World.title: Argentina's central bank reform bill reaches the lower house: what would change
World.content:
Argentina's central bank reform bill reaches the lower house: what would change

31st Friday, July 2026 - 23:11 UTC Full article

The reform is part of a package that includes what the government calls the fiscal shackle

Argentina's executive branch sent the bill to overhaul the central bank's charter to the Chamber of Deputies on Friday, a day after President Javier Milei outlined it in a nationwide broadcast. The measure will formally enter the parliamentary record on Monday and be referred to committees; the government hopes to pass it in August.

The text is organized around six pillars. The first replaces article 3 of the current statute to establish that the institution's primary and fundamental mission is to preserve the value of the currency. It thereby supersedes the multiple mandate set in 2012, under Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, which included financial stability, employment and economic development with social equity. According to the bill's rationale, a central bank charged with everything cannot be held accountable for anything. The bill also strips the board of powers to channel credit toward small businesses and regional economies.

The second pillar sets specific grounds for removing board members, limited to serious and manifest failures arising from precise facts. Removal would require an executive decree with prior approval by both chambers, by a two-thirds majority of members present. It scraps the bicameral committee mechanism used in 2010, when the government sought to remove Martín Redrado as bank president, and eliminates the presence of an Economy Ministry representative at board meetings.

The third pillar bars all channels of financing to the public sector. It repeals temporary advances, prohibits loans to the national government, the provinces, the City of Buenos Aires and municipalities, bans purchases of government paper in the primary market and eliminates the freely available reserves established by the 1991 convertibility law. The executive's message states that the current administration could have transferred up to 36.6 trillion pesos to the Treasury through advances, more than 80% of the monetary base, and that non-transferable notes on the bank's books totaled 69.4 billion dollars as of April 2025.

The fourth pillar restricts profit distribution: only realized and liquid earnings not stemming from exchange rate movements or gold valuation could be transferred, reserves must reach at least 50% of the bank's capital, and any transfer must go toward cancelling public debt. The practice of remitting accounting gains from exchange rate differences to the Treasury has been used by every administration since convertibility ended, including the current one. The remaining pillars address balance sheet cleanup and update operational and reserve rules.

The reform is part of a package that includes what the government calls the fiscal shackle, a mechanism for partially shutting down state operations in the event of sustained deficits, along with capital markets and insurance sector reforms. Santiago Bausili's appointment as central bank president still lacks Senate confirmation.

World.title: Nicaragua advances reform that would extend the presidential term to seven renewable years
World.content:
Nicaragua advances reform that would extend the presidential term to seven renewable years

31st Friday, July 2026 - 22:43 UTC Full article

Daniel Ortega said on July 19, at the ceremony marking the 47th anniversary of the Sandinista revolution, that there would be no more elections in the country

Nicaragua's National Assembly this week opened consultations on a constitutional reform bill that would extend the presidential term from six to seven years on a renewable basis and impose restrictions on the participation of the government's opponents. The text is due to be voted in early September.

The reform requires approval in two legislatures, meaning ratification would come in the first half of 2027. It is the second constitutional change in 18 months: the February 2025 amendment had already extended the term from five to six years, created the post of co-president for Rosario Murillo and reshaped the structure of the state, changes criticized by the UN, the OAS, the United States, the European Parliament and the opposition. That reform pushed general elections scheduled for November 2026 to November 2027.

The scope of the initiative is subject to opposing readings. Daniel Ortega said on July 19, at the ceremony marking the 47th anniversary of the Sandinista revolution, that there would be no more elections in the country, and announced laws to put up a wall against those he calls coup plotters. Parliament Speaker Gustavo Porras subsequently maintained that elections will be held, though under a constitutional framework shielding them from foreign interference. The full text of the bill has not been released.

During the consultations in parliament, Porras said the proposal also sets seven-year terms for the appointment of the army commander in chief and of police chiefs. Murillo said the process had been shared with the diplomatic corps and would be discussed with all sectors before approval.

Ortega's remarks prompted international reaction. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a call to action to countries in the region on July 21. Panama and the Dominican Republic recalled their ambassadors from Managua for consultations, and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva also voiced criticism. The governments of Mexico and El Salvador have not commented. According to El País, the US ambassador to the OAS, Andrew Stevenson, requested a meeting of foreign ministers to deliberate on collective measures, and specified that the resolution he is sponsoring does not authorize the use of armed force. Nicaragua announced its withdrawal from the OAS in 2021, and it took effect in November 2023.

A survey by the exiled opposition organization Hagamos Democracia put at 44.9% the share favoring more direct intervention by the United States or other international actors. The organization itself acknowledges that it did not define the term and that the questionnaire was framed around earlier remarks by Rubio; no sample size or margin of error is given. Some 38.9% of respondents anticipated that greater pressure would harden repression.

The regional context shifted after the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, in a US military operation in Caracas, which Ortega referred to critically in his speech.

World.title: Three confederations reject selling part of the World Cup to private funds; Conmebol asks for explanations
World.content:
Three confederations reject selling part of the World Cup to private funds; Conmebol asks for explanations

31st Friday, July 2026 - 22:05 UTC Full article

The confederation said it understands that developing football requires commercial and financial decisions

The South American Football Confederation asked FIFA on Friday for additional information and clarification on the FIFA Forward Enterprise project, without coming out for or against it, a day after the confederations of Europe and of North and Central America and the Caribbean rejected the plan.

In a statement published on its website and social media, the body, based in Luque, Paraguay, said it had requested details on the scope, structure, governance and potential effects of the initiative. It added that it had begun a consultation process with its ten member associations and convened a meeting of its Council to assess the proposal.

The confederation said it understands that developing football requires commercial and financial decisions, but that such decisions must always serve the game and never override its essence. It said it would continue acting with prudence and through institutional channels, and called for unity across the football family.

The stance contrasts with that of the other confederations that have spoken. UEFA and its 55 associations rejected the initiative on Thursday and warned they would withdraw their national teams from FIFA competitions if the plan proceeds, arguing the World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product. The same day, Concacaf and its 41 associations rejected it unanimously, with objections centered on the lack of procedural safeguards, a timeline they called artificially short and the absence of review by FIFA's governing bodies; it also called for football development to be funded from existing reserves, following the most profitable World Cup on record. On Friday, the Asian Football Confederation expressed solidarity with both positions.

Also on Friday, Carlos Cordeiro, senior adviser to Gianni Infantino, resigned, saying he had no part in drafting the proposal and opposes it unequivocally, considering it a bad deal for football.

FIFA responded on Thursday evening that the project does not involve selling football or ceding control of its governance, and that it would retain full control of the new company. It attributed part of the controversy to inaccurate information published in the media and offered to raise development funding to as much as 24 million dollars per association. Infantino appealed directly to the national associations, noting that the decision rests with them rather than with the confederations.

The vote is scheduled before the 211 associations on September 19 and requires 106 votes in favor. Accounts of the scale of the operation differ: figures cited include a subsidiary valued at 20 billion dollars and the sale of between 20% and 30% of commercial rights, with the fund Thrive Capital among those interested.

Conmebol comprises ten associations, the fewest of any continental confederation, limiting its weight in the vote. Hours before the statement, El País had reported, citing unidentified officials, that the confederation had decided to back the project tacitly.

World.title: Brazil's top court authorizes influence-peddling probe into Lula's eldest son
World.content:
Brazil's top court authorizes influence-peddling probe into Lula's eldest son

31st Friday, July 2026 - 18:35 UTC Full article

No charges have been filed. The authorization opens the preliminary evidence-gathering stage, after which prosecutors will decide whether to bring an indictment

Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice André Mendonça authorized the Federal Police on Thursday to open an investigation into Fábio Luís Lula da Silva, the eldest son of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, over indications of influence-peddling and corruption.

No charges have been filed. The authorization opens the preliminary evidence-gathering stage, after which prosecutors will decide whether to bring an indictment. The 51-year-old businessman, known as Lulinha, is presumed innocent.

Investigators suspect he acted, together with businesswoman Roberta Luchsinger, on behalf of the firm World Cannabis, linked to lobbyist Antônio Carlos Camilo Antunes, to facilitate the supply of medicinal cannabis-based products to the public health system. The approaches are alleged to have reached the Health Ministry and the presidential office. According to a witness statement taken by the Federal Police, Luchsinger introduced the lobbyist to the president's son. The deal never materialized.

The police request was filed in late July, during the judicial recess. It was initially reviewed by Alexandre de Moraes, on duty as acting court president, who sought an opinion from the Prosecutor General's Office. That office concluded that banking secrecy disclosures had revealed conduct unrelated to the earlier investigation into the national social security institute and recommended drawing a new rapporteur, which produced Mendonça.

Camilo Antunes already faces charges in that separate case, which concerns the diversion of up to 6.3 billion reais, some 1.24 billion dollars, in deductions applied to retirees and pensioners. Fábio Luís da Silva's links to the lobbyist were examined in that file, in which he is not listed as a subject of investigation.

His lawyers argue the new investigation stems from the failure to find irregularities in the earlier case. One of them, Guilherme Suguimori Santos, told Folha de São Paulo that a fresh theory cannot be constructed to start over and stretch the matter until the elections.

The president said he would not intervene. If his son is accused of anything, he will be treated as anyone's son, with no privilege, and he would never ask a police chief or a judge not to do their job properly, Lula said on the podcast Inteligência Ltda, adding that his son would have to prove his innocence, although the burden of proof rests with the prosecution.

Brazil votes on October 4, with the campaign formally beginning in mid-August. Lula is seeking a fourth term and polls give him a narrow lead over Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, whose father is imprisoned over the coup plot.

World.title: Italy and France tighten borders with Spain after 50,000 enter Ceuta
World.content:
Italy and France tighten borders with Spain after 50,000 enter Ceuta

31st Friday, July 2026 - 18:29 UTC Full article

Spain's Interior Ministry put at around 50,000 the number who entered since Thursday and at 48,300 those who had already returned voluntarily to Morocco, according to its latest Friday update

Italy ordered the reintroduction of border checks at its ports and airports with Spain on Friday, and France announced it would increase fivefold the officers deployed at its land border from Saturday, after tens of thousands of people entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta irregularly from Morocco.

Spain's Interior Ministry put at around 50,000 the number who entered since Thursday and at 48,300 those who had already returned voluntarily to Morocco, according to its latest Friday update, with departures running at a rate the government placed at 150 people per minute. The Government Delegation in Ceuta raised the death toll to 57, a provisional count that rose through the day. Most died attempting to reach the coast by swimming. Ceuta has around 83,000 inhabitants and its services were overwhelmed; Spain deployed the Army.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni presented the decision as a temporary suspension of Schengen free movement on maritime and air connections with Spain, adopted, she said, to protect national security. Rome later clarified that the checks would be random and apply only to non-EU citizens.

European rules do not permit what some governments have proposed. The Schengen Borders Code provides no mechanism for excluding a state from the free movement area, only the temporary reintroduction of checks by a country at its own borders, as a last resort and in the face of a serious threat to public policy or internal security. Former EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell said on Friday that no member state can unilaterally suspend another's participation. Sweden, Finland and Denmark had raised excluding Spain.

French Interior Minister Laurent Núñez said 334 police officers and gendarmes would join regular deployments on Saturday, after being tripled on Friday, supported by three aircraft, drones and reinforced patrols on trains. Emmanuel Macron expressed solidarity with Spain and offered Frontex resources.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez traveled to Ceuta and described what happened as a violation of Spain's territorial integrity, which he attributed to human trafficking networks rather than to Morocco, whose cooperation on repatriation he explicitly thanked. Spanish police unions said Moroccan authorities had eased exit controls, a claim that has not been officially confirmed.

EU ambassadors will meet on Monday and member state experts on Saturday under the bloc's crisis response mechanism, convened by the Irish presidency. The closest precedent is May 2021, when between 8,000 and 10,000 people entered over two days.

World.title: Fernández de Kirchner asks UN to suspend the ban keeping her off the ballot
World.content:
Fernández de Kirchner asks UN to suspend the ban keeping her off the ballot

31st Friday, July 2026 - 09:39 UTC Full article

Fernández de Kirchner, 73, was sentenced to six years in prison and permanent disqualification from public office for fraud in the awarding of public works contracts during her terms

The defense team of former Argentine president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner has filed an individual communication with the United Nations Human Rights Committee seeking suspension of the lifetime ban on holding public office imposed on her by the Argentine courts, her lawyers announced on Wednesday in Buenos Aires.

The filing includes three precautionary measures: provisionally lifting the disqualification, restoring the Supreme Court to its five members — it currently operates with three — and modifying her house arrest regime, including removal of her electronic ankle monitor. The defense also requested a full review of the conviction.

Fernández de Kirchner, 73, who served as president from 2007 to 2015, was sentenced to six years in prison and permanent disqualification from public office for fraud in the awarding of public works contracts during her terms. The sentence became final after being upheld by the Supreme Court, and she has been under house arrest since 2025.

The team comprises Argentina's Carlos Beraldi, Spain's Javier Borrego — a former judge of Spain's Supreme Court and of the European Court of Human Rights — and Brazil's Rafael Valim, who took part in Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's submission to the same committee during the proceedings stemming from the Lava Jato investigation.

The lawyers argue that the trial violated guarantees set out in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, a treaty with constitutional rank in Argentina, and say a permanent sanction contradicts the body's earlier findings. Valim said the precautionary request seeks suspension of a sanction that he argues runs counter to clear committee precedent. The allegations of judicial arbitrariness and persecution made by the defense and by the former president herself have not been independently substantiated.

In an interview on Thursday, Valim said the committee's decisions are binding and form part of Argentina's commitments before the United Nations. The mechanism, however, is not equivalent to an enforceable judgment: if the committee finds a rights violation, it issues recommendations for the state to adopt remedial measures, without means of compulsory enforcement. The lawyer also noted that Argentina's Federal Criminal Procedure Code provides for such a decision as grounds to review a final sentence.

Valim estimated the precautionary measures could be resolved within months and the merits could take years. He also argued that winning a primary election does not amount to holding public office, meaning the disqualification would not bar a candidacy, while acknowledging that this reading is contested. Whether the primary system will be in force for 2027 has not been settled.

In a letter circulated on social media, Fernández de Kirchner said the disqualification is in fact the principal penalty. Her son, lawmaker Máximo Kirchner, said the Peronist movement wants her as its 2027 candidate, in a field that also includes Buenos Aires province Governor Axel Kicillof.

World.title: Stability alone does not buy a house: Georgieva's message in Montevideo
World.content:
Stability alone does not buy a house: Georgieva's message in Montevideo

31st Friday, July 2026 - 08:02 UTC Full article

Stability cannot be put in a refrigerator, she said, and a house cannot be bought on stability alone: more growth is genuinely needed

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva praised Uruguay's macroeconomic and institutional strength on Thursday but urged authorities to take greater risks to turn that stability into growth.

Stability cannot be put in a refrigerator, she said, and a house cannot be bought on stability alone: more growth is genuinely needed. She was speaking at the annual economics conference organized by the Central Bank of Uruguay. In closing, she called for protecting what has been achieved while adding a little more courage to face the new international environment.

Georgieva highlighted the social consensus underpinning Uruguayan policy and described it as an asset in an increasingly polarized world. She noted that the country holds public debt of around 60% of gross domestic product and an electricity matrix that is 98% renewable. Among areas with potential she identified logistics capacity to serve neighboring countries, greater cost efficiency in public services, simplified procedures for small and medium-sized enterprises, and preparing society for the impact of artificial intelligence.

On monetary policy, she welcomed the reduction of inflation to 4.5% and the anchoring of expectations, but advised against rushing to set a lower target while external shocks persist, particularly on energy prices. She also backed the central bank's de-dollarization strategy, arguing that wider use of the national currency strengthens the capacity to respond to shocks the country cannot control, and recommended encouraging peso savings through better returns.

Central bank Governor Guillermo Tolosa had warned on Wednesday that Uruguayans' financial decisions remain shaped by fear inherited from the 2002 crisis. Georgieva compared that behavior with the experience of Bulgaria, her home country.

Turning to the global context, the IMF chief described a transition from a predictable order toward a system with multiple centers of gravity, and warned that protectionism and trade fragmentation could cut as much as 7% of world output. The fund projects global inflation of 4.7% this year and holds that a resurgence would raise debt servicing costs. She cited the conflict in the Middle East and tensions in the Strait of Hormuz among sources of vulnerability. On artificial intelligence, she estimated it could add up to 0.8 percentage points to annual global growth, while affecting 40% of jobs worldwide and as much as 60% in advanced economies.

Georgieva said Latin America has a unique opportunity to realize its potential through greater regional integration. Economy Minister Gabriel Oddone described the visit as a political one.

World.title: British journalist suggests channeling Enzo Fernández's taxes to Falklands defense
World.content:
British journalist suggests channeling Enzo Fernández's taxes to Falklands defense

30th Thursday, July 2026 - 23:08 UTC Full article

Winter made the suggestion on a television program hosted by Piers Morgan

British sports journalist Henry Winter has proposed that the taxes Argentine footballer Enzo Fernández pays in the United Kingdom be directed toward the defense of the Falklands, as a form of punishment after FIFA opened disciplinary proceedings against the Argentine Football Association.

Winter made the suggestion on a television program hosted by Piers Morgan. He said that were he in the British government, he would propose transferring the player's tax contribution, which he estimated at more than two million pounds a year, to the Islands for residents to decide how to spend it. The figure is Winter's own estimate of the footballer's private finances and has not been verified. The remarks were an opinion offered on a television show: there is no indication that the British government or FIFA is considering any such measure.

Fernández, however, is not among those charged. The proceedings opened by the Disciplinary Committee on July 29 cover Leandro Paredes, Nahuel Molina, Thiago Almada, assistant coach Roberto Ayala and Spain's Gavi, along with the AFA. The Chelsea midfielder was sent off during the final for two bookings, near the end of regulation time, and not for the incidents that followed the final whistle.

Winter also questioned the effectiveness of a financial penalty, arguing it would be negligible against the revenue Argentina earned from its run in the tournament, and proposed stripping Argentina of the match it has been allocated in the centenary edition of the 2030 World Cup. Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay will each host one game of that edition; the remaining matches will be played in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. Morgan, for his part, had posted a message after the semifinal containing a crude insult aimed at the Argentine squad and a reference to the outcome of the 1982 war.

The case against the AFA concerns four articles of the Disciplinary Code, among them the use of a sporting event for demonstrations of a non-sporting nature, and discrimination. FIFA cited allegedly discriminatory chanting and gestures, delayed kickoffs, failure to comply with protocols and the display of inappropriate messages. Those charged will be able to present their positions before a ruling.

The banner reading “Las Malvinas son argentinas” was displayed on July 16 in Atlanta, after Argentina's 2-1 semifinal win over England. There is a direct precedent: in 2014 FIFA fined the AFA 30,000 Swiss francs for unfurling the same message before a friendly against Slovenia.

Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, which is a British overseas territory. In a 2013 referendum, islanders voted overwhelmingly to retain that status.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Authorities capture CJNG leader, Navy backs US $115M sargassum strategy and Kia commits $649M to EVs
World.content:
The week of July 27th in Mexico ended with a major security win as agents captured the alleged intellectual author of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo’s assassination, a case that rattled Michoacán, a state burdened by organized crime, in late 2025.

President Claudia Sheinbaum, meanwhile, spent much of the week swatting away rhetorical grenades lobbed from abroad: she rejected Argentine President Javier Milei’s claim that Mexico was funding an “anti-Argentina campaign,” and brushed off White House adviser Stephen Miller’s assertion that cartels control Mexico’s political system, telling reporters the United States “must look at itself” on drug consumption. Closer to home, a cheating scandal consumed Mexico’s largest and most prestigious university, which confronted suspicions that AI and old-fashioned cheat sheets had corrupted its admissions exam. In a lighter moment, chefs in the capital’s Venustiano Carranza borough assembled a 100-meter, 1.5-tonne torta at the International Torta Fair, a Guinness-certified spectacle that drew hundreds of thousands of visitors.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mastermind of Manzo murder captured in Jalisco

Federal authorities on Thursday arrested Ramón Ángel “R1” Álvarez Ayala, the alleged mastermind behind the November 2025 assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said Álvarez Ayala, leader of a CJNG-linked cell known as “Los R’s,” was apprehended in Atotonilco, Jalisco, in an operation involving a high-speed chase and a shootout that left one of his bodyguards dead. García Harfuch later detailed R1’s criminal history, noting he was first jailed in 2012 for orchestrating a wave of violence in Guadalajara, was released in 2022, and resumed criminal activity soon after — allegedly ordering several killings, including that of influencer Valeria Márquez. His capture marks the 31st arrest connected to Manzo’s murder, a killing that shocked Mexico’s political and business classes and turned the independent mayor into a national symbol of local officials’ vulnerability to organized crime.

Mexicans now view China more favorably than the US, Pew finds

A new Pew Research Center survey found that Mexicans view China more favorably than the United States for the first time in nearly two decades of polling. Some 59% of Mexican respondents said they had a favorable opinion of China, compared to 40% for the U.S., and Mexicans were roughly three times more likely to express confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping than in Donald Trump. Canada showed a similar reversal, and Pew noted the trend held across most of the 36 countries it surveyed. Analysts attribute the shift largely to worsening views of Washington rather than improving perceptions of Beijing, with younger Mexican adults especially likely to favor China over the U.S.

Chemical spill near Arizona border triggers emergency response

Two separate freight train derailments prompted emergency responses over the weekend. In Ciudad Madero, Tamaulipas, authorities declared a Code Red and evacuated more than 200 residents after a Pemex-owned tank car carrying 70,000 liters of gasoline tipped over in a rail yard.

Farther north, a Ferromex freight train derailed in Naco, Sonora, spilling roughly 59,000 liters of sodium hydrosulfide, a corrosive chemical used in copper mining, just south of the U.S. border. Heavy rain then hampered cleanup efforts in Sonora, forcing families near the Cuauhtémoc ejido to temporarily leave their homes due to fumes. Sonora’s Civil Protection Agency said emergency measures were deployed immediately, while the National Water Commission is testing water and soil to determine whether the chemical reached waterways near Cananea. The Federal Attorney General’s Office has opened an investigation into the derailment, which occurred on a Grupo México-linked rail line and raised fresh concerns about industrial safety in a state that is already home to some of Mexico’s largest copper mining operations.

Del Toro caps historic Tour de France

Cyclist Isaac del Toro delivered Mexico’s best-ever Tour de France result, finishing third overall and taking the white jersey as the race’s best young rider — a result celebrated by President Sheinbaum. The 22-year-old from Ensenada, Baja California, made history early in the three-week race too, winning Stage 2 in Barcelona after teammate and four-time champion Tadej Pogačar eased up in the final meters to let the young rider take the victory, a gesture that left Del Toro visibly stunned. It was the first Tour stage win by a Mexican rider in 36 years, since Raúl Alcalá’s back-to-back victories in 1989 and 1990. Del Toro’s final-week performance in the Alps, where Pogačar again worked to protect his young teammate’s position, sealed a podium finish that surpassed Alcalá’s previous best of eighth place, cementing Del Toro’s status as Mexico’s greatest cyclist and a genuine contender for future Grand Tours.

Acapulco hydroelectric dam project scrapped

Sheinbaum canceled the long-controversial La Parota dam project near Acapulco, citing unresolved land expropriation issues and a lack of community agreements. In its place, the government will build radial wells along the Papagayo River, rehabilitate aqueducts and replace drinking water lines serving the city’s upper neighborhoods.

Foreign investment keeps flowing

Several new investment announcements underscored continued foreign interest in Mexico.

Houston-based Talos Energy agreed to acquire a 50% stake in Repsol’s offshore Block 29 in the Gulf of Mexico, home to the Polok and Chinwol oil discoveries.

South Korean automaker Kia announced a US $649 million investment to begin producing its EV3 electric SUV at its Pesquería, Nuevo León plant starting Aug. 4 — the model’s first production site outside South Korea, expected to create 500 jobs this year and 1,500 more by 2030.

On the consumer side, U.S. cookie chain Crumbl opened its first Mexico store in Roma Norte, CDMX, to 800-person lines, while gourmet hot dog chain Dog Haus debuted in Mérida, part of a broader wave of American food brands expanding south.

Mexican economy shows signs of life

The MND Economy Index™, a 10-pillar composite gauge of Mexico’s economic health, rose to 68.61 in its latest edition — its highest reading yet, driven by improving inflation and monetary policy scores even as economic growth remains the weakest-performing pillar. The improving picture was reinforced by other data this week:

Mexico’s export revenue hit a record US $389.72 billion in the first half of 2026, a 24.6% annual increase driven by a surge in non-automotive manufacturing exports.

The economy grew 1.5% quarter-over-quarter in Q2, Mexico’s best result since late 2020, aided by World Cup-related tourism spending.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard also weighed in on the trade relationship with Washington, downplaying Trump’s latest remark that he “doesn’t care” about the USMCA. “Obviously there are warnings every week, there are a lot of things,” Ebrard told reporters, adding that “as of today we’re doing well.” Sheinbaum echoed the sentiment, noting the two countries’ economies remain deeply integrated after decades of free trade.

Navy presents US $115M sargassum plan

With Quintana Roo facing its worst sargassum season on record, the Mexican Navy announced a 2-billion-peso plan to combat the seaweed influx choking Caribbean coast beaches. The strategy includes roughly 50 kilometers of new anti-sargassum sea barriers near Playa del Carmen, Cancún, Tulum, Puerto Morelos and Mahahual, along with new collection vessels aimed at eventually processing 4,000 tonnes of sargassum per day. Quintana Roo has already collected more than 92,000 tonnes of the macroalgae this year, with officials projecting the total could exceed 119,000 tonnes before year’s end.

World Bank aligns support with Plan México

World Bank Group President Ajay Banga made his first visit to Mexico in five years, meeting with Sheinbaum to align a new five-year Country Partnership Framework with the government’s Plan México industrial strategy. The framework will prioritize infrastructure, energy, water management and human capital development.

Banga also toured Grupo Naturasol, a family-owned agribusiness in México state that previously received International Finance Corporation financing, calling it a model for how smaller firms can plug into North American supply chains.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: When legacy media’s hypocrisy gets called out: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
I am increasingly finding myself analyzing the Mexico narrative as it’s told by different media outlets. Just this past week brought us another ludicrous example with The Atlantic magazine publishing an article titled “A Planeload of Informants” with the subtitle: “The United States is intensifying its hunt for narcos within the Mexican government. Is this all prelude to an attack?”

I guess The Atlantic was feeling left out of the party by other large media outlets writing breathtakingly sensationalist articles about Mexico. If you remember, leading up to the World Cup, The Economist magazine informed its readers that: “The World Cup will test Mexico’s control over its territory.” The Wall Street Journal told us that the “World Cup puts Mexico’s Cartel Crisis on the Global Stage.” And the New York Times has written at length of experts confidently predicting Mexico would enter a period of increasing violence after the February government operation against CJNG leader Mencho.

But they have all been wrong. Totally wrong. The post-Mencho spiral of violence? It didn’t happen. In fact, Mexico has seen its homicide rates hitting lows not seen in over a decade. The “World Cup test” of Mexico against the cartels? There was no test. The world watched with envy as foreigners partied alongside Mexicans across the country. Not a single article has been written acknowledging getting things so wrong. And so now we have the media moving on to the next big story: A potential attack by the United States on Mexico.

Let’s be clear about the history here: Mexico has, for decades, genuinely struggled with cartel violence, and I am not arguing otherwise. But what these outlets consistently omit is the context of the last year. Cooperation between the U.S. and Mexico against cartels is, in the words of officials on both sides, at unprecedented levels — a shift I’ve tracked in real time (see my columns on the World Cup coverage and Mexico’s business community). The result of that cooperation isn’t more violence; it’s homicides down by almost 50% this year. Apparently good news doesn’t sell subscriptions.

Which brings me to two personal anecdotes from this past week that I want to share:

Cancelling a 30-year subscription

The first took place at a friend’s dinner party in Mexico City. A few hours into some good conversation, he (quite randomly) asked me: “Do you still read The Economist magazine?” To which I responded that I do. He then said: “I have been a loyal subscriber for over 30 years, but I am about to cancel it. I am done with them.” His reasoning was enlightening: “I am tired of the narrative of their coverage. By cancelling my subscription with them, I am choosing to not pay attention to the reality that they are presenting.” He went on: “The predictive power of their writers and editors has changed … and as a result they are just flat out wrong on many topics.”

The words stuck with me as I have been increasingly feeling the same about The Economist. In just the past few months, I have actually written twice about how intellectually lazy, disingenuous and downright wrong their coverage has been regarding Mexico. Increasingly, as I read their coverage on the country, I have found myself wondering, “Why am I reading this? It’s not accurate. It’s sensationalist. And it doesn’t represent reality. Why am I paying to read something that I think is just plain wrong?”

As my friend’s cancellation shows, his decision reflects a broader pattern I’m seeing: As irresponsible coverage piles up, readers simply stop trusting — and stop paying for — outlets they once considered essential.

The conversation went further with others at the party explaining that, in contrast, they read Mexico News Daily precisely because it “provides optimism by showing me the Mexico that I want to believe exists today and believe can exist in the future.” The comment wasn’t made out of ignorance or a lack of information, but rather in a way that reinforced the optimism they have for Mexico. Said differently, they are choosing to align with a narrative of informed optimism versus colonialist click-bait pessimism. It’s unfortunate to increasingly see people tuning out of legacy media, but it’s easy to understand why they are doing it. As many outlets increasingly present a pessimistic, dystopian, doom-and-gloom view of much of the world — one that increasingly is out of touch with reality — many people are choosing to tune out.

The Economist’s Elon Musk interview

The second anecdote came earlier this week when I watched The Economist’s editor-in-chief, Zanny Minton Beddoes, interview Tesla/SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The nearly 90-minute-long interview went on fine for the first hour, but then turned decidedly testy. Ms. Beddoes at one point begins to take issue with Musk’s assessment of the current state of the U.K. (where The Economist is based and where she lives). She questioned his motives, repeatedly said he was incorrect, accused him of supporting “fringe” and “far right” parties and questioned when he had last visited the U.K. To be clear, the point here is not whether Musk’s take on the U.K. is right or wrong, that’s a separate debate entirely.

Here you have the head of The Economist, the British publication that has increasingly misconstrued, misrepresented and irresponsibly presented other countries around the world, getting extremely defensive about someone questioning the U.K. She repeatedly took offense to any of Musk’s critiques of her own country, claiming “People say that you’re racist,” “people loathe you,” “What is the motivation for [participating in tribalism]?” It was quite shocking to see the head of a publication that for decades has portrayed much of the rest of the world as dangerous, backwards and corrupt take so much offense to someone questioning the current state and future direction of her own country.

As she waged increasingly personal attacks against Musk, he finally had enough and responded with a dagger: “A lot more people hate you, the media — more than you realize. Do you realize the media is despised? Do you realize … the favorable view of journalists is like 15%? … They hate you.” It was a striking moment. Her defensiveness made her and her publication feel small, out of touch, aloof. It was a moment where I found myself even further questioning the true motives of The Economist.

Musk’s jab about journalism’s approval rating isn’t just a soundbite — it’s the direct consequence of the pattern I described above. When outlets choose sensationalism over accuracy, they erode trust in journalism broadly, pushing people toward sources — credible or not — that at least feel honest to them.

Is The Economist really trying to live by its founding mission from 179 years ago of taking part “in a severe contest between intelligence, which presses forward, and an unworthy, timid ignorance obstructing our progress”? Or are they more likely contributing to the obstruction of progress with increasingly ignorant and biased journalism? If the latter is in fact the case, as I sadly suspect it is, they will likely experience more people like my friend moving on.

I strongly believe that the role of the media is more important than ever. But we in the media also needs to work harder than ever to earn your trust and respect — and many outlets seem to have forgotten that.

Thank you for reading and supporting MND.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: After a young girl’s death, Mexico shuts down all militarized grade schools
World.content:
Following the death of a female student, the Education Ministry (SEP) ordered all so-called “military schools” shuttered by Aug. 31.

Furthermore, Education Minister Mario Delgado said such schools must immediately reimburse payments made for outstanding educational services, such as re-enrollment fees, school supplies and uniforms.

President Claudia Sheinbaum praised Delgado’s decision, while lamenting the 13-year-old girl’s death. “What happened in Tamaulipas is very sad,” she said. “Abuses occurring under the pretext of discipline cannot be allowed.”

The SEP resolution comes after the July 16 death of Dafne Zapata, who died during a summer camp at Marina Doenitz Military Academy in the state of Tamaulipas.

Dafne’s death prompted immediate demands for justice from family and friends, eventually leading to the arrest of three alleged perpetrators.

That day, Dafne’s mother was informed that her daughter was suffering from a cough and dehydration, only to be told minutes later that she had died.

An autopsy refuted the academy’s conflicting claims about Dafne’s death — sudden circulatory failure and accidental death were cited — indicating that she died from drowning.

Medical examiners also found bruises and signs of recent physical abuse, prompting the authorities to rule out natural causes and classify the case as femicide.

Soon thereafter, prosecutors arrested Jorge Luis Ponce Ortega, the school’s director, Estrellita Mora Díaz, a supervisor, and 18-year-old Danna Yanina, a teaching assistant.

Former students of the academy criticized the arrest of Yanina, staging a protest while proclaiming that she was another victim who was forced to carry out “disciplinary measures.”

The SEP has ordered a comprehensive review of all 31 military-style academies in the country, with Delgado saying, “There can be no true educational transformation if expressions of violence are permitted.”

The edict requires all 32 state education ministries to thoroughly review the authorizations, permits and Official Recognition of Studies they’ve granted and shutter all military-style schools and institutions.

Additionally, Delgado instructed local education authorities to order the immediate delivery of school documentation to students affected by this measure, including full or partial certificates of studies to guarantee the continuity of their education and to facilitate their incorporation into other educational institutions.

Dafne’s mother, Alejandra Quintos, this week proposed legislation to address security and safety issues at military-style institutions. The so-called Dafne Law would establish controls, security protocols and oversight mechanisms for military academies, summer camps and other such organizations, whether public or private.

With reports from El País, El Economista, La Jornada and Animal Político

World.title: Cookie craze hits CDMX: Crumbl opens first Mexico location
World.content:
The viral global cookie phenomenon known as Crumbl has arrived in Mexico.

Famous for its large gourmet cookies, weekly rotating menu and signature pink boxes, the U.S. bakery chain opened a store in the chic Mexico City neighborhood of Roma Norte on Tuesday.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Crumbl Mexico (@crumbl.mx)

It did not go unnoticed.

El Universal newspaper described Tuesday’s opening day as a “frenzy,” reporting that dozens of people arrived early in hopes of “being among the first to try the famous viral cookies” and “a line of approximately 800 people snaked around the block.”

The event attracted content creators and influencers to the shop at Calle Durango 225. They busily documented the atmosphere and shared images of the event on various digital platforms.

Crumbl’s approach breaks with traditional baking. Its menu isn’t fixed; it has over 270 recipes in its catalogue, but offers 3 or 4 new flavors each week.

The brand — founded in Logan, Utah, in 2017 — produces weekly Sunday night flavor reveals across platforms such as TikTok and Instagram to drive hype. The strategy has attracted long customer lines at its outlets in the U.S., Canada and Puerto Rico.

The limited edition cookies available in Mexico City through Saturday — the shop is closed on Sundays — are Tres Leches Cake, Confetti Cake and a S’mores Cookie.

Crumbl typically offers several other items on a Classic Cookies list. This week, there were four on the menu: Cookies and Cream, Pink Sugar, Milk Chocolate Chip Cookie and Chocolate Chip Cookie Thins.

The cookies come with a hefty price tag, however: One cookie costs 89 pesos; a pack of 4 costs 315 pesos; a pack of 6 costs 450 pesos; a package of 12 costs 885 pesos; and a monthly subscription (5 cookies shipped to your house) is available for 990 pesos.

Award-winning fast-casual restaurant enjoys solid first two months in Yucatán

Though not matching the ballyhoo produced by the Crumbl opening, Dog Haus opened its first restaurant in Mérida in June, its first permanent international restaurant.

The fast-casual gourmet restaurant — also known as Dog Haus Biergarten — is a hot dog, sausage and burger chain headquartered in Pasadena, California. It is known for its use of Black Angus beef and King’s Hawaiian rolls, earning recognition as a Menu Trendsetter by Nation’s Restaurant News.

The Mérida location is the first of three Dog Haus locations planned for Mexico in 2026, with openings planned for Mexico City and Tijuana.

With reports from El Universal, Animal Gourmet, Food and Travel México and Expansión

World.title: Opinion: Is China Claudia Sheinbaum’s surveillance model for Mexico?
World.content:
Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, elected in 2024 with nearly 60% of the vote, has continued many of her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s policies while placing emphasis on clean energy, public-private investment, and aggressive mass digitalization. Her flagship Llave MX platform, run by the new Digital Transformation and Telecoms Agency, aims to unify citizen data for easier access to government services and health records.

Central to this effort is República Sana (Healthy Nation) program, which seeks to integrate Mexico’s major public health institutions and advance toward universal healthcare. Enrollment will require a biometric digital identity card under the Unique Population Registry Code (CURP) system, including photos, fingerprints and possibly iris scans, with ambitious goals for broad coverage by 2030. The president argues that centralized biometrics will reduce bureaucracy and petty corruption.

However, critics such as R3D (Digital Rights Defense Network) caution that linking every government transaction, tax payment, medical visit and benefit to a single biometric identity could enable greater surveillance and data vulnerabilities. In a country where roughly 55% of the workforce operates in the informal economy, the system could also help formalize tax collections but at the potential cost of privacy and potential misuse.

The China precedent

China provides a clear cautionary reference point. By combining centralized digital identities with extensive surveillance cameras, it has developed tools for tracking, behavioral scoring and social control. Although Sheinbaum has pledged that her government will not spy on citizens, the infrastructure being built in Mexico — centralized databases tied to biometrics — has prompted concerns about possible function creep and future authoritarian risks.

The Chinese system developed gradually. It began with a national ID program in the 1980s, expanded to biometric collection in the 2000s, and was later integrated with facial recognition, financial records and other data. In Xinjiang, advanced tracking tools have been used for ethnic targeting. The broader lesson is that systems initially justified for efficiency and public safety can, in combination, expand in unintended ways. Mexico is unlikely to replicate China’s model, but the architecture merits careful scrutiny. Biometric collection is also mandatory for non-citizens at U.S. borders but widely applied on a “voluntary” basis for U.S. citizens, also raising serious concerns of potential function creep.

The surveillance infrastructure

Mexico’s digital agenda already connects with a large camera network. As mayor of Mexico City from 2018 to 2023, Sheinbaum expanded the city’s cameras significantly. Under current Mayor Clara Brugada, the Ojos que te cuidan (Eyes that protect you) program has added another 30,400 high-resolution units, bringing the total above 113,000 — the largest urban video surveillance system in the Americas, with plans to have 150,000 installed by 2030.

When combined with Llave MX’s national biometric registry and the Central Intelligence Platform, this network could support automated facial recognition and real-time tracking. Anthropologist Esteban Salmón’s research points to practical downsides in Mexico City, including false positives, issues with evidence handling and over-reliance on video in some prosecutions.

Similar systems elsewhere have shown higher error rates for darker-skinned individuals and women in facial recognition. In Mexico, this could disproportionately affect Indigenous and mestizo populations. Without strong safeguards, such tools risk unintended consequences for justice and civil liberties.

Oversight, security reforms, and implementation challenges

These issues are compounded by changes to independent institutions. The Sheinbaum administration has moved regulatory authority over telecommunications under the executive following the abolition of the independent Federal Telecommunications Institute.

In June and July 2025, the government passed the Investigation and Intelligence Law and the National Public Security System Law. These measures grant the Ministry of Security and Citizen Protection (SSPC) and the military-controlled National Guard broader access to biometric, telephone, vehicle, tax and property records. The new Central Intelligence Platform aims to interconnect these databases across government levels to help prevent and investigate violent crimes.

Critics including R3D and Article 19 have expressed concerns about limited judicial oversight and further militarization of security functions. This builds on earlier debates, including the Supreme Court’s 2021-2022 decision striking down a biometric phone registry on privacy grounds. Mexico’s history of data breaches also highlights risks associated with greater centralization.

Significant implementation challenges remain. Large segments of the rural population and many elderly Mexicans face barriers related to Internet access, devices and digital literacy. Without adequate support, digitalization efforts risk creating new forms of exclusion.

Mexico’s big tech and digital push

The Mexican government’s digital push has fostered significant relationships with global technology companies such as Nvidia, Microsoft, Palantir, and others for investments in data centers, AI infrastructure, manufacturing partnerships and talent development. Although there is no confirmed contract between the Sheinbaum administration and Palantir for core intelligence or biometric systems, the U.S. firm recently expanded its presence in Mexico through a major deal with GNP Seguros, the country’s largest insurer. Palantir’s Foundry and Artificial Intelligence Platforms are being used for fraud detection, risk monitoring and data integration.

Because these platforms also excel at mass surveillance, profiling and other operations with human rights implications, the company’s aggressive expansion in Latin America has raised questions about how private-sector AI tools could eventually feed into government surveillance architectures. The Sheinbaum administration also has agreements with Google, Meta and TikTok ostensibly focused on combating digital violence, but critics worry that broad partnerships with global tech giants could accelerate the centralization of citizen data.

What can be done

The system is still under development, which offers an important window for civil society to shape its direction. Mexico’s Supreme Court has previously pushed back against biometric overreach. That precedent, along with input from organizations like R3D and Article 19, can help strengthen oversight of the new Central Intelligence Platform. International standards from the Inter-American Court of Human Rights and the IACHR offer additional leverage. Immediate attention should focus on implementing regulations for the Investigation and Intelligence Law. Concerned legislators and privacy advocates can seek provisions for judicial oversight, data minimization, independent audits and penalties for misuse.

Broader engagement is also important. Trade unions, Indigenous communities, digital rights groups and others can advocate for greater transparency around Llave MX and the República Sana program, including independent oversight mechanisms particularly in relation to arrangements with global AI powerhouses.

Sheinbaum’s digital agenda is ambitious and officially presented as a way to improve efficiency, reduce corruption and expand access to services. At the same time, it assembles key elements of centralized data systems: biometric identities, integrated intelligence platforms, extensive camera networks and shifts in regulatory oversight. Its long-term character will depend on whether robust transparency safeguards, independent review and legal protections are incorporated from the outset. Getting the balance right between security, efficiency and rights will be essential — not just for Mexico, but for the broader struggle against digital authoritarianism in Latin America.

This article was written by It was originally published by Foreign Policy in Focus.

World.title: Mexican soccer officials break ranks with US and Canada by not rejecting FIFA’s World Cup privatization plan
World.content:
The Mexican Football Federation (FMF) is breaking ranks with its fellow soccer federations in the United States and Canada by refusing — for now — to reject FIFA’s plan to bring private investors into the World Cup’s commercial rights.

While the plan being pushed by FIFA President Gianni Infantino has drawn ire worldwide, the FMF said on social media it is undertaking a “process of study and analysis to make the decision that best suits the development of Mexican soccer,” without endorsing Concacaf’s swift rejection.

VIDEO | ⚽️ Infantino asegura que la creación de la filial comercial (FFE) es “una oportunidad para crecer” que podría elevar hasta 40M$ la ayuda a cada federación. pic.twitter.com/f7fLnCt91N — EFE Deportes (@EFEdeportes) July 30, 2026

Concacaf, the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football, held an urgent meeting this week in which the presidents of its 41 member associations “rejected the proposal” and voiced “deep concerns” about “the lack of due process” and an “artificially short deadline.”

Concacaf includes Mexico, the U.S. and Canada, the co-hosts of the recently completed 2026 FIFA World Cup. The rejection of the proposal was supported by the U.S. and Canada.

The regional confederation questioned why private equity is needed after “the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history” and pointed to FIFA’s “billions of dollars in reserves and no debt.”

The project Infantino is promoting calls for the creation of FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a commercial subsidiary that would run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup and sell minority, non‑controlling stakes to outside investors on a $20 billion valuation.

FIFA says FFE would raise up to $4.2 billion by working with J.P. Morgan and long‑term investors including Thrive Capital, an investment firm created by Joshua Kushner, brother of President Donald Trump’s son‑in‑law Jared Kushner.

The 211 member federations are being offered a one‑time $20 million payment plus a jump in regular FIFA Forward development funding from $8 million to $20 million for the 2027‑30 cycle, with further increases later.

FIFA says the additional money would support infrastructure, coaching, national teams, competitions, and women’s and grassroots soccer.

In a clarification posted on X, FIFA said “nobody is selling football” and argued that FFE would remain fully owned and controlled by FIFA, with governance and the global match calendar unchanged.

The backlash has been swift. The 55 member associations of the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) voted unanimously to boycott the World Cup and all FIFA competitions if the project goes ahead.

UEFA said football “is not FIFA’s to sell” and warned that “the soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially.”

In its vote Thursday, Concacaf cited the absence of any review by FIFA’s own governance bodies, but stopped short of threatening a boycott.

It tasked its FIFA Council members with pushing FIFA to tap existing reserves instead and to run any future plan through proper procedures under the FIFA statutes.

FIFA has promised to open working groups so federations can review more details before a Sept. 19 deadline, leaving Mexico to weigh whether to join with its confederation’s stance or support the proposal.

On Friday, the story took some more turns. Infantino’s senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned, saying “I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup” and calling the $20 billion commercial subsidiary “a bad deal for soccer.”

In a separate statement, FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff had been “deceived” by Infantino’s lack of openness and argued the plan is “the project of one person” that “must not go ahead.”

With reports from Mediotiempo, ESPN Deportes, TUDN, Proceso and Associated Press

World.title: Harry Styles concerts will boost Mexico City’s economy by 2 billion pesos
World.content:
Six Mexico City shows by pop mega-star Harry Styles, starting Friday and running through August 10, will inject more than 2 billion pesos (US $120 million) into the economy, according to the local chapter of the National Chamber of Commerce (Canaco CDMX).

Canaco says ticket sales will account for more than 80% of the economic windfall, with the rest coming from lodging, food, transportation and other services.

According to Canaco, the hospitality industry is expected to be among the main beneficiaries, with revenue from lodging projected to exceed 299.7 million pesos (US $17.2 million), as visitors arrive from across Mexico and abroad.

The food service sector is also expected to get a significant boost, with spending at restaurants, cafés and other establishments near the venue projected at 156 million pesos (US $9.0 million).

Ticketmaster Mexico estimates that around 60% of attendees at the GNP Stadium will travel to Mexico City for the shows, staying an average of two to three nights. The influx will significantly move the economic performance needle of the capital’s tourism sector and related industries.

Head of Canaco CDMX Vicente Gutiérrez Camposeco confirmed the figures in a statement, adding that the benefits from an event like the Styles concerts extend beyond the entertainment industry.

“It’s not just the event organizers who benefit,” he said. “Hotels, restaurants, shops, tourism services, transportation, ride-hailing platforms, travel agencies, suppliers, and thousands of small and medium-sized businesses that participate directly or indirectly in serving visitors also benefit.”

Mexico City is one of seven cities worldwide chosen by Styles to host a 2026 residency, and the one with the most concerts in the region, concert promoter Ocesa said. The soft rocker and One Direction graduate’s six GNP Stadium dates are likely to attract more than 400,000 fans.

Some 60% of them will be women, while 35% will be under 25 years old, according to Ocesa.

The Styles concert phenomenon reinforces Mexico City’s position as one of Latin America’s leading entertainment tourism destinations, providing not just culture and entertainment, but also, as Ocesa puts it, “acting as engines for economic development, job creation, tourism promotion, and the strengthening of the cultural industry.”

With reports from EFE and Excélsior

The Continent’s Mood Today

There is a distinct end-of-cycle weariness in the air, a sense that the continent is tidying up loose ends before a long, uncertain sleep. In Colombia, a former oil chief asks for a plea deal to close a chapter on a scandalous campaign; in Brazil, a steel giant frantically rearranges its debt to buy time. It is not panic—the COLCAP’s leap and the steady hand of Colombia’s central bank prove that—but it is the quiet, desperate choreography of entities trying to outrun their pasts. The earth itself joined this mood of release, a magnitude 5.6 quake near Pucallpa, Peru, rattling nerves across the Brazilian border without demanding a toll of blood, as if the Amazon shrugged in its sleep.

The triggers are specific and interlocking. CSN’s bond exchange, carrying a steep 11% coupon, is a flare sent up from the commodity trenches, while Colombia’s Grupo Cibest injects $70 million into Guatemala’s Banco BAM, a sign of capital still seeking fertile ground across borders. Meanwhile, Mercado Libre’s quiet trademark filing for ‘Balse’ suggests a coming retail war against Shein, a battle for the region’s wallets fought not in the streets, but in supply chains. From the auction of Brazil’s Santos terminal to Chile’s fragile industrial rebound, the day’s stories are all acts of reconfiguration—of debt, of corporate identity, of the ground beneath our feet.

Brazil – The Art of the Long Goodbye

Brazil on Friday was a masterclass in managed decline and aggressive future-proofing. The air in São Paulo’s financial districts was thick with the scent of ink and obligation as Companhia Siderúrgica Nacional (CSN) launched a massive $1.3 billion bond exchange, offering a painful 11% coupon to push its debt maturities further out on the horizon, as our reporting detailed. This is not a victory lap; it is a grim, necessary refinancing undertaken while warning of widening losses. The Ibovespa’s slight uptick felt less like enthusiasm and more like a quiet acknowledgment that a potential default had been, for now, elegantly sidestepped.

Yet, the state is also looking ahead with cold, hard calculation. The announcement of a $193 million auction for a container terminal in Santos, the nation’s logistical aorta, signals a pragmatic rush to modernize infrastructure regardless of the fiscal noise. This push-and-pull between private sector fragility and public sector ambition was framed by a deeper, demographic clock ticking in the background: our reporting on the IBGE’s projections reminds everyone that the country’s population will peak in 2041. Every bond issued, every terminal auctioned, is shadowed by the specter of a future, shrinking market. InfoMoney captured the political parallel, with Tarcísio opening his campaign on a platform of pure management—a promise to govern a country that is already learning to count its future inhabitants in smaller numbers.

Mexico – A Phantom Dissipates in the Boardroom

A strange, quiet jubilation settled over Mexican corporate law offices on Friday. The mood was not one of explosive victory, but of a deep, existential threat evaporating into thin air. The Rio Times reported that Orbia, the Mexican chemicals giant, had successfully escaped a $1.14 billion cartel lawsuit. A billion-dollar phantom, a legal Sword of Damocles that had hung over the company, was simply wiped away by a court ruling. The S&P/BMV IPC’s slight dip suggests the broader market was unmoved, but for Orbia, it was a rebirth by judicial decree.

This narrow escape contrasts with the broader, more pedestrian challenge highlighted by Expansión: the struggle to convert Mexico’s growing number of investment accounts into actual, lasting wealth. The democratization of finance is underway, but the mood is one of caution, a realization that opening an account is far easier than building a patrimony. The Orbia ruling, then, is a private miracle in a landscape where the real, daily miracle—turning savings into security—remains stubbornly elusive for the many.

Colombia – Holding Steady in a Political Storm

Colombia’s Friday felt like a tightrope walk performed with a straight spine. The Banco de la República, in a move of almost theatrical steadiness, held interest rates at 12% and announced it would start buying up reserves due to a cheap dollar, as reported by La República. The COLCAP soared by over 2%, a roar of approval from a market desperate for a technocratic anchor. The central bank stood as a pillar of orthodoxy, seemingly unmoved by the political weather.

But that weather is turbulent. Our reporting broke the news that Ricardo Roa, the recently departed CEO of Ecopetrol, is seeking a plea deal over alleged irregularities in President Gustavo Petro’s 2022 campaign, which he managed. It is a seismic political event wrapped in the quiet language of legal procedure. The contrast is dizzying: a stable, predictable monetary authority on one hand, and a state oil company’s former chief trying to negotiate his way out of a campaign finance scandal on the other. La República also noted Petro’s comments on gas imports, a reminder that energy sovereignty remains a live wire. The nation’s mood is a held breath, a bet that institutional gravity can withstand the pull of political chaos.

Argentina – The Weight of the Dollar and the Silence of the Showroom

In Buenos Aires, the mood is a brittle thing, a thin veneer of official celebration over a deep well of personal anxiety. iProfesional captured the dissonance perfectly: while Economy Minister Caputo celebrates that more dollars are entering the country than leaving, Argentine savers quietly bought up $2.4 billion in June alone. The people are voting with their wallets, and they are voting for the greenback, a deep-seated instinct that no macroeconomic statistic can soothe. The S&P Merval’s slight decline reflects a City that is, as iProfesional advises, recommending extreme caution for August.

The real economy is sending smoke signals. Car sales, a bellwether of middle-class confidence, suffered their worst collapse of the year, reshaping the very ranking of top brands. The story of a leading empanada business collapsing under 230 bounced checks and a billion pesos in debt is not just a business failure; it is a parable of the real cost of this transition. Our reporting on Argentina’s economy notes that inflation is down to 1.9% a month and poverty is at a seven-year low, but the showroom floors are empty and the empanada empire is in ruins. The ‘Milei miracle’ has a ledger, and on Friday, the debit column felt heavier.

Chile – A Faint Pulse in the Factory Floor

A cautious, almost superstitious hope flickered through Chile on Friday. After eight long months of decline, industrial production finally turned a corner, as Emol reported, reinforcing a fragile bet that the country might just dodge a technical recession. The sound of machinery stirring back to life is the most precious music in Santiago right now, a signal that the patient’s long fever might be breaking. The peso rallied, with the dollar falling sharply over the week, a sign of easing nerves.

Yet, the celebration is muted, a whispered prayer rather than a shout. Unemployment remains stubbornly high at 9.4%, a figure our own reporting confirmed, and Minister Rau could only offer the tentative hope that a ‘turning point’ has been reached. It is the language of the wince, not the victory cry. The joblessness is a cold, hard floor beneath the warm air of industrial output. Chile’s mood is that of a family watching a sick relative take their first spoonful of soup: desperately hopeful, but terrified of a relapse.

Peru – The Earth’s Reminder

Peru’s day was split in two: the solid, encouraging clink of construction steel, and the deep, terrifying growl of the earth. El Comercio reported that construction grew by a roaring 11.8% in the first half of the year, and Proinversión is accelerating a massive $40 billion infrastructure portfolio. The sol held steady, a quiet anchor of stability. The mood in Lima’s boardrooms was one of bullish, forward-looking momentum, a country building its way out of stagnation.

Then, the Amazon spoke. A magnitude 5.6 earthquake near Pucallpa, as reported by The Rio Times, sent tremors rippling across the border into Brazil. No damage, no casualties—just a deep, planetary reminder that all this building, all these adjudications and portfolios, occur on a living, restless crust. The quake was not a tragedy, but it was a metaphysical one. It punctured the illusion of control, leaving behind a mood of humbled awe. The day’s two stories—the soaring construction figures and the seismic shudder—are a perfect diptych of Peruvian existence: audacious ambition forever shadowed by the Andes’ ancient, unpredictable power.

The Shared Mood

The thread tying these six nations together on the last day of July is a shared act of renegotiation with reality. Brazil is renegotiating its debt maturities, Colombia its political accountability, Argentina its social contract with the dollar, and Chile its relationship with economic gravity. Even the earth in Peru seemed to be renegotiating its own internal pressures. This is not a continent in revolution, but in a vast, complicated, and deeply exhausting process of restructuring.

This points to a deeper regional psyche: a weariness with grand ideological experiments and a grudging turn towards the brutal, unglamorous work of technical management. From Tarcísio’s ‘management-focused’ campaign in Brazil to the Colombian central bank’s stoic rate hold, the day’s heroes are not caudillos but technocrats, not prophets but accountants. The shared mood is a collective, whispered confession that the miracles didn’t come, and now the bills are due. It is a sobering, adult feeling, as unglamorous and necessary as an 11% bond coupon or a plea deal signed in a quiet room.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the biggest corporate survival story in Latin America on Friday?

Mexico’s Orbia escaped a $1.14 billion cartel lawsuit, effectively wiping out a massive legal threat. Meanwhile, Brazil’s CSN launched a $1.3 billion bond exchange with a steep 11% coupon to push out its debt maturities, a costly but critical move to avoid a liquidity crisis.

How did Colombia’s political and economic realities collide on July 31?

The collision was stark. The central bank held rates steady at 12%, projecting an image of total institutional stability, while simultaneously, the recently departed CEO of state oil company Ecopetrol, Ricardo Roa, requested a plea deal over alleged campaign finance irregularities tied to President Gustavo Petro.

What natural event punctuated the economic news in Peru?

A magnitude 5.6 earthquake struck deep beneath the Amazon near Pucallpa, Peru. Tremors were felt across the border in Brazil, but no damage or casualties were reported. The event served as a powerful, humbling counterpoint to the country’s booming construction sector and infrastructure ambitions.

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Bourbon Street Music Club — Moema If you only make one stop, make it this landmark New Orleans-style jazz and blues club. On Saturday it runs afternoon Jazz Café sets and an evening headline show around 9 pm in a warm, intimate room — the surest bet in the city for great live music and a proper night out. Rua dos Chanés 127, Moema; shows from about R$38.

Tonight at a Glance —Live Samba or MPB House Authentic Brazilian music with a mixed crowd of locals and visitors; best nights are typically Friday and Saturday from 9 pm. —Rooftop Bar in Pinheiros or Itaim Stylish open-air drinks spot for a date or sunset warm-up; crowd is young professionals and digital nomads. —Boteco in Vila Madalena Classic São Paulo bar-hopping scene; ice-cold beer, simple food, and a lively street atmosphere. —Electronic Club in Barra Funda Warehouse-style venue with local and international DJs; crowd arrives very late, around 1 am. —LGBTQ+ Party in Centro Inclusive, high-energy party with pop, funk and electronic sounds; known for a creative, welcoming crowd.

On a Saturday night, São Paulo’s energy is unmatched, and knowing exactly how the city works separates a flawless night out from a frustrating one. This guide gives you the practical script—the comanda, couvert, payments, getting home safe, and the logic of the local circuit—so you can navigate any venue tonight like you belong.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm-up (7 pm – 9 pm): Start with sunset drinks at a rooftop or cocktails in a Pinheiros speakeasy. It is early by Brazilian standards but perfect for a seated table.

Prime time (9:30 pm – midnight): Hit a samba circle, MPB house or a buzzing boteco street in Vila Madalena. Live music typically starts around 9:30 pm or 10 pm.

After midnight (12:30 am – 5 am): Move to a club in Baixo Augusta, Barra Funda or a warehouse party. The local crowd floods in after 1 am and the night peaks around 3 am.

Late-night food (3 am – 5 am): Post-club, find a padaria (bakery) or a late-night lanchonete for a sandwich. These spots are scattered across central neighbourhoods.

Scenes & Sounds

Samba — Roots samba, samba-rock and pagode played live in crowded, sweaty rooms. The sound is percussion-heavy and highly interactive. Where: Barra Funda, Vila Madalena, and Centro

MPB — Brazilian Popular Music blending bossa, tropicalia and contemporary songwriting. More seated and intimate than samba. Where: Pinheiros, Vila Madalena, and Consolação

Electronic — From deep house to techno in industrial-style clubs and roving warehouse parties. International-level production and sound systems. Where: Barra Funda, Centro, and Cambuci

Forró — Northeastern dance music with accordion and zabumba; friendly, partner-dance focused and very welcoming to beginners. Where: Vila Madalena, Lapa, and various dedicated forró houses

Funk — Carioca-style baile funk and São Paulo’s own funk ostentação. Heavy bass and fast-paced rhythms, central to many LGBTQ+ and club parties. Where: Baixo Augusta and club parties across the city

Sertanejo — Brazilian country music, huge in São Paulo. Massive singalong hits in upscale venues. Where: Vila Olímpia and Itaim Bibi

Pick Your Night

Date night: A stylish rooftop in Itaim Bibi or a low-lit cocktail bar in Pinheiros. Arrive early for a quiet corner before the late-night rush.

Solo and safe: A lively samba house with communal tables or a bar counter in a busy boteco. Sit at the counter, order a caipirinha, and chat with the barman.

Dance till sunrise: A warehouse club in Barra Funda or an all-night LGBTQ+ party. Do not arrive before 12:30 am.

Meet locals: A packed samba circle or a forró dance floor. The structured partner dance makes it natural to interact.

Meet other expats: A bar in Pinheiros known for digital nomads or an international-themed party in Vila Madalena. Start at the bar.

World.content:

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Roda de Samba at Pedra do Sal This is the soul of Rio on a Saturday night. An authentic, open-air samba party at the historic birthplace of samba, packed with locals and in-the-know visitors. The music is live, powerful, and free, spilling into the surrounding streets with a raw, joyful energy you won’t find in any club. Go for the unparalleled atmosphere, the friendly crowd, and the strongest caipirinhas in the port zone.

Tonight at a Glance —Pedra do Sal The ultimate free street samba, an iconic Rio experience with a diverse, fun-loving local crowd. Best early evening. —Rio Scenarium A multi-floor antique-filled fantasy and a samba institution; tourist-friendly, visually stunning, and reliably brilliant. Best late night. —Substation A sweaty underground electronic club in Copacabana (the former Fosfobox space) for house, techno and pop. A gritty local favourite for dancing till sunrise. —Bar dos Descasados A romantic, secret-feeling rooftop bar in Santa Teresa with jaw-dropping views. Perfect date spot for sunset and early drinks. —The Home Rio’s cathedral of electronic sound and a world-famous LGBTQ+ club, reborn in the former The Week space in Saúde. A massive, spectacular Saturday-night party.

Tonight, Saturday 1 August 2026, Rio de Janeiro’s nightlife runs the full gamut, from the historic street samba of Pedra do Sal to colossal LGBTQ+ club nights and underground indie discos. The main circuit connects a sunset Santa Teresa rooftop, a late-night Lapa music hall, and a sunrise sweat in a Copacabana basement.

Tonight across Rio de Janeiro. (Photo internet reproduction)
