World.title: Chevron CFO bullish on Iraq after West Qurna 2, Nassiriya agreements
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Chevron boasts “significant potential” to expand its activities in Iraq over the next decade, according to Chief Financial Officer Eimear Bonner, highlighting the US oil company’s increasing trust in the country’s energy sector after recent deals with Baghdad.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Bonner said that Iraq remained one of Chevron’s top priority markets for future production expansion after the signing of preliminary agreements to pursue negotiations on the massive West Qurna 2 and Nassiriya oil fields.

She added that Chevron has been encouraged by its interaction with Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi and Iraq’s Ministry of Oil while discussions continue and that the corporation is also collaborating with Baghdad on diverse crude export routes to boost Iraq’s long-term energy security.

The statements bolster rising trust among foreign energy corporations after Al-Zaidi’s visit to the United States earlier this month, during which Iraq inked more than $60 billion in investment deals covering energy, infrastructure, banking, and technology.

World.title: Syria joins Saudi Arabia, Jordan in warning Iraq over Iran-backed militias
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Syria has joined Saudi Arabia and Jordan in warning Baghdad that strikes conducted from Iraqi soil against neighboring nations may result in military strikes against the armed groups responsible, according to Syrian military officials cited by regional media.

According to Al Jazeera and the US-funded Al Hurra, a senior Syrian military source said that Damascus will react to any strikes from Iraq by attacking the “terrorist militias” involved inside Iraqi territory.

The purported warning comes amid a steep increase in regional tensions after US-Saudi bombings against Iran-backed militias in Iraq in retaliation for drone assaults on Saudi oil installations, which Riyadh said were conducted from Iraqi territory.

The Iraqi government has frequently said that it would not allow Iraqi land to be used as a launchpad for attacks on neighboring nations.

Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi recently issued an order establishing a comprehensive security strategy aimed at enhancing state authority and preventing armed organizations from endangering regional security.

The new threat puts further pressure on Baghdad, as more neighboring nations indicate they may take direct action if cross-border assaults continue.

Iraqi authorities have attempted to prevent such a situation, claiming that security activities should be overseen by the Iraqi government rather than foreign forces.

Several Iran-backed organizations operating inside Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) are at the heart of the conflict, including Kataib Hezbollah, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, Harakat al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada.

While the PMF is technically part of Iraq’s security system, some of its sections have strong links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and have been accused by regional governments of carrying out strikes outside of Baghdad’s jurisdiction.

For Iraq, the diplomatic stakes go beyond security.

Baghdad has been attempting to reestablish ties with Syria as part of greater regional economic integration, including talks on resurrecting the old Iraq-Syria oil pipeline to the Mediterranean, which is considered strategically crucial for diversifying Iraq’s export routes outside the Gulf.

The purported Syrian warning comes at a critical moment for Al-Zaidi’s administration, which has spent recent months bolstering relations with Washington, Ankara, Riyadh, and Damascus while portraying Iraq as a secure destination for global investment.

The mounting threats from neighboring Arab governments highlight the importance of Baghdad demonstrating its ability to prevent armed groups from conducting strikes independent of the state.

Failure to do so risks increasing regional military tensions and jeopardizing Iraq’s aspirations to boost commerce, energy cooperation, and infrastructure projects with its neighbors.

The Syrian government has not issued an official warning, and IraqiNews.com has not independently confirmed the statements ascribed to the Syrian military source.

However, the claims reflect rising regional worry that strikes by Iran-backed militias operating from Iraqi soil could further destabilize the area and hamper Iraq’s diplomatic and economic goals.

World.title: Iran-backed militias threaten Iraq’s ties with US and Gulf
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Escalating tensions between Iran-backed militias are providing one of the most serious hurdles yet to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s ambitions to deepen ties with the United States and Gulf states while luring billions of dollars in international investment.

The most recent crisis followed US-Saudi airstrikes on Iran-aligned armed groups in Iraq, when Saudi Arabia accused militias operating from Iraqi territory of firing drones at oil installations in the kingdom’s Eastern Province.

Riyadh claimed that the operation targeted the militias responsible for the assaults rather than the Iraqi state or its military forces, but Baghdad denounced the strikes as a breach of national sovereignty.

The recent tensions are being fueled by numerous prominent Iran-aligned organizations operating inside Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), notably Kataib Hezbollah, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, Harakat al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada.

While the PMF is technically part of Iraq’s security apparatus, many of its groups have strong links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and have occasionally conducted operations outside of Baghdad’s chain of command.

Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi responded by calling an emergency meeting of the Ministerial Council for National Security, canceling a planned trip to Saudi Arabia, and announcing a comprehensive security strategy to prevent Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks on neighboring countries.

The administration also reiterated its resolve to keep all weapons entirely under state control.

That vow has gained importance after Al-Zaidi’s visit to Washington earlier this month, during which Iraq and the United States reiterated their commitment to completing the US-led coalition operation by the end of September 2026.

During the visit, Al-Zaidi pledged to ensure that all weapons eventually come into the control of the Iraqi state, citing it as a cornerstone of his government’s security strategy and a crucial step toward bolstering Iraq’s sovereignty and stability.

Since entering office, Al-Zaidi has maintained a policy of balancing Iraq’s ties with rival regional and international forces.

During recent travels to Washington, Ankara, and Tehran, he achieved huge investment and cooperation deals totaling tens of billions of dollars in the energy, banking, technology, infrastructure, and industrial sectors.

His administration has also attempted to strengthen connections with Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Turkey, and other Gulf nations via new transportation corridors, energy alliances, and trade agreements aimed at diversifying Iraq’s economy beyond oil and positioning the country as a regional center linking the Gulf to Europe.

According to analysts, Baghdad’s approach is highly dependent on proving that the Iraqi state, rather than armed groups, controls the country’s security and foreign policy.

Continued strikes from Iraqi territory risk eroding the country’s reputation with major regional allies and international investors, at a time when foreign investment has risen after years of turmoil.

The stakes rose when US President Donald Trump said that recent US-Saudi operations against Iran-backed militias were coordinated with the Iraqi government, a claim Baghdad has denied.

Observers believe it reflects rising discontent among Iraq’s leadership with armed groups accused of dragging the nation into regional conflicts that contradict Baghdad’s diplomatic and economic interests.

Al-Zaidi is currently facing the most significant test of his leadership.

Delivering on his promise to place all weapons under state control will be critical not only for Iraq’s internal security but also for maintaining trust with the United States, Gulf Arab states, and international investors, many of whom support many of the country’s largest economic projects.

Baghdad’s dilemma now extends beyond managing ties between Washington and Tehran.

It demonstrates that the Iraqi state possesses both the authority and the political will to prevent Iran-backed militias from using Iraqi territory to launch attacks that risk isolating the country, harming relations with Arab neighbors and the United States, and jeopardizing Iraq’s long-term economic recovery and investment goals.

World.title: Iraq faces growing fiscal strain
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is under increasing financial strain as plummeting oil earnings tighten government budgets, with Health Minister Abdul Hussein al-Mousawi saying that ensuring monthly public-sector wages has become the government’s top priority.

Speaking at a public meeting, al-Mousawi stated that the government requires approximately 10.8 trillion Iraqi dinars ($8.2 billion) per month to pay public-sector salaries, while current monthly oil revenues have fallen to approximately 2.5 trillion dinars, highlighting the growing gap between government obligations and income.

The statements are one of the most direct public acknowledgements by a top Iraqi official of the government’s financial challenges after months of decreased oil prices and fewer export profits.

Iraq’s government finances remain very vulnerable to variations in global energy markets because the vast bulk of public revenue comes from crude oil.

Official figures published this week indicated that oil accounted for over 84% of federal income in the first five months of 2026, but collections decreased by more than one-third compared to the same time the previous year as oil prices and export profits plummeted.

The health minister also warned of financing restrictions in the healthcare sector, citing worries about the supply of medications and the government’s capacity to sustain public services if financial pressures continue.

The fresh warnings follow weeks of increased regional tensions, which disrupted oil markets and added uncertainty to Iraq’s economic prospects.

As OPEC’s second-largest producer, Iraq relies on oil exports to fund wages, pensions, social welfare, and the majority of government expenditure, making the budget susceptible to long-term reductions in crude prices.

Economists have long cautioned that Iraq’s reliance on oil income makes the nation susceptible to external shocks, while a hefty public-sector pay bill constrains the government’s budgetary flexibility.

Previous administrations attempted to diversify income streams via tax changes and non-oil investments, but hydrocarbons remain the economy’s backbone.

The financial pressure comes at a critical time for Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s government, which has been promoting Iraq as a destination for billions of dollars in foreign investment following agreements signed with US, Turkish, and international companies in energy, banking, technology, and infrastructure.

Continued budgetary strain may make it more urgent to accelerate economic reforms, raise non-oil income, and improve public financial management to lessen Iraq’s reliance on petroleum exports.

They also emphasize that preserving investor trust will be contingent on the government’s ability to maintain macroeconomic stability while continuing to fund big development projects.

Despite the present issues, Iraq has large foreign currency reserves, which act as a financial cushion for the government.

However, experts warn that while reserves might help absorb short-term shocks, they are not a substitute for the fundamental changes needed to diversify the economy and reduce its dependence on unpredictable oil earnings.

World.title: Iraq expects record 22 million pilgrims for Arbaeen
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is prepared to welcome around 22 million pilgrims for this year’s Arbaeen pilgrimage, including up to 5 million overseas tourists, in what officials believe to be one of the country’s greatest religious gatherings and a significant boost to tourism and the local economy.

According to Iraqi official data, well over 22 million people are anticipated to attend the annual pilgrimage to the holy city of Karbala, with 4.5 million to 5 million pilgrims coming from outside Iraq.

The government has announced that tens of thousands of volunteers would be deployed to assist pilgrims, and Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has urged officials to boost the number of buses and other transport services to facilitate travel during the festival.

The surge of foreign tourists is projected to have a substantial impact on Iraq’s tourism, hospitality, transportation, and retail industries, with hotels, restaurants, transit operators, and local businesses benefitting from increased demand during the pilgrimage season.

Officials have extended transportation networks in preparation for this year’s pilgrimage, including more rail services, buses, and logistical assistance, as part of larger measures to boost connectivity and promote Iraq’s tourist industry.

The government has increasingly highlighted religious tourism as a crucial pillar of economic diversification, with millions of people visiting the country’s holy sites at Karbala, Najaf, Kadhimiya, and Samarra each year.

According to officials, continuing investment in infrastructure and tourist services will help Iraq become one of the Middle East’s major religious tourism destinations, while also creating jobs and helping local economies around the country.

World.title: Reports: Iraq PM threatened to resign over militia disarmament
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi has threatened to resign if Iran-aligned armed groups do not cooperate with his government’s efforts to bring all weapons under state control, according to reports citing political sources, highlighting the growing pressure on Baghdad to address one of its most difficult security challenges.

According to sources, Al-Zaidi warned leaders of Iraq’s Shi’ite Coordination Framework that if armed groups did not react to government efforts to disarm and completely submit to state authority, he would stand down.

IraqiNews.com was unable to independently verify the claims, and the Prime Minister’s office had no immediate response.

According to the sources, Al-Zaidi has been more dissatisfied by what he sees as a lack of cooperation on one of his administration’s fundamental commitments: guaranteeing that all weapons stay solely under the control of the Iraqi government.

The claims came days after US-Saudi airstrikes struck Iran-backed groups in Iraq in response to drone assaults on Saudi oil installations, which Riyadh said were launched from Iraqi territory.

The bombings forced Al-Zaidi to call an emergency security conference, cancel a planned trip to Saudi Arabia, and unveil a new security strategy aimed at preventing Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks on neighboring nations.

Armed organizations have emerged as one of Al-Zaidi’s most pressing problems.

Since entering office, he has attempted to solicit billions of dollars in foreign investment with trips to Washington, Tehran, and Ankara, while portraying Iraq as a stable location for oil, infrastructure, and technological projects.

Analysts believe Baghdad’s economic objectives are strongly dependent on its ability to show that the state, not armed groups, controls Iraq’s security strategy.

Repeated strikes conducted from Iraqi territory have strained ties with regional allies and risk weakening investor trust.

According to Western diplomatic sources published by Asharq Al-Awsat, key Iraqi officials, including Al-Zaidi and members of Iraq’s security apparatus, have received threats in connection with the government’s attempts to restrict weaponry outside of state control.

Unlike many regional leaders, Iraq’s prime minister leads by wide political agreement rather than a legislative majority, restricting his power to make unilateral choices.

Major security and political changes usually need agreement among Iraq’s different political blocs.

Al-Zaidi’s biggest power may not be the threat of resignation, but rather the international backing his administration has garnered as a result of recent accords with the United States, Turkey, and other allies.

These agreements, which span energy, finance, technology, and infrastructure, have boosted hopes that Iraq will attract tens of billions of dollars in investment if security improves.

Whether Al-Zaidi can translate that international momentum into domestic reforms will ultimately depend on gaining broader political support for his pledge to keep all weapons under Iraqi state control, which has become one of his government’s most closely watched tests.

World.title: Iraq denies launching strikes from its territory against neighboring nations
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The military spokesperson for the Iraqi commander-in-chief, Sabah al-Numan, confirmed on Thursday that neither a foreign nor local body has presented proof that recent regional drone attacks were launched from Iraqi territory.

In a statement to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA), al-Numan urged accusing parties to submit reliable proof, saying that Baghdad has yet to receive such data.

The development comes following statements made by the Saudi Ministry of Defense, alleging that drone attacks targeting key oil infrastructure in the past few days originated in Iraq.

The Iraqi official indicated that the government will neither tolerate unilateral military acts from within its borders nor accept foreign violations of its territorial sovereignty.

Al-Numan’s remarks come a day after the United States and Saudi Arabia launched coordinated airstrikes targeting several bases of Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), killing and injuring many fighters.

The joint operation targeted several logistical and weapons storage locations in different provinces in Iraq, escalating the current regional battle.

The PMF described the joint US-Saudi strike as a dangerous escalation and a clear breach of Iraqi sovereignty.

World.title: Iraqi oil flows to continue via Turkey’s Ceyhan as renewal deal is discussed
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Turkish sources told Reuters that crude oil shipments from northern Iraq to the Turkish port of Ceyhan will continue while the two countries seek an arrangement to extend the pipeline’s operation for another 12 months.

On July 27, a bilateral agreement that had been in place for decades ended. Despite expectations, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi did not sign a 12-month renewal deal during his meeting with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara on Tuesday.

According to a Turkish official, oil flows via the Iraq-Turkey pipeline, which is Baghdad’s only operational export pipeline, will continue while negotiations for a renewal deal are still in progress.

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar recently announced a 12-month extension agreement between the two countries.

During a joint press conference in Ankara, Erdogan stated on Tuesday that Turkey hopes to finalize a comprehensive energy cooperation agreement as soon as possible.

An extension is intended to provide additional time for discussions on a complete accord. Turkey aims to fully utilize the 1.5 million barrels per day pipeline and consider expanding it to oil fields in southern Iraq.

Turkish data suggests that the pipeline currently transports approximately 170,000 barrels per day.

World.title: Long hours hurting resident docs’ mental health, NMC tells SC
World.content:

NEW DELHI: Long and crushing working hours have become a serious challenge for resident doctors, causing them psychological distress and mental health problems. Flagging the issue in an affidavit before Supreme Court, National Medical Commission (NMC) has stressed that reasonable working hours and time for rest are a must for their wellbeing and proper functioning, as well as proper patient care. It, however, expressed its inability to ensure the same, saying the matter falls within the domain of central and state health authorities.In the affidavit filed in response to a PIL by a group of doctors seeking healthy working conditions, the commission placed the findings of its task force, which had projected a grim picture of what doctors have to endure.âThe demanding schedules, including long and multiple 24-hour duties (sometimes 3-5 consecutive duties), were significant stressors for most post graduate doctors. These extended hours without adequate rest led to physical and mental exhaustion, negatively impacting their performance and health,â commission said, referring to the report.Doctorsâ organisation âUnited Doctors Frontâ had approached the court demanding healthy working conditions, pointing out that cases of doctorsâ suicides are on the rise and claiming that 150 such cases have been reported in five years.

World.title: Railway Board panels suggest premature retirement of 5 officers
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Review committees of Railway Board have recommended premature retirement of five Group âAâ officers in âpublic interestâ, a decision which officials said was aimed at sending out a strong message of âzero tolerance for corruption, lack of integrity and inefficiencyâ.

While two of these officers belong to senior administrative grade (SAG), being equivalent to joint secretary-level officers, the other three are junior administrative grade (JAG) railway officers, who are at director or joint director level. âIntegrity, discipline and accountability in public service remain non-negotiable. Actions taken under the provisions of Indian Railway Establishment Code are aimed at upholding these core values,â railway ministry said in an official statement.

It said the review committees had carried out detailed assessment of the officersâ service records in accordance with prescribed procedure. The review included examination of annual performance appraisal reports, integrity records, vigilance inputs, disciplinary history and service records. âThe committees unanimously recommended premature retirement of the officers in public interest,â the ministry said.

World.title: E20: AAP plans pro-choice rally to PM residence
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Stepping up his campaign against the rollout of E20 fuel, AAP national convener

Saturday announced a march to PMâs residence Tuesday to submit petitions against the ethanol-blended fuel programme, while demanding that consumers be given the option to choose betw-een pure petrol and E20 at fuel stations.

Addressing AAPâs âNational Townhall Against E20â at Constitution Club, Kejriwal alleged Centre had âimposedâ ethanol-blended fuel on consumers without adequate consultation and claimed it was causing financial losses to vehicle owners. He said petitions would be collected Monday, before a delegation of about 100 people marches to PMâs residence the following day.

Kejriwal placed three demands before Centre -- provide both pure petrol and E20 at fuel stations, price E20 lower than pure petrol, and reduce petrol prices to below Rs 84 per litre.

He argued that consumers should be free to decide which fuel they wish to purchase.

Claiming govt has repeatedly maintained E20 is safe for vehicles, Kejriwal challenged Centre to make public the scientific studies supporting the policy. âGovt keeps saying studies have found E20 does not damage vehicles. If such studies exist, they should place the reports in the public domain,â he said, adding that several people had shared experiences of reduced mileage and vehicle problems during the town hall.





He also alleged govt was only delaying the introduction of higher ethanol blends like E25 and E30 until the controversy surrounding E20 subsides. âThere are no studies going on. They are simply waiting for the issue to die down. Once it settles, they will bring E25, E30 and continue increasing the ethanol content,â Kejriwal claimed, advising consumers to opt for electric vehicles until E100-compatible vehicles become commercially available.

At the town hall, several owners, mechanics, delivery workers and experts claimed E20 had affected vehicle performance, increased maintenance costs and reduced mileage. Among them was a couple who commute daily from Delhi to Gurgaon. The husband said their 2014 petrol car earlier delivered 14 km per litre but now gives about 9 km per litre, significantly increasing monthly fuel expenses. His wife, who works in the automobile sector, claimed dealerships were receiving complaints from owners of newly-purchased vehicles regarding mileage and performance, but employees had no clear answers to offer.

World.title: Monsoon hope as WMO sees an El Niño counter
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The risk of overall monsoon rainfall being âbelow normalâ continues to loom over India due to a strengthening El NiÃ±o, but World Meteorological Organisationâs (WMO) latest monthly global seasonal climate update, released late Friday night, offered a ray of hope.

It predicted the possibility of a âpositiveâ Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), which could offset to an extent the negative impact of El NiÃ±o.

El NiÃ±o is a climatic pattern of warming of surface waters of central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean and is associated with a weak monsoon and harsher summer in India. IOD, on the other hand, has to do with the difference in sea surface temperatures between western and eastern parts of tropical Indian Ocean.

It helps in formation of stronger monsoon winds.

âA positive IOD is expected to develop... Combined with exceptionally warm global oceans and the likelihood of a positive IOD, the developing El NiÃ±o is expected to shape weather patterns across many parts of the world in the months ahead,â WMO said.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

If WMOâs forecast comes true, there is a possibility of improved rainfall conditions in south peninsular India â the region which had reported a high cumulative rainfall deficit of 22% as of Aug 1 â in particular and over many parts of the country in general.





Monsoon may avoid deficient phase with positive IOD

It may prevent India from slipping from âbelow normalâ phase to âdeficientâ monsoon phase at the end of the rainy season.

El NiÃ±o Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and IOD are two key factors that govern variation in monsoon rainfall. Though IMD Friday flagged the continuation of âneutralâ IOD conditions through the remaining period of southwest (summer) monsoon, it, at the same time, referred to climate forecasts from some international forecasting centres suggesting that positive IOD conditions are likely to develop during Sept.

World.title: Judge Ujjal Bhuyan questions SC collegium’s opacity
World.content:
NEW DELHI: SC judge Ujjal Bhuyan has questioned opacity in the collegiumâs decisions on judicial appointments.

âI have noticed that the last three collegium resolutions contain no reasons whatsoever.

Is this a step back from the principle of transparency?â said Justice Bhuyan at a panel discussion on Saturday.

âBy withholding reasons, we also create space for individuals to enter the judiciary who may later describe groups of people as âantsâ and make other remarks that are wholly unconstitutional,â he said.

Citizens have right to know deliberations on elevation, transfer of judges: Bhuyan

To prevent the entry of such people, âthere should be some discussion, there should be some reasons givenâ, said Justice Ujjal Bhuyan.

Though the judge didnât name anyone, the comment was an apparent reference to a remark by an Allahabad high court judge at a social event in 2024.

He was speaking at the launch of the Judicial Transparency Index: Assessing Disclosure of Information by the Supreme Court and the High Courts, prepared by the Justice, Access and Lowering Delays in India (JALDI) Initiative at the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy.

The judge stressed that deliberations on the elevation and transfer of judges by the SC collegium largely remain confidential, contrary to the principle of judicial transparency.





âWhile carrying out the next assessment on the scale of Judicial Transparency Index, I may request the JALDI team to also look into the aspect of opacity of the collegium system. Deliberations on elevation and transfer of judges remain confidential. Reasons for rejecting or deferring a recommendation are rarely disclosed in full. And the criteria applied are not codified in any publicly disclosed instrument. It is a very important issue.

Citizens have a right to know what is happening in the courts. They have a right to know who would be their judges.

They have a right to know judgments. These should be in the public domainâ, Justice Bhuyan underlined.

The report is the first systematic study assessing transparency practices across Indiaâs higher judiciary and evaluates disclosure of information by the Supreme Court and high courts across judicial processes, institutional governance and administration, and judicial and administrative personnel.

Referring to a previous collegium resolution reiterating the recommendation of senior advocate Saurabh Kirpal for appointment as a judge, Justice Bhuyan said he found the reasons recorded by the Supreme Court convincing but noted that despite more than three and a half years having passed, no appointment materialised.

Key findings of the JALDI report reveal that only five high courts have published a budget on their websites for FY 2025-26 while none has published the criteria governing case allocation.

Of the 813 judges in the higher judiciary, only 87 have publicly disclosed their assets even as only two high courts publish disciplinary sanction orders pertaining to district judicial officers.

âThe findings highlight that the level of judicial transparency varies across courts and demonstrate that while individual disclosure measures have emerged...they have not yet translated into a holistic approach...â a release from Vidhi said.

World.title: July GST collections up 15.4% to Rs 2.1 L cr on higher imports
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: GST collections rose 15.4% to Rs 2,11,205 crore in July, the second highest since the new structure was implemented last Sept, on the back of a 29% jump in integrated GST (IGST) on imports. This was also the highest pace of growth since rate rationalisation.The rise in IGST on imports in July (for transactions in the previous month) may be attributed to higher prices of crude and other commodities in the wake of the West Asia conflict.The impact of strong economic activity in June, when factory output grew at its fastest pace in nearly two years, was also visible on the tax numbers, seen as an advance indicator of economic activity. Some of the price hikes in FMCG and automobile sectors would have also buoyed collections. Central GST mop-up was pegged 12.3% higher at just under Rs 40,000 crore, while state GST grew 8.7% to nearly Rs 48,000 crore."The high GST collections tie in very well with the 7.3% increase in industrial production during June. It reflects continued economic resilience despite the challenges in the external environment...Thesteady growth in GST collections each month indicates that overall domestic consumption is becoming largely insulated from seasonal variations and external headwinds," said MS Mani, partner at Deloitte India.Some experts, however, are worried about the continued rise in imports. "...one cannot ignore the elevated levels of import GST collections, which remain a nagging concern. This points to a persistent gap in domestic manufacturing capability despite the range of successful PLI and Atmanirbhar Bharat interventions rolled out over the past few years.It is likely that the sustained push by policymakers towards localisation of around 100 products (being talked about) over a period of time will help bridge this gap," said Saurabh Agarwal, partner at EY India, a consulting firm.Net of refunds, which were 13% higher at almost Rs 30,000 crore, collections went up 15.8% to Rs 1,81,237 crore.Haryana logged the highest growth of 28%, followed by Gujarat and Puducherry (26%), Karnataka and Goa (23%), and Maharashtra (20%). Chhattisgarh (23% fall), Jharkhand and Manipur (20% decline) were among the laggards.

NEW DELHI: Cabinet Friday approved two strategic tunnel projects and the approach roads on NH-244 in J&K at an estimated cost of around Rs 9,800 crore to provide all-weather connectivity between Kashmir Valley and Jammu region while improving access to Chenab Valley,.The projects comprise Singhpora-Vailoo tunnel and Sudhmahadev-Dranga tunnel, along with their approach roads, on the Anantnag-Chenani corridor. These are expected to strengthen road connectivity in Doda, Kishtwar and Udhampur districts, and reduce travel time.While the development of the 39km Singhapora-Vailoo stretch will have 10km unidirectional twin-tube tunnels, the 13km Sudhmahadev-Dranga section will have 8km tunnels. The projects would be completed in five years and will be fully Centre-funded.The tunnels are aimed at bypassing difficult stretches of NH-244 that are frequently affected by adverse weather disrupting traffic and isolating several areas during the winter months. World.title: Morning Digest: Eight killed as extremely heavy rain batters Kerala; magnificent seven as Indian boxers put on a show at CWG, and more
World.content:
Eight killed as extremely heavy rain batters Kerala

Eight people died in rain-related incidents in Kerala as a spell of intense rain battered the State from Friday (July 31, 2026) night into Saturday (August 1, 2026), triggering landslips, flash floods, and widespread destruction, particularly in hilly regions. This comes barely a month after a deadly debris slip triggered by extreme rainfall claimed eight lives at a tunnel construction site in Wayanad.

Varanasi police book MPs Rahul Gandhi, Pappu Yadav and Awadesh Prasad for ‘insulting Sanatan Dharma’

The Varanasi police on Saturday registered a First Information Report (FIR) against Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi and Members of Parliament Pappu Yadav and Awadhesh Prasad over a play they staged on the Parliament premises in Delhi on the alleged donation theft at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya.

Stricter punishment, speedy probe as President Murmu assents to tweaked anti-paper leak Bill

An amended law that empowers states to set up fast-track courts for speedy trials of accused and enhance punishment in public examination question paper leak cases has received the assent of President Droupadi Murmu. In a gazette notification issued on Friday (July 31, 2026), the law ministry said President Murmu has given her assent to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, after it was cleared by both Houses of Parliament earlier this week.

Arrested terror suspect had planned to infiltrate CJP protest, says West Bengal Special Task Force

The West Bengal Special Task Force (STF) on Saturday (August 1, 2026) said a terror suspect arrested on Friday (July 31, 2026), identified as Hamim Mondal, had plans for subversive action during protests by the Cockroach Janta Party in Delhi. The police have also picked up his associate, Arpita Sarkar, from Sahebganj in Jharkhand and transferred her to Kolkata.

Protest for Amit Shah’s resignation over July 20 action will continue: AISA chief Neha

Demanding Union Home Minister Amit Shah’s resignation over the July 20 crackdown on anti-paper leak protesters in Delhi, AISA president Neha said the movement has evolved into a wider campaign seeking accountability from the Centre over the alleged police action.

Veteran Nepalese mountaineer Purja dies in avalanche on Broad Peak in PoK

Veteran Nepalese mountaineer Nirmal Purja died in an avalanche on Broad Peak, located in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir’s Gilgit Baltistan, his expedition company said on Saturday (August 1, 2026). Purja, 43, was among 10 climbers swept away by the avalanche that struck Broad Peak, located in the Karakoram range near K2, at an altitude of around 7,000 metres on Thursday (July 30).

Commonwealth Games: Magnificent seven as the Indian pugilists put on a show

India capped its finest-ever boxing campaign at the Games, with seven gold medals and three silver. Sachin Siwach rallied to down Tryagain Morning Ndevelo of Namibia in a thrilling men’s 60kg gold medal bout. Earlier, Preeti Pawar opened the floodgates for India. It was then Jaismine Lamboria’s turn to showcase her technical brilliance against Northern Ireland’s Michaela Walsh in the women’s 57kg final.

Gulveer wins bronze in 5000m, first Indian to win two athletic medals in CWG

Gulveer Singh etched his name in Commonwealth Games history, once again, at the 2026 edition in Glasgow after he became the first Indian, man or woman, to win a medal in the 5000m event on Saturday (August 1, 2026). Moreover, the 27-year-old broke fresh ground by becoming the first Indian track and field athlete to win multiple medals in a single Games.

3 people killed, at least 21 wounded in Moscow restaurant bombing, Russian officials say

A bomb detonated at ​a ​restaurant on Saturday (August 1, 2026) in ‌central ⁠Moscow killing at least three people, including the bomber, Russian state media ​said, ​citing ​local officials. At least 21 people were also injured when the explosive device detonated at the restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square in Moscow, the National Anti-Terrorism Committee said, quoted by Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.

NEET-UG counselling to begin on August 4, academic session from September 8

The first round of counselling for admission to MBBS and other undergraduate medical courses under the All India Quota (AIQ) will begin on August 4 and the academic session for the 2026-27 batch will commence on September 8, according to the Medical Counselling Committee.

With 7 medals, Indian para team delivers best-ever CWG show, equals medals from all past editions

Indian para sports athletes scripted history in the Glasgow Commonwealth Games as they equaled the haul of all the previous editions put together, winning seven medals, including one gold and silver on Saturday (August 1, 2026). The 28-member Indian para sports contingent ended their campaign with seven medals — 3 gold, 2 silver and 2 bronze. On Sunday (August 2), Indians will feature in track cycling and para track cycling events.

One inmate killed, six wounded in Sri Lanka prison riot, says police

At least one inmate was killed, and another six were taken to hospital after a riot at a prison outside Sri Lanka’s capital on Saturday (August 1, 2026), police said. The violence at the Mahara Prison outside Colombo came about a month after clashes at another overcrowded jail killed 10 guards and 21 inmates in Sri Lanka’s worst prison riot in years.

Employees of Hindustan Machine Tools (HMT), Kalamassery, on Saturday submitted a memorandum to Rajya Sabha member John Brittas, seeking his intervention to resolve the prolonged financial crisis in the public sector unit.

The memorandum noted that despite assurances made during a meeting with Union Heavy Industries Minister H.D. World.title: Plane carrying European tourists crashes in Peru, killing 13 people on Nazca Lines viewing flight
World.content:
A plane carrying European tourists to view the famed Nazca Lines crashed into a field outside the Peruvian city of Nazca, killing 13 people, local authorities said.

Nazca’s municipal government said the plane departed from the nearby city of Ica on Saturday and was operated by Peruvian company Aerodiana. On its website, the airline said that it has offered scenic flights over the Nazca lines for the past 14 years using Cessna Grand Caravan planes.

The Nazca Lines are a group of extensive geoglyphs scraped into the desert around Nazca hundreds of years ago by Peru’s Indigenous inhabitants. The lines form images of animals that can only be fully appreciated from planes or viewing towers.

Among the dead were seven Italian citizens between the ages of 18 and 54, two 52-year-old Spaniards and two Germans of 77 and 78 years, Peru’s Transportation Ministry said. The other two fatalities were the pilot Américo Salazar and copilot Irenka Guanilo del Carpio, it said in an official report.

President Keiko Fujimori expressed regret over the accident and said a “temporary suspension” of the airport was being considered, though the decision will be made once she receives reports from the relevant ministries.

Peruvian authorities said the accident is under investigation. Aerodiana was not immediately available for comment.

World.title: Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das | The three faces of a revolt
World.content:
From satire to sit-in is the most popular, and perhaps the easiest, explanation for the student protest movement that culminated in the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. This explanation is empowering in its simplicity. But it is incomplete.

By now, everyone knows how the story goes. On May 15, 2026, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant likened unemployed youth turning to activism and social media to “cockroaches”, triggering widespread backlash. Seizing on the remark, Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student in Boston, launched a satirical online platform for fellow “cockroaches”, transforming an insult into a rallying cry for disaffected youth. Within the first 24 hours, 50,000 people signed up. That number swelled to more than a million within five days, while the movement’s Instagram account surged past 22 million followers.

Yet behind the viral posts, soaring follower counts and colourful symbolism stood a trio: Abhijeet Dipke (30), Ashutosh Ranka (30) and Saurav Das (27), whose skills complemented one another. They come from different parts of the country, different social backgrounds and possess markedly different temperaments.

Those who have spent time around Jantar Mantar since the movement began describe Mr. Dipke as politically intuitive, though at times a touch emotional, and the beating heart of the movement. On July 18, after activist Sonam Wangchuk was removed from Jantar Mantar, it was Mr. Dipke who argued that the movement should escalate its demands. Instead of limiting itself to seeking Mr. Pradhan’s resignation, he proposed demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Mr. Dipke loves discussing A.R. Rahman’s music and reciting Shah Rukh Khan’s dialogues from Swades. He brought a sense of lightness to the protest, spending time in the evenings talking to the protesters, posing for pictures with them and cracking a joke every now and then.

Mr. Ranka, meanwhile, has been described as decisive, though at times authoritarian, and quicker to lose his temper than others. He remains the mind of the movement and its principal strategist. Mr. Das, the youngest of the three, is known as much for his affable demeanour as for his outreach skills, though colleagues say he can occasionally be indecisive.

If Mr. Ranka and Mr. Dipke rave about Shah Rukh Khan starrer Swades and Aamir Khan’s Rang De Basanti, Mr. Das represents the other end of the social spectrum where his favourite series is Modern Family — a mockumentary about a multigenerational family based out of Los Angeles.

Association with AAP

One obvious thread connecting the three is their association with the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), a link none of them has sought to conceal. Both Mr. Dipke and Mr. Ranka have worked for the party, while Mr. Das’s proximity to former Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal is hardly a secret.

Mr. Dipke was born in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (formerly Aurangabad), Maharashtra, into a Dalit family, though his caste identity largely remained in the background during the protest. “He is a student leader who is also a Dalit and not the other way round,” a leader associated with the 36-day protest said. One occasion on which he publicly asserted his caste identity came after ink was thrown at him at Jantar Mantar on July 18. His response was brief: “Blue is my colour. Jai Bhim.”

He studied journalism at Tilak Maharashtra Vidyapeeth in Pune before moving to the U.S. in 2023 to pursue a Master’s degree in Public Relations at Boston University. Mr. Dipke worked in political communications and was associated with the AAP social media team between 2020 and 2023, working closely with senior leader Manish Sisodia.

Mr. Ranka’s journey to the CJP was unlike that of most protest leaders. Born and raised in Jaipur, he studied Materials Science and Engineering at IIT-Kanpur, where he was elected president of the Students’ Gymkhana, an early indication of his interest in public life.

He served as a Delhi Assembly Fellow during 2019-20, working closely with the team of former Delhi Chief Minister and current Leader of Opposition Atishi during the pandemic, before pursuing a Master’s in Public Administration at the London School of Economics. He subsequently worked with McKinsey & Company and with Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, before gradually moving away from the worlds of consulting and international policy in favour of Indian public life.

Mr. Ranka also worked on the AAP campaign for the February 2025 Delhi Assembly election, focusing exclusively on the New Delhi constituency, where Mr. Kejriwal was the candidate. He was part of the team examining voter deletions and continued to publicly defend Mr. Kejriwal and the party even after the election. His most recent article as AAP’s “national spokesperson” was published on March 16.

Unlike many political organisers, Mr. Ranka has never hidden his ambitions. He has often expressed a desire to focus on Rajasthan politics. Following the 2025 Assembly election, he turned his attention to the State, running campaigns to protect a 100-acre forest near Jaipur. More recently, he gave Rajasthan Education Minister Madan Dilawar a three-month ultimatum to address issues faced by students at Rajasthan University, warning that the CJP would otherwise seek the vice-chancellor’s resignation.

Saurav Das, the movement’s young spokesman, became its public face. A journalist before he became a protest leader, he understood how newsrooms functioned, how narratives were shaped and, more important, how to keep a movement in the headlines.

Mr. Das spent part of his childhood in Puducherry and speaks a smattering of Tamil. He studied Journalism and Mass Communication at Amity University, Noida, graduating in 2019. He is best known for his detailed profile of former Chief Justice of India D.Y. Chandrachud for The Caravan, and has also written for Frontline and other publications.

‘The language of Gen Z’

Mr. Das is also the co-founder of Climate Action Front, an initiative focused on climate governance, sustainability and environmental policy. Alongside journalism, he has been working on his debut book, Complicit Silence: The Court’s Role in India’s Quiet Suffering, which examines the judiciary’s role in contemporary India through a series of case studies involving citizens seeking justice. Videos of Mr. Das dancing after Mr. Pradhan’s resignation also went viral, attracting admiration as well as criticism. Mr. Das defended the celebrations as “the language of Gen Z”, arguing that young people express political victories differently.

None of the three had ever led a protest of this scale before they laid siege to the government near the 18th century observatory, Jantar Mantar. Nor had the majority of the protesters who took to the streets of Delhi, in response to their call. For now, the three insist that the CJP will continue to function as a pressure group rather than a political party.

World.title: U.S. Justice Department subpoenas New York Times journalist in North Korea leak probe
World.content:
The Justice Department ​has subpoenaed the records of a freelance journalist for ‌the New York Times as part of a ​probe into the sourcing of ⁠a 2025 story about a botched U.S. military operation in North Korea, the newspaper said on Saturday (August 1, 2026).

Freelancer Matthew Cole was subpoenaed in February by Virginia prosecutors seeking more than two years’ worth of his notes as well as his testimony, according to the newspaper. Reuters could ⁠not immediately independently verify the information, but a spokesman for the Times said Mr. Cole is disclosing the subpoena.

“We support ​Matthew Cole’s decision ‌to make public a subpoena that the government has attempted to keep secret,” New York Times spokesperson Charlie Stadtlander said in an ‌emailed statement.

The story co-written by Mr. Cole detailed how ​Navy SEALs in early 2019 killed several unarmed North Koreans during a ⁠mission to plant a listening device near the country’s coast, citing two dozen unnamed sources.

A spokesperson for ‌the Justice Department did not address Mr. Cole’s specific case, but said that the DOJ “will use all available legal tools to uncover those who unlawfully disclose national defence information.”

Stadtlander called the subpoena of Mr. Cole “another brazen and illegal attack from ‌the administration designed to deny the public information of ​vital importance.”

The New York Times article said the newspaper is paying for Mr. Cole’s ⁠legal representation. Cole’s reporting “helps the public understand what the government ⁠is doing in its name,” said his attorney, David A. O’Neil. “He will not ‌be intimidated by efforts to suppress information that the administration considers unflattering,” O’Neil said.

World.title: An amateur singing circle spanning Chennai city
World.content:
Paadarivom Padipparivom traces its origins to the lockdowns of 2020. Former IT professional Naggeshwerran S., aged 43, known as NGR in the music community, noticed a pattern while scrolling through the Smule karaoke app.

A singalong on wheels today The Bus Singalong is Paadarivom Padipparivom’s latest initiative. The Bus Singalong on August 2 with two routes across Chennai was initially planned with one bus for around 50 participants. When registrations opened through the group’s mobile app, around 40 people signed up within one and a half hours. The response led to the addition of a second bus, taking the total registrations to around 85–90. The bus sing-along event will take place from 3:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. Registrations have now closed, as the organisers have already received 90 registrations and booked two buses, which have reached full capacity. Looking ahead, the organisers are exploring the possibility of hosting their next sing-along event aboard the Cordelia Cruise. While discussions are still in the preliminary stages, those interested can stay updated by following the group’s Instagram page for future announcements and registration details.

“People were singing because they enjoyed it, but many of them were also being mocked online. We realised there were many people who wanted to sing but did not know where to learn,” says Naggeshwerran.

A decision to do something about this led to free live sessions on Facebook and YouTube, where participants got to learn one Tamil song every week. The lessons were as simple as they can be: songs were broken down into simple sounds and rhythmic patterns. “I have been singing since 1992, but I never learnt Carnatic music. Friends would teach me using sounds instead of swaras. We thought if this method worked for me, it could work for others too,” he says. The first session, held on May 4, 2020, drew close to 500 viewers, far exceeding the organisers’ expectations. Requests for regular classes soon followed, leading to the formation of Paadarivom Padipparivom.

The community now operates from two studios —Madipakkam and Saligramam which serve as its primary spaces for learning and singing. Each studio can accommodate around 25-30 people and hosts regular singing classes, rehearsals, karaoke sessions and community singalongs. Members also gather there for Jam Along Vaanga, where they perform solo or duet songs before an audience.

As participation grew, the community began extending beyond its studios. An invitation from Cookgramam restaurant in Anna Nagar led to regular singalong sessions at the venue on the first and third Friday of every month. The sessions, which combine music with a shared meal, accommodate around 65 to 70 participants and are consistently full. The group has since partnered with an event venue in Adyar for larger singalong sessions and has also received requests from a venue on OMR to host similar events. A majority of those who join are above the age of 30. “Most activities in music are designed for children or youngsters. We wanted to create something for people in their thirties, forties, fifties and beyond. Many of them are not looking for a career in music. They simply want a place where they can sing without being judged,” says Naggeshwerran.

The organisation follows a structured cinema music curriculum rather than teaching only individual songs. Learners are introduced to concepts such as pitch, rhythm and expression through familiar film songs. Since 2020, the team has released lessons for nearly 300 Tamil film songs, each available on YouTube for learners to revisit.

As interest grew, the organisers realised members wanted opportunities to sing outside the classroom. This led to the launch of Jam Along Vaanga, a karaoke programme where participants perform solo or duet songs before an audience. “We call it ‘Bathroom to Green Room’. Many people only sing inside their homes. We wanted to create a path where they could first learn, then practise and finally perform before an audience,” says Naggeshwerran.

The community now has around 3,000 members across WhatsApp groups, with participants from 26 countries joining both physical and online events.

An auction of singers

The group also organises Paattu Paraak, a singing competition inspired by the Indian Premier League. Participants are grouped into teams of six through a conceptual auction, without any exchange of money. Teams then compete in a cricket-style format, chasing each other’s total scores across multiple rounds. The finals are organised as fundraising events, with the proceeds donated to charitable organisations. In the past two years, funds raised through the competition have been contributed to Akshaya Homes, a free residential home for destitute senior citizens.

Registrations for all events are managed through the group’s PP Music mobile app. Participants can register, make payments and reserve slots for singalongs, competitions and other programmes through the app. Paadarivom Padipparivom has kept the registration fee for a singalong event at ₹299 to make it accessible to more people. Members with an annual subscription can attend events without paying separately, as the fee is included in their membership.

Beyond registrations, the app functions as a learning platform. Users can access free teaching videos, submit recordings of songs for feedback from mentors, and receive personalised comments on areas for improvement. It also features a “Voice Bank”, where aspiring singers can store their recordings, a digital library of solo and duet lessons in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Hindi for annual members, competition registrations, and a chat section that allows members to interact with one another.

For further details, contact 86680 18282 or @ppmusic0405 on Instagram

World.title: Presidential nod delay hits judiciary appointments
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The delay in presidential assent to judicial appointments has begun to affect the functioning of the superior judiciary, with the term of an additional judge of the Sindh High Court (SHC) having already expired and four additional judges of the Peshawar High Court (PHC) facing a similar situation within days, despite recommendations by the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (JCP) for the continuation of their services.

Justice Khalid Hussain Shahani of the SHC was appointed as an additional judge on Jan 29, 2025, for a one-year term. On Jan 22 this year, President Asif Ali Zardari approved a six-month extension in accordance with the JCP’s recommendation, extending his tenure until July 29.

Before the expiry of his tenure, the JCP, at its meeting on July 20, recommended another six-month extension and forwarded the recommendation through the constitutional channel to the president, who is the appointing authority. However, the summary has remained pending with the Presidency and no notification has yet been issued.

With no formal approval forthcoming, Justice Shahani’s term expired on July 29. Despite this, the SHC included his name in the latest roster of judges constituting benches, anticipating that the notification would be issued in the meantime.

SHC judge’s term lapses as four PHC judges face similar uncertainty

Sources in the Presidency maintained that an additional judge could not continue to hold office beyond the expiry of his tenure unless the president formally approved the extension and the Law Ministry issued the notification.

The sources recalled the case of former Islamabad High Court judge Justice Shaukat Aziz Siddiqui, whose confirmation as an additional judge was rejected by then president Asif Ali Zardari in October 2012 despite the JCP’s recommendation. The matter was later resolved by the Law Ministry, but when it reached the Supreme Court, the apex court observed that, following the 18th and 19th Constitutional Amendments, the president’s role in the appointment of judges had become largely ceremonial and that he was bound to act on the prime minister’s advice.

When contacted, SHC Registrar Asif Qureshi said he would examine the matter.

A similar situation is emerging in the Peshawar High Court (PHC), where the tenure of four additional judges — Justice Farah Jamshed, Justice Inamullah Khan, Justice Sabitullah Khan and Justice Aurangzeb — is due to expire on Aug 4.

The four judges were appointed as additional judges on Feb 4, 2025. When the JCP met on Jan 15 to consider the confirmation of 10 PHC additional judges, it confirmed six as permanent judges while recommending a six-month extension for the remaining four. The president subsequently approved the extension, which is now nearing completion.

The JCP has since recommended a further extension for the four judges, but the matter, like that of Justice Shahani, is awaiting presidential approval.

The uncertainty comes days after the Presidency also delayed assent to the appointment of additional judges to the Islamabad, Lahore, Sindh and Balochistan high courts, prompting concern within judicial and legal circles. The recommendations, approved by the JCP on July 20 and 21, have yet to be notified, while the government is said to be examining constitutional options should the delay persist.

Pakistan Bar Council Vice Chairman Pir Masood Chishti said an additional judge whose notification had not been issued by the president could not continue to perform judicial functions after the expiry of his or her tenure. “Once the president grants approval and the Law Ministry issues the notification, the judges can resume office,” he said.

Supreme Court Bar Association Presi­dent Haroon Rashid criticised the continued delay, arguing that the president could not indefinitely withhold confirmation of, or appointments recommended through, the constitutional process.

Published in Dawn, August 2nd, 2026

World.title: ‘US may not have enough forces to defend Israel against Iran’
World.content:
• Top American commander warns navy is stretched too thin; US has used nearly half of its THAAD interceptors

• Pentagon may face choice between US interests and Israel

• Missile defences consumed faster than they can be replaced; war tests Washington’s ability to fight on multiple fronts

WASHINGTON: A warning from one of America’s top military commanders has exposed a growing dilemma for Washington: The United States may no longer have enough naval forces to simultaneously defend Israel against Iranian missile attacks and protect its own interests across the Middle East.

General Alexus Grynkewich, commander of US European Command, has privately informed Pentagon officials that American naval assets are becoming stretched too thin as the conflict with Iran continues, according to reports by The Washington Post and other news outlets.

The general reportedly warned that without another US Navy destroyer assigned to the region, commanders could eventually face a difficult choice between protecting American forces and continuing missile-defence operations for Israel.

News outlets noted that the significance of the warning lies not only in the shortage itself, but in who delivered it.

Grynkewich is not an outside analyst; he is one of the senior officers responsible for managing US military commitments. His message reflects an internal military concern that America’s global commitments are exceeding available resources.

Navy destroyers equipped with the Aegis combat system have become a central part of Israel’s missile defence. These ships can track incoming ballistic missiles and launch advanced interceptors such as SM-3 and SM-6 missiles.

But these destroyers are also among America’s most valuable global military assets. They are needed in the Pacific to deter China, in Europe to reassure Nato allies, and in the Middle East to protect American bases and shipping routes.

His warning highlights a difficult military calculation: Every ship sent to defend Israel is a ship unavailable for another potential crisis. The warning comes amid reports that the United States has carried a substantial share of the burden in defending Israel from Iranian missile attacks.

Pentagon assessments cited by The Washington Post indicate US forces fired more than 200 THAAD interceptors during the Iran conflict — roughly half the Pentagon’s reported inventory — along with over 100 interceptors launched from Navy ships.

Israel also used its own Arrow and David’s Sling systems but relied heavily on American support during the most intense missile exchanges.

The issue is not simply the number of missiles fired. Advanced interceptors are expensive, complex weapons that take years to manufacture and replace. Recent assessments have warned that prolonged combat could place pressure on US stockpiles of critical air-defence weapons.

For decades, American military strategy has rested on the belief that Washington can respond to multiple crises simultaneously. The United States maintains alliances in Europe, commitments in the Middle East, and a growing military focus on the Indo-Pacific.

The warning from US European Command suggests that this assumption is being tested. The problem facing Pentagon planners is not whether the United States has the strongest military in the world — it does.

The problem is whether even the strongest military has enough ships, missiles, and industrial capacity to sustain simultaneous commitments. A conflict with Iran may therefore be revealing a broader vulnerability: America’s military power is vast, but not unlimited.

According to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies cited by CNN, the military has used a significant portion of its advanced missile inventory in recent weeks of fighting.

The assessment estimates that American forces have consumed about 45pc of their Precision Strike Missiles, at least half of their THAAD interceptors, and around 50pc of their Patriot interceptors.

The analysis also indicates the US has used roughly 30pc of its Tomahawk cruise missiles, over 20pc of its Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles, and around 20pc of its SM-3 and SM-6 interceptors.

Either way, the message from inside the Pentagon is clear: Modern warfare is consuming advanced weapons faster than they can be replaced, and even the US military must make choices when several crises demand the same resources.

Published in Dawn, August 2nd, 2026

World.title: Iranian oil smuggling drops 60pc, claim sources
World.content:
KARACHI: The influx of smuggled Iranian oil has drastically declined as tankers were hit inside Balo­chistan, causing heavy losses to those involved in this illegal business, according to sources in the oil sector.

The oil companies have been demanding that oil smuggling be stopped, but it has continued for years. However, the arrival of Iranian petroleum products increased after the US-Israeli war on Tehran began, pushing crude oil prices above $100 per barrel.

“Over the past month and a half, at least six oil tankers coming from Iran were destroyed by terrorists, but the actual number is not known,” said the source familiar with those in the oil business. However, it was not confirmed by other sources.

Since the US-Israeli attack on Iran on Feb 28, the entire world was shocked due to due to closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which is the world’s most critical energy transit chokepoint, carrying roughly 20pc of global oil, 20pc of liquefied natural gas (LNG), and about one-third of the world’s fertiliser trade.

Influx slows after terrorists destroyed six tankers in 45 days

Reserves of petroleum products began to decline in countries like Pakistan, which depend largely on imported fuel.

Pakistan faced the same situation, but the country did not experience rationing of oil and gas products. Reserves for 25 days were available, while more ships entered Pakistan during the war.

However, the influx of Iranian oil increased significantly. Smuggled petroleum products were available not only in Balochistan but also in Sindh, up to Karachi. Many say that Punjab also benefited from these smuggled oil products, which helped the country avoid rationing of oil products, as seen in India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka in the region.

“It is difficult to determine the proportions of previous and current influxes, but smuggling has decreased significantly, by at least 60pc,” the source claimed.

In FY26, Pakistan spent a record $16.86bn on the import of petroleum products, which was around 22pc of the country’s total import bill. Notably, despite higher prices, the share of petroleum products in the import bill remained within the average. Each year, Pakistan has to spend 22-25pc of its total imports on oil products.

According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, the import bill for petroleum products in FY25 was $15.94bn.

Pakistan’s illegal trade with Iran is worth more than $2 billion per year, and a number of products, such as edible oil, food products, washing powder, soaps, etc., are readily available in Karachi.

It is widely believed in the circles of trade and industry that the smuggling of oil products from Iran was deliberately ignored by the authorities due to the war and to avoid a crisis from a possible shortage of oil supplies across the country.

The government has consistently been passing on the increase in oil prices to consumers, but has successfully avoided a shortage-like situation.

World.title: Allies’ rift continues to widen as AJK polls enter 2nd phase
World.content:
• Multiple rounds of talks between PPP, PML-N leaders fail to defuse tensions

• Sanaullah questions Zardari’s election as president after PPP’s Form-47 jibe

• Saeed Ghani alleges PML-N govts came to power through rigging every time

• Sharif family meets at Jati Umra to take stock of ‘mounting’ political challenges

MUZAFFARABAD/LAHORE: Despite multiple rounds of talks between the PML-N and the PPP in Azad Jammu Kashmir, the tensions between the two allies over the results of the Mirpur elections did not subside, with leaders from both parties continuing to trade rigging allegations ahead of the second phase of the AJK elections.

The second phase will be held today in nine constituencies of Muzaffarabad division and all 12 refugee constituencies.

The PPP and the PML-N — coalition partners in the Centre — have been engaged in a war of words since the PML-N emerged victorious in Mirpur in the first phase of AJK elections.

In the latest exchange, PML-N senior leader Rana Sanaullah remarked on President Asif Ali Zardari’s role as he responded to PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s allegations of rigging in the 2024 general elections. Rana Sanaullah, the prime minister’s aide on political affairs, was addressing a gathering in Jhelum valley alongside Kashmir Affairs Minister Amir Muqam.

“If you call the votes secured by the prime minister votes of Forms-47, then on what forms has the president gotten votes on?” Mr Sanaullah said.

“If you say to Mian Nawaz Sharif that he became the prime minister for the first time or every time through rigging, […] then remember, it is also discussed here that someone also became the prime minister for the first time after breaking apart the country,” he said in reference to PPP founder Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who became the president of Pakistan in December 1971 after the secession of then-East Pakistan following the 1970 elections.

The PML-N stalwart also took a jibe at Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, whose recent remarks have sparked a fresh debate in political circles on the matter of creating new provinces. Calling Mr Naqvi a “blessed one” of President Zardari, the PML-N leader said the interior minister had “made the [political] journey of 30 years in three-and-a-half years”. “You began from where and have now reached where, and now you realise that this system is completely dysfunctional.”

‘PML-N always rigged polls’

Earlier in the day, PPP leader Saeed Ghani alleged that the PML-N had never won a general election without rigging. This followed a press briefing by Punjab’s education and sports ministers, where they said that the chief ministers of Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had nothing to show for their performance.

Addressing a press conference in Karachi, Ghani said: “The PPP did not secure power through rigging in any of the elections held till today. On the other hand, the PML-N has never secured power without rigging.”

The PPP leader alleged that the PML-N had come to power due to rigging in the 2024 polls. The PPP leader alleged that Nawaz Sharif, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz “lost their own seats and then blame us”.

Talks to defuse tensions

To defuse the tensions, senior leaders of both parties met multiple times in Azad Kashmir over the weekend to “explore a legal resolution” to the dispute. The latest round of talks followed two earlier meetings on Thursday and Friday. Another round was scheduled for Saturday afternoon, but could not be held as the PML-N leaders returned to Islamabad.

A PML-N source told Dawn that discussions focused on the PPP’s allegations and its demand for re-polling in certain constituencies. “It was not planned or pre-planned rigging but isolated acts at places where supporters of one candidate enjoyed numerical dominance over their opponents. Such incidents have unfortunately been part of the territory’s polling atmosphere and have also been witnessed in previous elections,” the source quoted the PML-N leaders as telling their counterparts.

According to the sources, the PPP initially raised objections to the results in four constituencies — Charhoi, Sehnsa and Nakyal in Kotli district, and Barnala in Bhimber district. However, it later withdrew its allegations regarding Sehnsa and Barnala. Saturday’s discussions centred on Charhoi, where PPP AJK president Chaudhry Yasin lost to PML-N’s Raja Riasat, and Nakyal, where PPP candidate Javed Iqbal Budhanvi was defeated by PML-N’s Raja Ayaz Ahmed.

Sharifs meet at Jati Umra

The Sharif family held discussions at Jati Umra. According to a statement issued by the PM’s Office, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif held consultations with his elder brother and PML-N chief Nawaz Sharif at Jati Umra to take stock of mounting political challenges, including the rift with the PPP over the AJK elections.

A senior PML-N leader told Dawn that the party leadership had taken serious note of the PPP chairman’s increasingly combative rhetoric against the Sharif family over the AJK polls and his warning that the PPP could reconsider its support for the federal government if the remaining phases of the elections were manipulated in favour of the PML-N. Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz and Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar also attended the meeting.

JAAC proposal

Separately, the PPP chairman claimed that he received a positive response from the banned Joint Awami Action Committee to his letter proposing the establishment of a truth and reconciliation commission. He welcomed the committee’s willingness to engage with the proposed commission, describing it as “a possible institutional path forward”, and noted that the proposal had also been endorsed by the AJK Legislative Assembly.

Mr Bhutto-Zardari said he would study the committee’s proposals carefully before consulting AJK Prime Minister Raja Faisal Mumtaz Rathore, who would, in turn, approach the federal government and other stakeholders “to seek their initial views and assess whether sufficient common ground exists to take a consensus proposal forward”.
