World.title: How Trans-Caspian Cable Fits Kazakhstan’s Evolving Connectivity Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA — For decades, Kazakhstan’s connectivity strategy was measured in highways, railways and pipelines. Today, that vision is expanding. As global competition increasingly depends on the movement of data alongside the movement of goods, the country is investing in a new layer of strategic infrastructure — one designed not to carry cargo, but information.

Among the clearest examples of this shift is the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable project. The first-ever underwater telecommunications link across the Caspian Sea will connect Aktau and Sumqayit, creating a new digital corridor between Central Asia, the South Caucasus and Europe.

The project reflects a broader vision articulated by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who has increasingly framed Kazakhstan’s connectivity agenda as extending beyond physical transport routes to include cross-border digital infrastructure. In his September 2024 State of the Nation Address, he called for the project to be completed, describing it as essential for “creating a digital infrastructure linked with international corridors and cross-border data flows.”

Several months later, speaking at an informal meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Organization of Turkic States in Budapest, Tokayev expanded that vision beyond Kazakhstan.

“This project will significantly improve digital communication between our countries and will be a strategic step towards strengthening regional integration. Such initiatives open up opportunities to create a new digital corridor across the Eurasian continent,” he said.

The regional context continues to evolve. As the cable enters its final construction phase, regional leaders are once again gathering, this time in Cholpon-Ata for an informal Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, underscoring how cooperation between the countries increasingly extends across transport, energy and digital connectivity.

Nearly two years after Tokayev first identified the project as a strategic priority, it is entering its most tangible phase. Kazakhstan is now carrying out the final stages of the project, with commercial commissioning expected by the end of 2026. The latest phase has shifted from engineering preparation to offshore construction.

According to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development’s release from July 31, regulatory, customs and organizational procedures have been completed, including the approval of equipment required for the offshore works, allowing construction to proceed without administrative delays.

Preparatory work in 2025 included desktop and offshore engineering surveys, selection of the optimal route avoiding anchorage zones and military training areas, environmental approvals from the Mangystau Region authorities, and the production and factory testing in China of a specially armored submarine cable equipped with ROPA optical amplifiers.

With the planning phase complete, attention has shifted from engineering design to execution at sea. The cable, previously delivered from China to the port of Kuryk together with three cable baskets weighing a combined 600 tons, was transported to Baku aboard a specialized logistics vessel. It has now been transferred into the cable tank of the cable-laying vessel, which has departed Baku and is laying the line toward Aktau.

The operation is being carried out by a cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons and equipped with dynamic positioning technology to ensure precise installation on the seabed. Around 70 crew members are involved, including technical supervisors and representatives of Kazakhtelecom. The project is being implemented by CaspiLink B.V., the joint venture established by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom.

A dedicated jointing room has also been installed onboard to allow engineers to repair or reconnect the cable if required during installation. Both the Kazakh and Azerbaijani cable ends have already undergone testing. Subject to favorable weather conditions, installation of the submarine cable is expected to be completed within the next 15 to 20 days, while the overall commissioning process remains on schedule for completion by the end of 2026.

The significance of the project, however, extends well beyond the technical operation. As economies become more deeply integrated through both physical and digital infrastructure, international corridors are no longer defined solely by the goods they carry. They are increasingly shaped by the data they enable to move across borders. While the cable spans just 380 kilometers across the Caspian seabed, the vision behind it reaches much further. The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable reflects Kazakhstan’s ambition to remain an important link in the movement of both goods and data across Eurasia.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Air Taxis, Energy Security and Middle Corridor
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from international media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights the country’s plans to launch Central Asia’s first air taxi service, developments in energy security, transport connectivity and regional diplomacy.



Speaking alongside Putin, Kazakh President calls for freeze of Ukraine war

Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said on Saturday ​that a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine might be reached ‌if the sides froze the conflict and resumed negotiations, reported Reuters on July 25.

Speaking alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin at a Russia-Kazakhstan forum in the Siberian ​city of Omsk, Tokayev praised Putin’s “utmost diplomatic flexibility.”

“If I may offer my humble opinion, since I have been asked, perhaps it is time to freeze this conflict and return to the Istanbul formula 2.0,” he said.

Moscow ​and Kyiv participated in talks in Istanbul soon after Russia’s full-scale invasion in early 2022 and again in 2025, though the discussions failed ​to produce a breakthrough.

Tokayev proposes launching digital transport corridor between Kazakhstan and Russia

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed launching a pilot digital transport corridor between Kazakhstan and Russia to further develop logistics and boost bilateral trade, reported Trend on July 25.

According to the press service of the President of Kazakhstan, Tokayev made the proposal while addressing the 22nd Kazakhstan-Russia Interregional Cooperation Forum in Omsk.

The president said Kazakhstan and Russia have unique opportunities to shape Eurasia’s transport and logistics architecture.

“Kazakhstan and Russia, which share the world’s longest continuous land border, are destined to play a leading role in developing the transport and logistics architecture of the Eurasian continent,” Tokayev said.

US, Kazakhstan discuss energy security, Caspian oil exports

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Kazakh Foreign Minister Yermek Kosherbayev held high-level talks Wednesday on regional energy security and the stability of global oil supply chains, reported ED News on July 29.

“The two officials discussed the importance of energy security, including the reliable and uninterrupted export of Kazakhstan-origin oil via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), for regional stability and prosperity,” said State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott.

Rubio expressed gratitude for Kazakhstan’s support of US President Donald Trump’s peace initiatives and signaled interest in deeper economic ties, he added.

The Kazakh Foreign Ministry confirmed the conversation covered the “Enhanced Strategic Partnership” and preparations for Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s upcoming trip to the US for the G20 Summit in December.

Middle Corridor opens new route for Kazakh exports

Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) has organized the first-ever multimodal shipment of mineral fertilizers from the city of Ekibastuz to the United Kingdom, AzerNEWS reported on July 28.

The shipment is being carried via the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, using both rail and maritime transport. The cargo will travel through Kazakhstan, across the Caspian Sea, and onward through Azerbaijan and Georgia before being transported by sea from the ports of Poti and Batumi to the Port of Felixstowe in the United Kingdom.

The new route will enable Kazakhstan’s fertilizer producers to increase exports to the UK market. The use of the Middle Corridor will also help diversify logistics routes and ensure more reliable cargo deliveries.

Kazakhstan set to become first Central Asian country to launch air taxi service

Kazakhstan is preparing to become the first country in Central Asia to introduce electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) air taxis into its transport system, reported Reuters Connect on July 24.

“The Prosperity eVTOL aircraft, developed by Chinese manufacturer AutoFlight, was unveiled during a demonstration flight at the Kazanat Hippodrome in Astana. The event was organized by Kazakhstan’s Alatau Advanced Air Group (AAAG) in cooperation with AutoFlight.

The aircraft can carry one pilot and five passengers, reach speeds of up to 200 kilometers (124 miles) per hour, and travel about 200 kilometers (124 miles) on a single charge.

The air taxi service is expected to launch in Alatau, a new city being built from the ground up under Kazakhstan’s digital city concept,” reads the article.

World.title: Kazakhstan Joins Top Five Gold Buyers Amid Reserve Strategy Shift
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan ranked among the world’s five largest central bank gold buyers in the second quarter of 2026, purchasing 15 tons of the precious metal as monetary authorities worldwide accelerated efforts to strengthen reserves amid persistent geopolitical uncertainty and shifting global financial conditions.

According to the latest World Gold Council (WGC) report, the National Bank of Kazakhstan (NBK) was the fourth-largest purchaser globally during the quarter, behind only Poland (51 tons), China (33 tons) and Uzbekistan (16 tons). Jordan and the Czech Republic each added six tons, while Ghana, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and the Kyrgyz Republic made smaller purchases.

Kazakhstan’s acquisition came during a record quarter for central bank demand. Global official sector purchases reached 289 tons between April and June, the strongest second-quarter result on record and a sharp rebound from just 57 tons in the first quarter. The WGC attributes the recovery to a combination of geopolitical tensions, lower gold prices compared with first-quarter peaks, and central banks’ continued efforts to diversify reserve assets.

The trend appears far from temporary. According to a recent World Gold Council survey, 89% of central banks expect global official gold reserves to increase over the next year, while a record 45% plan to expand their own holdings.

For Kazakhstan, the latest purchases continue a long-term strategy rather than representing a short-term reaction to market volatility.

According to Amir Aktanov, an analyst at Halyk Finance’s Analytical Center, central banks have remained net buyers of gold for 15 consecutive years, purchasing more than 1,000 tons annually over the past three years. He also described sustained official demand as one of the key drivers behind the metal’s recent rally.

Kazakhstan has been one of the most consistent participants in that trend. Between 2011 and 2021, the National Bank steadily expanded its gold reserves, purchasing more than 335 tons over the decade. Although the regulator shifted its reserve management strategy in recent years, it also announced in February 2025 that it had suspended gold sales from its foreign exchange reserves, citing the complex geopolitical situation worldwide.

The renewed purchases in the second quarter suggest that reserve diversification remains a priority as policymakers seek assets perceived as resilient during periods of economic and geopolitical uncertainty. The broader gold market reflects the same dynamics.

Total global gold demand, including over-the-counter trading, remained stable year-on-year at 1,269 tons during the second quarter, while demand for the first half of 2026 increased 2% to 2,522 tons. In value terms, however, global demand reached a record $380 billion, highlighting the impact of elevated prices.

Kazakhstan’s position among the world’s largest buyers underscores both the strategic importance of gold in its reserve policy and the broader shift among central banks toward assets viewed as relatively insulated from geopolitical and financial shocks.

With official institutions expected to remain major buyers through the coming year, central bank demand is likely to continue providing structural support for gold prices, even as market attention shifts between inflation, interest rates and global political risks.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: Victoria Park masterplan for Brisbane 2032 unveiled
World.content:
Pedestrian bridges will link Victoria Park with the Brisbane CBD and National Aquatic Centre in a masterplan for the Olympic and Paralympic Games released today.

About two-thirds of the park will be green, public space under the draft for Victoria Park Precinct, part of a $7.1 billion infrastructure program joint-funded by the state and federal governments for Brisbane 2032.

It includes Brisbane Stadium, the National Aquatic Centre at Centenary Pool, upgrades to Brisbane Showgrounds and "expanded" parklands and public spaces.

An artist's impression of a deck pavilion looking over expanded Yorks Hollow. (Supplied: Queensland government)

Victoria Park was chosen for the new Games stadium by the Crisafulli government in 2025, a U-turn the premier acknowledged was the "only option".

It's been the target of ongoing protests which peaked earlier this year with the arrest of several activists who opposed its development because of cultural and historic ties.

Minister for the Games, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, said the plan would make the park more accessible.

"I think it will be more utilised than it has ever been seen before. Bearing in mind, two years ago this was a closed off golf course, that no-one in the community could utilise," Mr Bleijie said.

"I think the opportunity for community sport well after the Games is going to be more profound than has ever been the case before. It used to be a dump site, then it was a golf course, and we're opening it up and two-thirds will be available to the public use."

The government has promised the precinct will be accessible and connected to the rest of the city. (Supplied: Queensland government)

The government said it was investigating cycling and pedestrian links over the Inner City Bypass and rail corridor to link the precinct to the city and Fortitude Valley, and has promised it will be accessible to all "regardless of age, ability".

York's Hollow wetland will also be expanded and an "urban forest" planted to "soften" the landscape.

Consultation on the draft plan opens on Monday and runs until September 27.

World.title: Glorious athletics campaign ends in an empty stadium near midnight
World.content:
The final moment of celebration in Australia's glorious athletics campaign at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games was hilariously understated.

Approaching midnight, Lachlan Kennedy, Calab Law, Josh Azzopardi, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius finally walked onto the podium to receive their gold medals for the men's 4x100-metre relay.

The crowd had long since filed out of Scotstoun Stadium when the medal ceremony, which was supposed to happen two and a half hours earlier, kicked off.

The track and field that had hosted seven golds, five silvers and five bronze medals for Australia on a jam-packed day, had been leaf-blown, cleaned and stripped of most of its Games paraphernalia.

The stadium was empty when the medal ceremony took place. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Only a handful of volunteers, family, stadium crew, media members and team support staff remained to applaud the historic relay winners, Australia's first since 1974.

A protest by the initially disqualified Canadian team had finally succeeded, reinstating the Olympic champions to the silver medal spot and cutting short Ghanaian celebrations of bronze deep in the bowels of the Glasgow Warriors' rugby club home ground.

In a credit to organisers, the pyrotechnics still fired, the flags were still raised by military personnel in full regalia, and the anthem still played over the stadium PA.

Lachlan Kennedy, Josh Azzopardi, Calab Law, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius eventually got their moment. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Advance Australia Fair was sung even more drone-fully than usual without the safety of a crowd to hide the nasal tones of the Aussie accent, before the small gathering shuffled off the track.

It was a bizarrely low-key moment for one of the crowning achievements of this breakout meet for Team Australia, equalling the most medals won by the track and field team at a Commonwealth Games on foreign soil.

Of the 12 gold medals, 11 silver, and 11 bronzes, none sums up what the team has and can become more than this relay triumph.

Administrators, cheerleaders and athletes alike have been spruiking this new golden generation for Australian Athletics, which has pumped countless hours and very countable dollars into the nation's relays program in recent years.

Team Australia athletes pose for a photo after the women's and men's 4x100 metres relay finals on day nine of the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Paul Harding)

In the past four years, Commonwealth Games Australia invested $11.6 million into the Green2Gold2Great program.

That covered a wide range of athletes, with $500,000 dedicated to relays specifically.

In that time, Australia's teams have found some phenomenal success across a number of events.

In 2025, there were green and gold teams in all six events at the World Athletics Relays for the first time ever and the mixed 4x400m team won silver.

At this year's World Relays, the men's 4x400m picked up an Australian record and bronze.

Calab Law handed over to final runner Rohan Browning with Australia in first place. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

So well drilled are these teams that when it came time for the heats on the final morning of the athletics program, both the men's and women's teams could rest individual 100m medallists Kennedy and Torrie Lewis.

Azzopardi put aside his bitter disappointment at only being brought to Glasgow as a relay runner to contribute to the cause, describing the heats as "a training run".

That is a far cry from the team that missed out in Birmingham because Browning took a tumble in the heats.

They missed the 2024 Olympic final despite running faster heat times than the top three in the opposite heat, mucked up the final change in last year's world championships final, and missed a medal by just 0.24 of a second at World Relays in May.

This gold medal puts the world on notice, and there is still more room to grow.

Lachlan Kennedy, Joshua Azzopardi, Calab Law and Rohan Browning celebrate victory in the men's 4x100m relay final at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

It is a credit to the system and their confidence in it that they didn't rush Glasgow 100m finalist Eddie Nketia into the team, even for the heats, opting instead for quick-start specialist Ius to lead off.

Kennedy replaced him for the final, playing his role to perfection, handing off cleanly to Azzopardi deep in the box, before Law and Browning came home in 38.07.

"We knew what we had in us, we're training well, we compete domestically all year against each other, [so] we're pretty used to each other. I think it's a big part of why we're so successful. Train together all year, camps all year," Kennedy said.

Kennedy said there is no first and second squad in their team, but 1A and 1B, described as "green and gold" by Browning, who flagged the looming arrivals of Gout Gout and Nketia once they have more time to train with the team that now carries a golden aura.

"I hope there are kids at home tonight watching this who aspire to grow up and be part of this team," Browning said.

"Not just aspire to the baggy green or the Wallabies or the Australian AFL team, aspire to be part of the Australian relay team."

We have already seen glimpses of it, with former Cronulla Sharks under-17 player Zavier Peacock opting for the track and finishing second behind Gout at this year's junior Australian titles.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

And veteran Kurtis Marschall was spurred on by their performance.

The back-to-back-to-back Commonwealth Games pole vault champion started his competition first and finished last on a frigid summer's night in Glasgow, getting the chance to watch his teammates pick up medals as he made his way up to a Games record of 5.85m, claiming the last Aussie gold of the program.

"The system is working. The boys' relay tonight was just phenomenal. They inspired me to get over the line," he said.

"We just want to keep pushing this sport along more and more and more. It's the best sport in the world and deserves more eyes, so we're just doing our part."

The whole stadium was watching his crowning moment and while no-one saw "the boys" get theirs, they weren't there to see the work it took to get there either.

World.title: Young people suffer as data gaps limit understanding of pregnancy loss
World.content:
A new study has found pregnancy loss is common in Australia, but experts warn gaps in data may mean the unique needs of young people are not being addressed.

A first-of-its-kind study on miscarriage and pregnancy loss, released by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) on Wednesday, analysed data from five states and territories.

It found almost one in three women who gave birth in 2022 had previously experienced at least one miscarriage. One in 10 had experienced two or more.

Previous estimates found between one in four and one in five pregnancies ended in loss.

If you or someone you know needs help: Red Nose Grief and Loss 24/7 Support Line on 1300 308 307

Grief and Loss 24/7 Support Line on 1300 308 307 Pregnancy, Birth and Baby (advice from maternal child health nurses) on 1800 882 436

(advice from maternal child health nurses) on 1800 882 436 PANDA (Perinatal Anxiety and Depression Australia) on 1300 726 306

(Perinatal Anxiety and Depression Australia) on 1300 726 306 Bears of Hope (infant loss support for families) on 1300 114 673

While the scoping study sheds light on the prevalence of pregnancy loss, and that loss before 20 weeks' gestation is common, the data does not break down the experiences by demographic group or geographic location.

There is currently no routine national collection and monitoring of pregnancy loss data.

"Gaps in national data on pregnancy loss prevalence and care mean there's still much to learn about these experiences," AIHW spokesperson Deanna Eldridge said.

"There is a lot more work to be done. This is a scoping study, but this is just an amazingly important first step," co-founder and executive director of the Early Pregnancy Loss Coalition, Isabelle Oderberg, said.

Young people's experience of pregnancy loss

While the data does not provide an insight into how common pregnancy loss is for younger Australians, Ms Oderberg said there was anecdotal evidence to suggest this type of loss impacted younger people differently.

"I think that miscarriage is so often dismissed in general. But I think when you're younger and a medical professional sees you as not necessarily being at the end of your reproductive journey, they tend to be even more dismissive," Ms Oderberg said.

Loading...

Well-meaning but ultimately unhelpful sentiments around a person's age and ability to have children in the future can make younger people feel like their loss is not real or is not worthy of grieving.

"Language is often the only tool we have to remove the silence around grief because we can use our words to acknowledge the loss and its impact," Marjolein Kammers, from the University of Queensland's School of Psychology, said.

"At the same time, language is also often the very thing that creates the silence by diminishing or dismissing the emotional impact, for example, 'You are young, you can try again,'" Dr Kammers said.

" Pregnancy loss is the real loss of a developing baby as well as the loss of hopes and dreams … The language we choose can either validate that experience or silence it. "

Laura Baxter experienced this firsthand after going through a miscarriage when she was 24 years old. She was using the contraceptive pill and did not realise she was pregnant when she started experiencing heavy bleeding and extreme pain.

Loading TikTok content

"It was a whole different level of pain, and I collapsed to the floor," Ms Baxter said.

She eventually got an appointment to see her regular GP, who ordered a scan.

"Straight away she said, 'Okay, so you've had a miscarriage. We know this because we found', and I quote, 'retained products of conception on the scan,'" Ms Baxter said.

Ms Baxter said her doctor treated her miscarriage as a routine occurrence, and when Ms Baxter became emotional, told her, "I guess it is a little bit of a loss in some way."

She said she was told to "have a bleed" to remove the residual tissue, and was reassured that she was young and should be able to conceive again when she was ready.

Ms Baxter said the experience left her feeling dismissed and like her miscarriage had been minimised.

"From that experience with my GP, I felt like I shouldn't be grieving, that I should just move on," she said.

Lack of awareness in young people

TV personality Alex Crisp did not know much about miscarriage until she experienced her own.

"It wasn't until I was 29 when I had my first conversation about miscarriage because a good girlfriend of mine had gone through it," she said.

Alex Crisp did not know how common miscarriages were until she experienced pregnancy loss. (Supplied)

She decided to post on social media about her loss, in an effort to "open up a conversation" on miscarriage.

" We should be normalising this discussion. I think there are so many people who suffer in silence. "

Her post gained traction, and Ms Crisp said she received messages from people all over the world who had experienced pregnancy loss, or who simply wanted to send their well-wishes.

While her loss was still raw, Ms Crisp said the reaction was not expected, but had helped her heal.

" In the weirdest way, it really helped in my grieving. "

She believed young people's openness on social media, and their willingness to address trauma, would create lasting change.

"Social media can absolutely open the door for that kind of conversation for people who feel like they don't have that [support] in their life," Ms Crisp said.

"It's almost as if we wait until this [pregnancy loss] happens to us that we talk about it, and I think we need to shift that mentality."

World.title: Garma land council announcement sparks concern in region
World.content:
The announcement of a new remote Northern Territory land council has taken some Yolŋu leaders by surprise, with a key clan group elder initially rejecting the prospect of taking part.

Yothu Yindi Foundation chairman and Gumatj elder Djawa Yunupiŋu yesterday made the bold announcement at the Garma Festival of the plan to create the new Dilak Land Council.

"This land council is the vision of our elders who knew one day, when the time was right, the power would be brought back fully into the hands of the land owners," he said.

The announcement came on the 50th anniversary of the federal Aboriginal Land Rights Act, and would mark the first new land council to be formed in the NT in about 35 years.

If the Dilak Land Council comes to fruition, it will be a breakaway from the powerful Northern Land Council (NLC), which controls mining royalty distribution across the Top End.

Mr Yunupiŋu pledged the new council would still work in partnership with the NLC.

Djawa Yunupiŋu announced a land council to be led by the Dilak of north-east Arnhem land. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

In reaction to the announcement, an elder of another of the Gove Peninsula's leading clan groups, the Rirratjiŋu, has told the ABC he would not join the new council.

"I'm not happy and I'm not going to it," Rirratjiŋu Aboriginal Corporation chairman Wanyubi Marika said.

"I have to go back to my lawyers and find a way how to work on this. At the moment I don't agree with it, I just stick to the Rirratjiŋu current Northern Land Council program and support to Rirratjiŋu."

'Top of the mountain': New breakaway land council announced at Garma Fifty years since the creation of the Aboriginal Land Rights Act, a major shake-up of the land rights system has been announced at the Garma Festival.

The Gumatj and Rirratjiŋu clans have had a tense modern history together, and had been caught up in years-long court battles over the division of mining royalties in the region.

While those tensions have been healing in recent years, Mr Marika said he felt "frustrated and confused" by the latest move, and criticised what he said was a lack of consultation.

"This thing was thrown into my face, like an ambush," he said.

"I don't want to be surprised like that, because I never went through those discussions in the past. That kind of surprise is not accepted by me, or by the Rirratjiŋu clan.

"I will be open [to consultations], but I will not agree from Rirratjiŋu point of view.

"Because, strongly, we, in a power under the Northern Land Council, and under the Land Rights Act, we have more power, control over our land and for development and for working with our government and stakeholders … and not other clan groups that are involved."

Mr Yunupiŋu said in a further statement that Mr Marika and other Rirratjiŋu elders were consulted over the new land council prospect as were all of Gove's 13 clan groups.

"We will continue to engage with all the other clans as we progress this important work," he said.

Yiŋiya Guyula has also voiced some concerns over the new Dilak Land Council proposal. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Arnhem Land politician voices concern

Another senior Yolŋu elder and local leader, independent NT politician and Djambarrpuyŋu clan elder Yiŋiya Guyula, has also voiced some concerns over the new Dilak Land Council proposal.

"I've not been included in these current discussions of a new land council announced at Garma and neither have my clan elders," he said.

"The name Dilak is something that is worrying for me because we need to make sure that a new land council is inclusive of all Yolŋu, and the Dilak Council is a group currently associated with the Miwatj area in the eastern part of our Yolŋu country and we need to have a close look at who is included in this land council and who is creating the foundation for a very powerful new body.

"There are many clans across Yolŋu country.

"We need to create equality for all Yolŋu clans and we don't want to fall into a trap of a new land council that is not truly representative of Yolŋu rom [law]."

However, Mr Guyula also said that he would back a Yolŋu-run land council for the region.

"I am very interested to hear more," he said.

"I am supportive of a Yolŋu land council but this process needs to come under the Yolŋu system of law, led by our people, and inclusive of all our clans without balanda [non-Indigenous people] influence or control in the background."

Malarndirri McCarthy says the looming closure of a Rio Tinto mine will bring big changes to north-east Arnhem Land. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Formal process still to go through

Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy would have to sign off on a formal proposal to authorise the creation of the Dilak Land Council before it could happen.

Yesterday she said she was yet to receive such a proposal.

Ms McCarthy also acknowledged that Mr Yunupiŋu's family had been speaking about the prospect of a new land council for many years, and said the announcement was respectful.

"There was absolute respect and I think that was important too, because they know that there's still many steps to go before anything is official," she said.

The announcement of the land council comes at a precarious time for the Gove Peninsula, as the region prepares for the end of its major employer, a Rio Tinto bauxite mine, in 2029.

Also during the Garma Festival, NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro announced that an "in-principle" agreement had been made with the Rirratjiŋu clan, which would ensure the town lease of Nhulunbuy would be handed back to the Rirratjiŋu after the end of the mine.

World.title: Love story: We brought home three orphaned children on the same day
World.content:
Mark and Anna Dombkins were a young married couple, enjoying life with their six-month-old son in Wollongong/Dharawal lands, when a show documenting the horrors of an international orphanage changed the trajectory of their lives.

It compelled the pair to move overseas and adopt displaced children into their own loving and growing family.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

We had no idea what our family would become

Anna: Mark and I met at our church youth group.

He was just such a good human that I started to be like, "OK, this could be serious, he could be the one."

We did talk about wanting to have kids, we wanted to have a bigger family, which to us kind of meant maybe three or four biological children.

Loading...

Mark: When I met Anna, we were probably 16, and I just remember thinking, "she's beautiful and such a kind, endearing, warm person".

We both came from families where we had one sibling.

A mutual friend we had — there were five kids in his family — and I used to go to his place after school all the time, and it'd be a riot, it was so much fun.

I really liked the idea of a big family.

We needed to do something

Anna: Our son Jackson was six months old when we stumbled across a documentary called The Dying Rooms.

It was created by some journalists who went into orphanages in China and took a hidden camera.

We saw not just one room, but rooms and rooms full of babies who were never held and never picked up by anybody.

And there we were with this one little baby who was so loved, and there was always a line-up of people ready to hold him.

It just broke our heart.

It was just a very clear moment where we sat there thinking, "OK, we need to do something."

That's when we really just decided to grow our family in part through adoption.

Why don't we move to Africa?

Anna: We spent three years trying to adopt a child in Australia and we hadn't even been approved to start on the seven-year waiting list yet.

By that stage we were delighted to have another baby of our own, Jemima.

Mark and I were walking along the beach one day and I said to Mark, "what if we just move to Africa?"

And he just said, "yes, let's do that."

Between that conversation and landing in Tanzania was about six months, so it was a whirlwind.

Tanzania just ticked all the boxes; it was safe for us to live in with two young children, it was a place we could both work [Mark as a teacher and me as a school counsellor] and live, and we could legally adopt as Australians.

Finding the [particular] baby home was one of the things that led us to Tanzania because our big priority was finding children who were legitimately abandoned and where the processes were honourable and ethical.

Anna lived in Tanzania for three years. (Supplied)

Mark: I didn't want to get old in 20 years, look back and go, "we both felt strongly about this thing, but we just didn't have the guts to make it happen.

So, relocating to Africa, it was almost a relief that Anna would suggest it.

Reading the stories from the baby home [we found] and what the team there were aspiring to do, which was keep biological families together wherever possible, was also such a relief.

Because our intention was to do something good, but we didn't want good intentions to have bad impacts that we weren't aware of.

We brought home three of them on that one day

Anna: We'd been in Tanzania a couple of months when we got an email about a set of twins who needed a family.

The baby home had gone through the processes to try and find other ways they could be reunified with their biological family and those had all failed.

I remember just seeing Shay and Charlie in this sea of other babies. Jemima and I sat with them, and the connection was pretty immediate.

Then as we spent time with Amy, who ran the baby home, she told us that the twins actually had a brother [Jabari] who was only nine months older.

He was so malnourished, he wasn't likely to survive.

And really, she was saying, "can you take him home?"

Anna and Mark adopted twins Shay and Charlie, and their older brother Jabari. (Supplied)

So, we brought home the three of them on that one day.

We then had one four-year-old and four one-year-olds at home.

But it was just the most beautiful thing watching two sets of siblings come together and make a family.

And watching Jabari, the brother who was so unwell, come to life before our eyes with good food and love and care, was just incredible.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

Baby number six was on the way

Anna: We spent three years in Tanzania before we moved back to Australia.

Max was born when the family of seven returned to live in Australia. (Supplied)

We'd been home two weeks when I started feeling really tired.

And then we discovered baby number six was on the way.

It was crazy timing, but it was something we look back on now and think we never would have planned that, but it was so perfect.

Having Max just bookended our family in a way that allowed Shay, Jabari and Charlie to also welcome another child.

It's their story now, we get to cheer them on

Mark: A big family is both exhausting and so rewarding — it is beautiful chaos.

You see through their eyes, like the innocence and just the beautiful naivety of kids where they don't see colour and they don't see all the things that the world sees.

Anna and Mark with their children, (from left) Jabari, Shay, Max, Jemima, Charlie and Jackson. (Supplied)

Just learning about their love in all the most beautiful ways just really grounds and teaches you as an adult.

And to have gone on that journey with [Anna], the person I love and my best friend … and being truly known by someone and knowing someone in that way through the highs and lows ... it's just made it even more special.

Anna: They make us better and yes, we have helped them, but really our other children are so blessed by having them in our family as well.

They have a broader perspective.

They have a deeper emotional capacity, and their world has expanded by having the family that we have.

It's a wild ride and it takes everything we have every day, but there's so much joy in it.

Anna and Mark's foundation, Forever Projects, is working to end the orphan crisis in Tanzania through income creation for women. (Supplied)

Mark and I have been each other's support through it all and we see each other's best and worst self.

And we're there for each other through it all.

We don't know what the future holds for our kids, but we just can't wait to watch.

It's their story now and we just get to cheer them on and watch.

World.title: Teenage boy dies after being struck by two cars on Hindley Street
World.content:
A teenage boy has died after being struck by a car in Adelaide's CBD last night.

SA Police said the man was hit by a car before falling into the path of a four-wheel-drive on Hindley Street.

The Greenwith man was rushed to hospital, but died shortly after.

Police said emergency services were called to the popular city nightlife area close to 11PM on Saturday night.

Hindley Street was closed while police managed the scene.

Major Crash Investigators also attended to examine the circumstances around the incident.

The crash occurred on Hindley Street, Adelaide CBD. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

The street was reopened around 2:15 AM on Sunday morning.

Police are urging anyone who witnessed the crash and who hasn't yet spoken to them to contact Crime Stoppers.

The man's death was the 70th life lost on SA roads this year.

World.title: After javelin gold, Aussie star heads straight back to hospital work
World.content:
Sydney doctor Mackenzie Little has finally become a golden girl with the javelin as she led one last parade of Commonwealth Games field event medallists in the green and gold.

The remarkable 29-year-old Little, a doctor at Northern Beaches Hospital, can barely even call herself a part-time athlete these days, such is her busy medical life, but she still proved too good for her opponents as she finally lifted a major international title.

She nailed victory with her first throw and then revealed she will be jetting straight back to work on Tuesday as an ear, nose and throat registrar.

On a night when pole vaulter Kurtis Marschall completed Australia's golden track-and-field program by soaring to a Games-record 5.85 metres and a third-straight title, Little's achievement felt even more astonishing.

"I'm so I'm relieved and excited — this is so fantastic. Nailing the first throw is maybe something to do with how my training's been a bit quality over quantity in the last couple of years," she said.

"I wish I could say, you know, that I'm really, really training my butt off, but I'm just having to fit things in around my job. I'm having to make the most of sometimes challenging situations, not having all the time in the world.

"I perform surgeries and see outpatients in clinics and take care of patients who are in the ward sick in hospital. Then in the evenings, I'll get to training, but I've had to change my training locations this year to stay within 30 minutes of the hospital. When you're on call, you need to — overnight and in the evenings — be within 30 minutes of the hospital in case of emergencies.

"I'm gonna go and fly home straight away and get back to work."

On a tricky night for throwers in the Scotstoun Stadium on the last evening of track and field competition, Little believed her technique of throwing low and hard to cut through the wind helped her to a season best 61.88m with an opener that no-one else threatened.

New Zealand silver medallist Tori Moorby hurled 60.08m in the third round to grab the silver, while Kenya's Irene Jepkemboi took the bronze.

Kurtis Marschall reacts after securing his third Commonwealth Games gold medal in the pole vault. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Marschall, winner at both the Gold Coast and Birmingham Commonwealth Games, finished the night in style by becoming only the third Australian ever to win three titles in a row in the same event, and ending with a leap that surpassed his hero Steve Hooker's 5.80m in Melbourne 20 years ago.

Entering the competition late, the hot favourite from Adelaide held his nerve to defeat South African silver medallist Kyle Rademeyer and England's bronze winner Owen Heard (both 5.70m).

It was the latest big achievement for the 29-year-old, who earlier in the season handed a once-in-a-blue-moon defeat to the sport's modern-day legend, Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis.

"I just wanted to solidify myself in the record books, like I already did with the gold medal, but I definitely wanted to jump that 5.85 and take it off Steve," Marschall said.

Brooke Buschkuehl in action and on her way to bronze in the long jump. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Melbourne's Brooke Buschkuehl, the indefatigable 33-year-old mum, also made it a hat-trick of medals, but again missed out on the one she really wanted as she added a bronze in the long jump to go with her two silvers from Gold Coast and Birmingham.

Promising Wollongong teenager Delta Amidzovski, the 19-year-old world junior long jump champion, finished fourth, just five centimetres off a podium place.

World.title: WA Labor and Liberals battle it out over Karnup train station promise
World.content:
NationalWAPublic transport WA Labor and Liberals battle it out over Karnup train station promise Hannah Murphy August 2, 2026 — 12:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state government has announced it will build and open a new train station in Perth’s outer suburbs as it fights to keep its hold on Secret Harbour ahead of the upcoming byelection. Premier Roger Cook announced the $156 million train station for Karnup on Sunday, with Transport Minister Rita Saffioti confirming she would be allocating $10 million to begin planning the station. Mock ups of the Karnup Station posted on the Building for Tomorrow website. Building for Tomorrow Karnup is in the Secret Harbour electorate, which used to be held by WA Defence Minister Paul Papalia before he announced his retirement last month. Running in his place is Labor candidate Georgia Tree, who previously came under fire for living outside of the electorate. She has since moved in with family to stay inside her voter base. Karnup train station was first flagged for the Mandurah Line back in 2013, and has faced extensive delays since.



Related Article Metronet ‘We like to win’: Saffioti and Hastie go head-to-head over Lakelands station Cook said on Sunday population growth in the southern suburb meant the Karnup train station was now top of their agenda. “As part of our long-term MetroNet vision, we have always planned for a train station here at Karnup, and today we can announce work will start on the Karnup train station project in 2028,” he said. Cook said WA’s share of the project would be funded by land sales, while they would seek the other half from the federal government. Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said the train station was “always part of the plan”, but accepted the project had been sped up by the upcoming byelection.



“In relation to the timing, look, we would probably have made this announcement over the next six to eight months, but of course we have bought that announcement early,” she said. “Because we have got so much certainty now with the planning ... it’s all coming together.” An artist impression of a proposed new Karnup development, which is expected to bring thousands of new residents to the suburb south of Perth requiring access to rail. Saffioti said the project had been initially held up due to zoning laws and funding issues, due to the prioritisation of the nearby Lakelands train station. Ultimately, Saffioti said the station would be an “elevated design” with more than 400 car parking pays and an eight bus interchange.



The Labor government’s announcement comes just five days after opposition leader Basil Zempilas said he would be looking to revive the project if elected. Related Article WA election Secret Harbour byelection heating up as One Nation announces candidate “Labor promised Karnup Station in 2013, again in 2017 and again in 2021. Nearly a decade after Labor came to government, there is still no money in the State Budget, no construction timetable and no delivery date,” he said. “Locals have waited long enough. They deserve a firm commitment, not another promise designed to get Labor through an election.” Zempilas said the Liberals would commit $90 million to the project and commence building in 2029, and Saffioti slammed the figure as “undercosting”.



“There’s no way they’ll deliver it for $90 million,” she said. “Look, they said they’ll deliver an Ellenbrook rail line in 2008, and they never did. They said they’ll deliver max light rail. They came out with a under-costed ‘back of the envelope’ commitment.” Liberal local candidate Ryan Robertson offered his own support for the project, but said only his party had listened to residents about what they wanted from the train station. City of Rockingham councillor Ryan Robertson is WA Liberal’s candidate for Secret Harbour. Facebook/Ryan Robertson “People in Secret Harbour and surrounding suburbs are tired of being told Karnup station is coming,” Mr Robertson said.



“They have watched Labor make the same promise election after election while the station has remained unfunded and undelivered. “Karnup station is essential infrastructure for the future of this fast-growing community.”

World.title: ‘Sad for politics’: ICAC probe isn’t a ‘boon’ for Labor, says Minns
World.content:
NationalNSWOperation Rosny ‘Sad for politics’: ICAC probe isn’t a ‘boon’ for Labor, says Minns Mostafa Rachwani August 2, 2026 — 12:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW Premier Chris Minns has waved away any benefits Labor may gain from the week’s explosive ICAC revelations into dealings within the NSW Liberal Party. The inquiry has spent the past week digging into links between the NSW Liberals, Catholic Schools NSW and business figures in Sydney. Only two of the 10 persons of interest have appeared so far. Premier Chris Minns has waved away any benefit his party may derive from ICAC’s Operation Rosny. Sitthixay Ditthavong And despite a week of incisive questions surrounding how the Reformers, a group of the party’s conservative religious faction, received and used their funding, the premier has remained diplomatic. Asked if the inquiry was a “gift” to Labor ahead of the state election in March, Minns pointed to a surge in support for One Nation as a potentially “worrying” consequence.



“It’s interesting and perhaps worrying for me that over the same time that this inquiry has been taking place, One Nation’s vote has skyrocketed, and they’ve got nothing to do with this ICAC investigation,” Minns said on Sunday. “My concern is that people say, ‘Well, I’ve seen Labor at ICAC, and I’ve seen the Liberal Party at ICAC. I’m going to vote for a third party this time.’” Loading “So I don’t think it’s necessarily the big boon for our political party that many believe.” Speaking outside the North Cronulla Surf Life Saving Club to announce a $10 million investment in the club’s facilities, Minns looked to maintain a stoic position on the inquiry.



“I’ve been reluctant to offer a long-running commentary about it because I feel like this is an independent process, an independent inquiry,” he said. “I also think it’s sad for politics when people who are in elected positions are acting in this way because it casts a pall over all of us, everybody in politics.” Asked if, after watching the inquiry probe whether the group at the centre of the inquiry misappropriated funding or broke fundraising rules, the premier could only say the government would “monitor that”. It comes as the federal Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume has insisted the inquiry was “distant” from Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.



Taylor became embroiled in the scandal after one of the witnesses, former NSW Liberal Party staffer Dylan Whitelaw, claimed he had agreed to a donation to support the Reformer’s activities. Taylor is not directly involved in the inquiry and he is not a person of interest. Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume. Dominic Lorrimer He has repeatedly declared that “no payments were made” to the NSW Reformers. Hume doubled down, telling ABC’s Insiders that the issue is “distant” from Taylor and that ICAC should “be allowed to go through its processes free of political interference”.



Related Investigation

Investigation Inside Operation Rosny She went on to admit she didn’t “actually understand” the activities of the Reformers, but added that “each of our state divisions should be undertaking a review of its own constitution and its own membership to make sure that we are the fighting fit, electoral machine that we should be in the lead up to both state and federal elections.” Pressed on whether she would condemn the groups’ activities, Hume said it was a matter for ICAC in NSW and that she was “a Victorian”.
