World.title: Multiple people killed in shooting at Idaho burger restaurant
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMass shooting Multiple people killed in shooting at Idaho burger restaurant Rebecca Boone and Martha Belleisle Updated August 2, 2026 — 11:36am ,first published 10:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twin Falls, Idaho: A shooting at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant in southern Idaho in the US has left multiple people dead and others injured, police say. The shooter is among the dead, Twin Falls police chief Matthew Hicks said in a news conference. Police are still trying to determine the shooter’s identity and motive. “We believe the threat to the community is over,” Hicks said, adding that he did not yet know exactly how many were killed or wounded, and officials were still in the process of notifying next of kin. “It was a very chaotic scene.” A still image captured from video by a witness shows the scene of a shooting that started at an In-N-Out Burger restaurant. Kevin Bell Jr. via AP At least three people were killed and two were injured, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed officials, though it was unclear whether the shooter was included in those fatalities.



The number of victims is “expected to be higher,” city spokesperson Josh Palmer told the Times. Lane Koehn, 34, said he was at a red light near the In-N-Out restaurant when he saw a person with an AR-style rifle emerge from the drive-thru. A man with a pistol started firing at the shooter. He then saw someone in an In-N-Out uniform drag a person, also uniformed, bleeding from a gunshot wound in her chest across the car park. The employee, Koehn and the man with the pistol stayed until paramedics arrived for her. “She was pretty bad off, but I don’t know. I hope she made it,” Koehn said.



Koehn said he was told by the police to evacuate because the shooter was still active. He said the shooter fired at least three or four rounds, and it was not clear whether or not anyone in particular was targeted. Shooter dressed in black Video taken by a driver from across the street captured a shooter, who appeared to be dressed in black, walking up to a white car carrying a long rifle, opening the driver-side door and the boot. The person then walked to the boot and reached inside. At that point, the driver who shot the video left, fearing that the man might be getting more weapons.



Twin Falls resident Haley Dodaro, 43, and her mother went to In-N-Out for lunch on Saturday afternoon. While waiting in the drive-thru line, they saw people running across the road and workers bolting out of the restaurant. At first, Dodaro thought there might have been a fire, but then a man directing traffic in a reflective vest said there was a shooter. Police and fire crews respond to the shooting in Twin Falls. KMVT via AP “So that’s when we knew there was a shooting. People were running out, crying and screaming. It was very scary,” Dodaro said in a text message to the Associated Press. The nearby Magic Valley Mall was closed, and people had been told to shelter inside, according to an employee who spoke to NBC News. “We are currently in a lockdown,” he said. “There has been a mass shooting.”



St Luke’s Magic Valley spokesperson Taylor Marschner said in a statement that the medical centre was “working closely with law enforcement and emergency responders as they manage the situation”. Twin Falls, a city of about 56,000 people, is about 205 kilometres south-east of Boise and about 120 kilometres north of the Nevada border. According to the London Telegraph, the Twin Falls branch of In-N-Out Burger opened only nine days ago, with local residents queuing overnight to be among the first to eat there. World.title: ‘Find something that I can prove is Greg’: Family makes fresh appeal in 1989 cold case
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaMissing person ‘Find something that I can prove is Greg’: Family makes fresh appeal in 1989 cold case Carolyn Webb August 2, 2026 — 11:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When they were growing up on a farm near Portland, in western Victoria, Paul Delaney and brother Greg were best mates. They fought like siblings do, but every day they would be out riding motorbikes or horses, or playing tennis. “We did everything together,” Paul says. Pamela Delaney with two of her sons, Brendan (left) and Paul, in front of their former house in St Albans Park. In 1989, the area was part of Whittington. Eddie Jim Greg is often in Paul’s thoughts, but no longer in his life. On July 12, 1989, Greg vanished from the family home in Geelong. He was 21 years old.



On Sunday, as part of National Missing Persons Week – August 2-8 – the Delaneys are making what Paul terms “a last-ditch effort” to find out what happened, although they no longer believe Greg is alive. Paul and their mother, Pamela, want anyone with information on the disappearance to come forward. Newspaper clippings kept by the Delaney family about Greg’s disappearance. Eddie Jim “I’ve said to the police, find me a finger, something that I can prove is Greg, and I can bury it and say, ‘goodnight, goodbye’,” Pamela says. In July 1989, Greg was working as a chef at Greenmount resort on the Gold Coast in Queensland, but had flown back to Victoria to visit his family in the Geelong suburb of Whittington, now called St Albans Park, where they’d moved in 1988.



Greg spent the night of July 11 drinking and watching television in the Ottoman Court house. Paul remembers waking at 3am or 4am to find Greg in the lounge, ranting to himself. Paul says he told Greg to go for a walk, to sober up. Greg tripped over a lamp. The noise woke their father, Paddy, who came out and swore. Greg walked out of the house. Greg Delaney (left) as a young man and an Australian Federal Police image of what he might look like now, aged 58. The next night, when Greg didn’t return, police were called. Searches found nothing. Greg was described as 165 centimetres with a medium build, brown hair, blue eyes and a fair complexion. He was last seen wearing blue jeans, white Adidas sneakers and a jumper with black and white squares.



Paul says Greg might have hitchhiked to see his girlfriend in northern NSW. This was months before serial killer Ivan Milat is known to have murdered hitchhikers he picked up on the Hume Highway west of Sydney. Paul fears that this is what happened to Greg. The last known photo taken of Greg Delaney (far right), at lunch the day before he walked out of his family home. The Australian Federal Police have released a new image of what Greg might look like today, age 58, if still alive. Detective Leading Senior Constable Mark Woodhead, from the Geelong crime investigation unit, says: “This investigation remains open so if anyone has any information, no matter how small, now is the time to come forward.”



Greg’s father, Paddy, died in 2003. Pamela says that if Greg was alive, he “would have been in touch with me”. Tears still come when she talks about the eldest of her four sons. She wants to solve this mystery. “Everyone knows he’s gone. But we’d love to have a grave to visit,” she says. Anyone with information is urged contact Crime Stoppers at 1800 333 000 or submit a confidential report at www.crimestoppersvic.com.au. World.title: Four portable power banks that go the extra mile
World.content:
TechnologyGadgets Four portable power banks that go the extra mile Tim Biggs August 2, 2026 — 11:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The stress of carrying around battery-powered tech and not being sure when you’ll find the next wall plug is real. And though there are heaps of power banks available on the market, picking one you can rely on isn’t straightforward. When weighing up a portable battery it’s vital to choose a good brand, but you’re also looking to strike a balance between capacity, ports, size, speed and price, with each given different weight depending on your needs. Commonly, you can find compact units that hold 10,000mAh, charge at up to 30W, and cost about $70. That’s reasonable value for keeping a phone topped up all weekend, but below are four notably well-built premium units I have tested and recommend, that will give you a little extra. The all-rounder Odds are you won’t need 100W most of the time, but it is nice to have. I used the P63 to charge my MacBook Pro at full speed from very low to completely full in a couple of hours, while working, and it used less than half of the bank’s stored power. You can be assured your phone and most other devices will charge at their full speed from the main USB-C port, whether it’s an iPhone that takes 40W, a handheld gaming console that takes 65W, or a laptop that takes 90W.



If you’re mainly concerned about one device, this is a brilliant bank; it fills fast when you plug it into the wall, and has enough capacity to totally replenish your phone four or five times. But it will also happily charge multiple devices. You can charge two USB-C devices at up to 65W and 45W, or one USB-C and one USB-A at 65W and 18W. Charging three at a time clearly tests the limits of the bank though. The main port will still give 65W, but the other two get the bare minimum. And the unit will get hot. The P63 looks and feels nice, which is unusual for a power bank, though it is a massive fingerprint magnet. A glossy panel gives the impression of a big screen, but in truth there’s only a simple display underneath that shows the percentage battery left. What appears at first to be a corded lanyard is actually a short USB-C cable in disguise, one which is capable of carrying the full 100W. It’s a clever way to prevent you from forgetting a cable but, although it feels well-made, I’m hesitant to put any kind of stress on a power cable, so I wouldn’t hang it off anything. The magnetic option Simply snapping a magnetic charger to your phone when needed is a lot tidier than plugging in a cable. I primarily tested the 10,000mAh Fortix model, which had plenty of juice to fully charge my phone twice with some left over. It attached solidly, and was big enough that I could grip it like a pop socket, but it also made the phone quite bulky. If you want to keep using the phone as normal while you charge, a slimmer option like the $80 5000mAh Fortix might be better. There are number of these designs on the market, including one made by Apple specifically for its iPhone Air, and most (including this one) have both a magnetic charger and a USB-C. There are also many that feel a bit thin and flexy though, which you don’t want in a battery.



The 15W wireless charge speed is below the MagSafe maximum of 25W, but I found I was happy to start charging sooner and keep charging longer because I didn’t have to sit down with a bulky pack and a cable, or banish my phone to my backpack. If you have earbuds or other devices that can charge wirelessly (MagSafe AirPods are especially good here) you can top them up wirelessly with the Fortix while you sit at a cafe. But you can also just use a cable, and you’ll get a slightly faster 20W. If you do two devices at once, both will have greatly reduced speeds, but it works. In addition to iPhone, these will also work on any Qi2 Android phone. I tested them on a Google 10 Pro and they worked perfectly. On Samsung phones, because of the low camera bump, I had to tilt the battery a little, which doesn’t affect performance but is not ideal. While there are cheaper magnetic battery banks out there, these are the most solid-feeling I’ve used. And I do appreciate that they are made with a cutting edge semi-solid state battery design, meaning they have minimal liquid content (so much less danger of fires) and should last for thousands more charges than an equivalent lithium-ion battery. One downside of the overall design is the lack of a screen; you only have a little row of LED dots to show how much juice you have left. The wall plug The BoostCharge Hybrid looks and works like any other travel charger; it’s a big black brick with one USB-C, one USB-A and easily removable prongs (it comes with all the regions so you can take it overseas with no adapter). When plugged into your wall it’s a 25W charger. However, it’s also got a 5000mAh battery stored inside, so it will continue charging the connected devices at a maximum of 20W when you unplug it from the wall. Of course none of these numbers stack up to the beefiest dedicated batteries, but this is also a legitimately pocketable device. And it may seem like a minor thing, but having the one fist-sized device act as a charging brick and a portable battery bank can be really convenient.



As you move around from place to place you plug it into a wall socket when you can — it will top up any attached device first and then fill up its internal battery — and then you just put it in your pocket when you need to leave and your device will continue charging. I also find myself using this device at home surprisingly often, which isn’t something I can say for any other battery bank, because it’s always plugged in and full. I have a big 100W charger at my desk for topping up gadgets, but if I happen to need something in another room and the battery is dead (often a tablet, headphones or a game controller), I’ll plug it into this charger and then take it with me. The obvious trade-off is that you could get much faster charging and more battery capacity if you used two separate devices. And of course if you had a battery bank plus a charger with multiple USB-C ports, you’d be able to top up your phone and battery significantly quicker when you found an outlet. But the selling point here is an all-in one solution at the expense of some speed. The overkill scenario It may not be pocketable, but the Prime’s thin brick shape makes it easy enough to grip and carry. It looks like a premium product, and if you have a work set-up that might demand heavy charging (say a laptop plus a phone), it’s a sleek power source that won’t take up much room. The 100W input means you can half-fill the bank in less than half an hour, assuming a strong enough wall plug, and then you can use that stored energy to charge two USB-C devices simultaneously at up to 100W each. Either port can boost to 140W if you’re only charging a single device. There’s also a USB-A that gets 20W if both the USB-Cs are full, or 22.5W otherwise. Yes, if you’re doing the maths, that’s a total 220W maximum output. And yes, it does get warm.



Another big benefit is the colour screen on the front, which you can cycle between an overview display showing remaining battery, one showing the exact wattage going through each of the three ports, and one showing the temperature. Being able to see power stats at a glance can be helpful if you’re not sure you’re getting the full speed, maybe because of a lower-spec cable or a device’s settings. This power bank also has Bluetooth for use with Anker’s app, where you can tweak some settings (such as power delivery preferences to keep temps low and increase longevity) and see live power stats. Editor's pick Gadgets Four new gadgets for your next cold weather adventure This unit also connects to Anker’s line of desktop charging bases, which could streamline your set-up by charging devices at home and serving as a spot to drop the bank and make sure it stays juiced up. But by that point you may be dropping $400 on a charging set-up, which is pretty tough to justify. On the other hand, if money is no object, Anker also has a $300 version of this power bank that has a 26,000mAh capacity and 300W max output (140W on both USB-Cs simultaneously, plus the USB-A). A note on battery safety High-capacity rechargeable batteries can be dangerous. If they overheat or malfunction, the resulting fire can be explosive and difficult to extinguish. However, while all batteries can potentially go wrong, almost all incidents are due to one of two factors; poorly made devices, or inappropriate handling. So here are some tips to minimise the risk.



When buying devices with a battery inside, stick to known brands and trusted stores. Well-made devices have battery management systems and thermal cut-offs, along with properly built and wired components. Avoid cheap, unbranded battery packs and mystery cables.

If you’re unfamiliar with a brand, check for regulatory marks. These include the FCC and CE marks, but the one that shows a device meets Australian requirements is the Regulatory Compliance Mark, which is a circled tick inside a triangle.

Batteries generate heat. Unplug devices once they are charged, and never leave things charging unattended on a soft surface like a bed or blanket. Don’t charge with hot devices, and avoid keeping them in hot environments like cars.

Avoid dropping, crushing or tampering with any battery-powered device, and inspect regularly for damage. If the plastic casing is cracked, any wires are damaged, connectors are bent or the device appears swollen, do not use.

Modern USB devices negotiate safe power levels with chargers, meaning it is not inherently dangerous to plug a device that only needs 5W into charger that can do 100W. But sticking to high-quality chargers and cables ensures these built-in safety handshakes work properly. While battery packs are ideal for travelling, it’s worth noting that you should always check airline rules. Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage. Units under 100Wh (a measure of total energy potential, generally equivalent to a power bank with around 27,000mAh capacity) are allowed in carry-on luggage, so the above four recommendations and the large bulk of consumer power banks can fly. But the actual use or charging of power banks on planes is now largely prohibited. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

Homicide detectives have been called in to investigate after a man was found dead at a bus stop on a main road in the state’s south west in the early hours of Sunday morning. Police say St John Ambulance were called about an unresponsive man found at a bus stop on the Boulevard in Australind just after 1 o’clock Sunday morning. Officers from Australind and surrounds attended to help the man. Hannah Murphy The man, believed to be in his 20s, was found with critical injuries and was taken to Bunbury Hospital. However he was declared dead. Police said two men in their 30s were in custody and homicide squad officers are helping with the investigation.



No charges have been laid at this time. It has been a busy weekend for WA police across the state, with the news of the Australind death coming just hours after police announced they had arrested a man over an alleged stabbing that took place in the courtyard of Brookfield Place in the city. Police said a group of men got in a fight outside a cafe near Brookfield Place on St Georges Terrace in the city centre late on Friday evening. The incident is believed to have happened around the Brookfield Place area, on St Georges Terrace. Bloomberg During the fight, one man was stabbed in the back.



He was rushed to Royal Perth Hospital by two other men in a white Toyota Corolla hatchback, who are believed to have briefly handed him over to emergency department staff before immediately leaving. The man, aged in his 30s, sustained life-threatening injuries and had emergency surgery. He is now in a serious but stable condition. Police confirmed on Sunday they had since arrested a 36-year-old man from Darch over the alleged attack, and charged him with one count of grievous bodily harm. He has been refused bail and is due before court this morning. Earlier on Friday, police said they had since arrested and charged a teenager over an attack on an Uber driver in Perth’s north.



Related Article Taxis Uber is winning the rideshare war, but our addiction to the app may backfire Officers said two young boys were collected from a house in Balga by a rideshare car, and once inside, they began threatening him and brandished capsicum spray. The driver pulled over at a petrol station in Greenwood and got out, but the boy followed him and allegedly sprayed him. The two boys then left on foot, but were later picked up by police. World.title: Vincent Pastore, whose Sopranos character ratted out Tony, dies aged 80
World.content:
CultureTV & radioVale Vincent Pastore, whose Sopranos character ratted out Tony, dies aged 80 August 2, 2026 — 10:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Vincent Pastore, a veteran actor who played mobsters and tough guys, and was best known for playing Salvatore “Big Pussy” Bonpensiero on The Sopranos, has died. He was 80. Bob McGowan, who had managed Pastore since his run on The Sopranos, told the Associated Press that he learnt of his death on Saturday from another client and actor on the show, Vincent Curatola. Vincent Pastore, the veteran actor known for his role in The Sopranos, has died. Pictured in 2024. Getty He said that he had been found in his home on New York’s City Island after not being heard from for a few days. McGowan said he’d been trying to reach Pastore about a possible job.



“He was the most loyal client and he always gave to charity,” McGowan said, “and he was the kind of guy who would help anybody, which is rare in my business.” Michael Imperioli, a longtime friend and collaborator with Pastore, said on Instagram that it seemed as though he had known Vinny forever. The Sopranos cast, with James Gandolfini centre and Vincent Pastore at the far right. Reuters “We did lots of work together and travelled all over the USA as well as Italy and Australia. Lots of good times. Lots of laughs,” Imperioli said. “Vinny was a kind-hearted brother who cared deeply about his family and friends. I will miss him always.” Pastore appeared in movies dating back to the 1980s and had roles in big movies, including Goodfellas and Awakenings, both in 1990.



He often played gangsters. And it was one of those roles he’s best known for: his 30-episode run as Salvatore “Big Pussy” Bonpensiero, the friend of Tony Soprano who becomes an FBI informant in The Sopranos. He was born in the Bronx and grew up in suburban New Rochelle, New York. He enlisted in the navy during the Vietnam War and later attended Pace University, according to his biography on IMDb. He is survived by his daughter, Renee Pastore. AP Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: WA Labor and Liberals battle it out over Karnup train station promise
World.content:
NationalWAPublic transport WA Labor and Liberals battle it out over Karnup train station promise Hannah Murphy August 2, 2026 — 12:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state government has announced it will build and open a new train station in Perth’s outer suburbs as it fights to keep its hold on Secret Harbour ahead of the upcoming byelection. Premier Roger Cook announced the $156 million train station for Karnup on Sunday, with Transport Minister Rita Saffioti confirming she would be allocating $10 million to begin planning the station. Mock ups of the Karnup Station posted on the Building for Tomorrow website. Building for Tomorrow Karnup is in the Secret Harbour electorate, which used to be held by WA Defence Minister Paul Papalia before he announced his retirement last month. Running in his place is Labor candidate Georgia Tree, who previously came under fire for living outside of the electorate. She has since moved in with family to stay inside her voter base. Karnup train station was first flagged for the Mandurah Line back in 2013, and has faced extensive delays since.



Related Article Metronet ‘We like to win’: Saffioti and Hastie go head-to-head over Lakelands station Cook said on Sunday population growth in the southern suburb meant the Karnup train station was now top of their agenda. “As part of our long-term MetroNet vision, we have always planned for a train station here at Karnup, and today we can announce work will start on the Karnup train station project in 2028,” he said. Cook said WA’s share of the project would be funded by land sales, while they would seek the other half from the federal government. Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said the train station was “always part of the plan”, but accepted the project had been sped up by the upcoming byelection.



“In relation to the timing, look, we would probably have made this announcement over the next six to eight months, but of course we have bought that announcement early,” she said. “Because we have got so much certainty now with the planning ... it’s all coming together.” An artist impression of a proposed new Karnup development, which is expected to bring thousands of new residents to the suburb south of Perth requiring access to rail. Saffioti said the project had been initially held up due to zoning laws and funding issues, due to the prioritisation of the nearby Lakelands train station. Ultimately, Saffioti said the station would be an “elevated design” with more than 400 car parking pays and an eight bus interchange.



The Labor government’s announcement comes just five days after opposition leader Basil Zempilas said he would be looking to revive the project if elected. Related Article WA election Secret Harbour byelection heating up as One Nation announces candidate “Labor promised Karnup Station in 2013, again in 2017 and again in 2021. Nearly a decade after Labor came to government, there is still no money in the State Budget, no construction timetable and no delivery date,” he said. “Locals have waited long enough. They deserve a firm commitment, not another promise designed to get Labor through an election.” Zempilas said the Liberals would commit $90 million to the project and commence building in 2029, and Saffioti slammed the figure as “undercosting”.



“There’s no way they’ll deliver it for $90 million,” she said. “Look, they said they’ll deliver an Ellenbrook rail line in 2008, and they never did. They said they’ll deliver max light rail. They came out with a under-costed ‘back of the envelope’ commitment.” Liberal local candidate Ryan Robertson offered his own support for the project, but said only his party had listened to residents about what they wanted from the train station. City of Rockingham councillor Ryan Robertson is WA Liberal’s candidate for Secret Harbour. Facebook/Ryan Robertson “People in Secret Harbour and surrounding suburbs are tired of being told Karnup station is coming,” Mr Robertson said.



“They have watched Labor make the same promise election after election while the station has remained unfunded and undelivered. “Karnup station is essential infrastructure for the future of this fast-growing community.”

World.title: ‘Sad for politics’: ICAC probe isn’t a ‘boon’ for Labor, says Minns
World.content:
NationalNSWOperation Rosny ‘Sad for politics’: ICAC probe isn’t a ‘boon’ for Labor, says Minns Mostafa Rachwani August 2, 2026 — 12:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW Premier Chris Minns has waved away any benefits Labor may gain from the week’s explosive ICAC revelations into dealings within the NSW Liberal Party. The inquiry has spent the past week digging into links between the NSW Liberals, Catholic Schools NSW and business figures in Sydney. Only two of the 10 persons of interest have appeared so far. Premier Chris Minns has waved away any benefit his party may derive from ICAC’s Operation Rosny. Sitthixay Ditthavong And despite a week of incisive questions surrounding how the Reformers, a group of the party’s conservative religious faction, received and used their funding, the premier has remained diplomatic. Asked if the inquiry was a “gift” to Labor ahead of the state election in March, Minns pointed to a surge in support for One Nation as a potentially “worrying” consequence.



“It’s interesting and perhaps worrying for me that over the same time that this inquiry has been taking place, One Nation’s vote has skyrocketed, and they’ve got nothing to do with this ICAC investigation,” Minns said on Sunday. “My concern is that people say, ‘Well, I’ve seen Labor at ICAC, and I’ve seen the Liberal Party at ICAC. I’m going to vote for a third party this time.’” Loading “So I don’t think it’s necessarily the big boon for our political party that many believe.” Speaking outside the North Cronulla Surf Life Saving Club to announce a $10 million investment in the club’s facilities, Minns looked to maintain a stoic position on the inquiry.



“I’ve been reluctant to offer a long-running commentary about it because I feel like this is an independent process, an independent inquiry,” he said. “I also think it’s sad for politics when people who are in elected positions are acting in this way because it casts a pall over all of us, everybody in politics.” Asked if, after watching the inquiry probe whether the group at the centre of the inquiry misappropriated funding or broke fundraising rules, the premier could only say the government would “monitor that”. It comes as the federal Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume has insisted the inquiry was “distant” from Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.



Taylor became embroiled in the scandal after one of the witnesses, former NSW Liberal Party staffer Dylan Whitelaw, claimed he had agreed to a donation to support the Reformer’s activities. Taylor is not directly involved in the inquiry and he is not a person of interest. Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume. Dominic Lorrimer He has repeatedly declared that “no payments were made” to the NSW Reformers. Hume doubled down, telling ABC’s Insiders that the issue is “distant” from Taylor and that ICAC should “be allowed to go through its processes free of political interference”.



Related Investigation

Investigation Inside Operation Rosny She went on to admit she didn’t “actually understand” the activities of the Reformers, but added that “each of our state divisions should be undertaking a review of its own constitution and its own membership to make sure that we are the fighting fit, electoral machine that we should be in the lead up to both state and federal elections.” Pressed on whether she would condemn the groups’ activities, Hume said it was a matter for ICAC in NSW and that she was “a Victorian”. While waiting in the drive-thru line, they saw people running across the road and workers bolting out of the restaurant. At first, Dodaro thought there might have been a fire, but then a man directing traffic in a reflective vest said there was a shooter. Police and fire crews respond to the shooting in Twin Falls. KMVT via AP “So that’s when we knew there was a shooting. People were running out, crying and screaming. It was very scary,” Dodaro said in a text message to the Associated Press. The nearby Magic Valley Mall was closed, and people had been told to shelter inside, according to an employee who spoke to NBC News. “We are currently in a lockdown,” he said. “There has been a mass shooting.”



St Luke’s Magic Valley spokesperson Taylor Marschner said in a statement that the medical centre was “working closely with law enforcement and emergency responders as they manage the situation”. Twin Falls, a city of about 56,000 people, is about 205 kilometres south-east of Boise and about 120 kilometres north of the Nevada border. According to the London Telegraph, the Twin Falls branch of In-N-Out Burger opened only nine days ago, with local residents queuing overnight to be among the first to eat there. World.title: ‘Find something that I can prove is Greg’: Family makes fresh appeal in 1989 cold case
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaMissing person ‘Find something that I can prove is Greg’: Family makes fresh appeal in 1989 cold case Carolyn Webb August 2, 2026 — 11:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When they were growing up on a farm near Portland, in western Victoria, Paul Delaney and brother Greg were best mates. They fought like siblings do, but every day they would be out riding motorbikes or horses, or playing tennis. “We did everything together,” Paul says. Pamela Delaney with two of her sons, Brendan (left) and Paul, in front of their former house in St Albans Park. In 1989, the area was part of Whittington. Eddie Jim Greg is often in Paul’s thoughts, but no longer in his life. On July 12, 1989, Greg vanished from the family home in Geelong. He was 21 years old.



On Sunday, as part of National Missing Persons Week – August 2-8 – the Delaneys are making what Paul terms “a last-ditch effort” to find out what happened, although they no longer believe Greg is alive. Paul and their mother, Pamela, want anyone with information on the disappearance to come forward. Newspaper clippings kept by the Delaney family about Greg’s disappearance. Eddie Jim “I’ve said to the police, find me a finger, something that I can prove is Greg, and I can bury it and say, ‘goodnight, goodbye’,” Pamela says. In July 1989, Greg was working as a chef at Greenmount resort on the Gold Coast in Queensland, but had flown back to Victoria to visit his family in the Geelong suburb of Whittington, now called St Albans Park, where they’d moved in 1988.



Greg spent the night of July 11 drinking and watching television in the Ottoman Court house. Paul remembers waking at 3am or 4am to find Greg in the lounge, ranting to himself. Paul says he told Greg to go for a walk, to sober up. Greg tripped over a lamp. The noise woke their father, Paddy, who came out and swore. Greg walked out of the house. Greg Delaney (left) as a young man and an Australian Federal Police image of what he might look like now, aged 58. The next night, when Greg didn’t return, police were called. Searches found nothing. Greg was described as 165 centimetres with a medium build, brown hair, blue eyes and a fair complexion. He was last seen wearing blue jeans, white Adidas sneakers and a jumper with black and white squares.



Paul says Greg might have hitchhiked to see his girlfriend in northern NSW. This was months before serial killer Ivan Milat is known to have murdered hitchhikers he picked up on the Hume Highway west of Sydney. Paul fears that this is what happened to Greg. The last known photo taken of Greg Delaney (far right), at lunch the day before he walked out of his family home. The Australian Federal Police have released a new image of what Greg might look like today, age 58, if still alive. Detective Leading Senior Constable Mark Woodhead, from the Geelong crime investigation unit, says: “This investigation remains open so if anyone has any information, no matter how small, now is the time to come forward.”



Greg’s father, Paddy, died in 2003. Pamela says that if Greg was alive, he “would have been in touch with me”. Tears still come when she talks about the eldest of her four sons. She wants to solve this mystery. “Everyone knows he’s gone. But we’d love to have a grave to visit,” she says. Anyone with information is urged contact Crime Stoppers at 1800 333 000 or submit a confidential report at www.crimestoppersvic.com.au. World.title: Four portable power banks that go the extra mile
World.content:
TechnologyGadgets Four portable power banks that go the extra mile Tim Biggs August 2, 2026 — 11:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The stress of carrying around battery-powered tech and not being sure when you’ll find the next wall plug is real. And though there are heaps of power banks available on the market, picking one you can rely on isn’t straightforward. When weighing up a portable battery it’s vital to choose a good brand, but you’re also looking to strike a balance between capacity, ports, size, speed and price, with each given different weight depending on your needs. Commonly, you can find compact units that hold 10,000mAh, charge at up to 30W, and cost about $70. That’s reasonable value for keeping a phone topped up all weekend, but below are four notably well-built premium units I have tested and recommend, that will give you a little extra. The all-rounder Odds are you won’t need 100W most of the time, but it is nice to have. I used the P63 to charge my MacBook Pro at full speed from very low to completely full in a couple of hours, while working, and it used less than half of the bank’s stored power. You can be assured your phone and most other devices will charge at their full speed from the main USB-C port, whether it’s an iPhone that takes 40W, a handheld gaming console that takes 65W, or a laptop that takes 90W.



If you’re mainly concerned about one device, this is a brilliant bank; it fills fast when you plug it into the wall, and has enough capacity to totally replenish your phone four or five times. But it will also happily charge multiple devices. You can charge two USB-C devices at up to 65W and 45W, or one USB-C and one USB-A at 65W and 18W. Charging three at a time clearly tests the limits of the bank though. The main port will still give 65W, but the other two get the bare minimum. And the unit will get hot. The P63 looks and feels nice, which is unusual for a power bank, though it is a massive fingerprint magnet. A glossy panel gives the impression of a big screen, but in truth there’s only a simple display underneath that shows the percentage battery left. What appears at first to be a corded lanyard is actually a short USB-C cable in disguise, one which is capable of carrying the full 100W. It’s a clever way to prevent you from forgetting a cable but, although it feels well-made, I’m hesitant to put any kind of stress on a power cable, so I wouldn’t hang it off anything. The magnetic option Simply snapping a magnetic charger to your phone when needed is a lot tidier than plugging in a cable. I primarily tested the 10,000mAh Fortix model, which had plenty of juice to fully charge my phone twice with some left over. It attached solidly, and was big enough that I could grip it like a pop socket, but it also made the phone quite bulky. If you want to keep using the phone as normal while you charge, a slimmer option like the $80 5000mAh Fortix might be better. There are number of these designs on the market, including one made by Apple specifically for its iPhone Air, and most (including this one) have both a magnetic charger and a USB-C. There are also many that feel a bit thin and flexy though, which you don’t want in a battery.



The 15W wireless charge speed is below the MagSafe maximum of 25W, but I found I was happy to start charging sooner and keep charging longer because I didn’t have to sit down with a bulky pack and a cable, or banish my phone to my backpack. If you have earbuds or other devices that can charge wirelessly (MagSafe AirPods are especially good here) you can top them up wirelessly with the Fortix while you sit at a cafe. But you can also just use a cable, and you’ll get a slightly faster 20W. If you do two devices at once, both will have greatly reduced speeds, but it works. In addition to iPhone, these will also work on any Qi2 Android phone. I tested them on a Google 10 Pro and they worked perfectly. On Samsung phones, because of the low camera bump, I had to tilt the battery a little, which doesn’t affect performance but is not ideal. While there are cheaper magnetic battery banks out there, these are the most solid-feeling I’ve used. And I do appreciate that they are made with a cutting edge semi-solid state battery design, meaning they have minimal liquid content (so much less danger of fires) and should last for thousands more charges than an equivalent lithium-ion battery. One downside of the overall design is the lack of a screen; you only have a little row of LED dots to show how much juice you have left. The wall plug The BoostCharge Hybrid looks and works like any other travel charger; it’s a big black brick with one USB-C, one USB-A and easily removable prongs (it comes with all the regions so you can take it overseas with no adapter). When plugged into your wall it’s a 25W charger. However, it’s also got a 5000mAh battery stored inside, so it will continue charging the connected devices at a maximum of 20W when you unplug it from the wall. Of course none of these numbers stack up to the beefiest dedicated batteries, but this is also a legitimately pocketable device. And it may seem like a minor thing, but having the one fist-sized device act as a charging brick and a portable battery bank can be really convenient.



As you move around from place to place you plug it into a wall socket when you can — it will top up any attached device first and then fill up its internal battery — and then you just put it in your pocket when you need to leave and your device will continue charging. I also find myself using this device at home surprisingly often, which isn’t something I can say for any other battery bank, because it’s always plugged in and full. I have a big 100W charger at my desk for topping up gadgets, but if I happen to need something in another room and the battery is dead (often a tablet, headphones or a game controller), I’ll plug it into this charger and then take it with me. The obvious trade-off is that you could get much faster charging and more battery capacity if you used two separate devices. And of course if you had a battery bank plus a charger with multiple USB-C ports, you’d be able to top up your phone and battery significantly quicker when you found an outlet. But the selling point here is an all-in one solution at the expense of some speed. The overkill scenario It may not be pocketable, but the Prime’s thin brick shape makes it easy enough to grip and carry. It looks like a premium product, and if you have a work set-up that might demand heavy charging (say a laptop plus a phone), it’s a sleek power source that won’t take up much room. The 100W input means you can half-fill the bank in less than half an hour, assuming a strong enough wall plug, and then you can use that stored energy to charge two USB-C devices simultaneously at up to 100W each. Either port can boost to 140W if you’re only charging a single device. There’s also a USB-A that gets 20W if both the USB-Cs are full, or 22.5W otherwise. Yes, if you’re doing the maths, that’s a total 220W maximum output. And yes, it does get warm.



Another big benefit is the colour screen on the front, which you can cycle between an overview display showing remaining battery, one showing the exact wattage going through each of the three ports, and one showing the temperature. Being able to see power stats at a glance can be helpful if you’re not sure you’re getting the full speed, maybe because of a lower-spec cable or a device’s settings. This power bank also has Bluetooth for use with Anker’s app, where you can tweak some settings (such as power delivery preferences to keep temps low and increase longevity) and see live power stats. Editor's pick Gadgets Four new gadgets for your next cold weather adventure This unit also connects to Anker’s line of desktop charging bases, which could streamline your set-up by charging devices at home and serving as a spot to drop the bank and make sure it stays juiced up. But by that point you may be dropping $400 on a charging set-up, which is pretty tough to justify. On the other hand, if money is no object, Anker also has a $300 version of this power bank that has a 26,000mAh capacity and 300W max output (140W on both USB-Cs simultaneously, plus the USB-A). A note on battery safety High-capacity rechargeable batteries can be dangerous. If they overheat or malfunction, the resulting fire can be explosive and difficult to extinguish. However, while all batteries can potentially go wrong, almost all incidents are due to one of two factors; poorly made devices, or inappropriate handling. So here are some tips to minimise the risk.



When buying devices with a battery inside, stick to known brands and trusted stores. Well-made devices have battery management systems and thermal cut-offs, along with properly built and wired components. Avoid cheap, unbranded battery packs and mystery cables.

If you’re unfamiliar with a brand, check for regulatory marks. These include the FCC and CE marks, but the one that shows a device meets Australian requirements is the Regulatory Compliance Mark, which is a circled tick inside a triangle.

Batteries generate heat. Unplug devices once they are charged, and never leave things charging unattended on a soft surface like a bed or blanket. Don’t charge with hot devices, and avoid keeping them in hot environments like cars.

Avoid dropping, crushing or tampering with any battery-powered device, and inspect regularly for damage. If the plastic casing is cracked, any wires are damaged, connectors are bent or the device appears swollen, do not use.

Modern USB devices negotiate safe power levels with chargers, meaning it is not inherently dangerous to plug a device that only needs 5W into charger that can do 100W. But sticking to high-quality chargers and cables ensures these built-in safety handshakes work properly. While battery packs are ideal for travelling, it’s worth noting that you should always check airline rules. Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage. Units under 100Wh (a measure of total energy potential, generally equivalent to a power bank with around 27,000mAh capacity) are allowed in carry-on luggage, so the above four recommendations and the large bulk of consumer power banks can fly. But the actual use or charging of power banks on planes is now largely prohibited. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter every Friday. Sign up here.

World.title: Two men in custody after man found dead at WA bus stop
World.content:
Breaking NationalWACrime Two men in custody after man found dead at WA bus stop Hannah Murphy August 2, 2026 — 10:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Homicide detectives have been called in to investigate after a man was found dead at a bus stop on a main road in the state’s south west in the early hours of Sunday morning. Police say St John Ambulance were called about an unresponsive man found at a bus stop on the Boulevard in Australind just after 1 o’clock Sunday morning. Officers from Australind and surrounds attended to help the man. Hannah Murphy The man, believed to be in his 20s, was found with critical injuries and was taken to Bunbury Hospital. However he was declared dead. Police said two men in their 30s were in custody and homicide squad officers are helping with the investigation.



No charges have been laid at this time. It has been a busy weekend for WA police across the state, with the news of the Australind death coming just hours after police announced they had arrested a man over an alleged stabbing that took place in the courtyard of Brookfield Place in the city. Police said a group of men got in a fight outside a cafe near Brookfield Place on St Georges Terrace in the city centre late on Friday evening. The incident is believed to have happened around the Brookfield Place area, on St Georges Terrace. Bloomberg During the fight, one man was stabbed in the back.



He was rushed to Royal Perth Hospital by two other men in a white Toyota Corolla hatchback, who are believed to have briefly handed him over to emergency department staff before immediately leaving. The man, aged in his 30s, sustained life-threatening injuries and had emergency surgery. He is now in a serious but stable condition. Police confirmed on Sunday they had since arrested a 36-year-old man from Darch over the alleged attack, and charged him with one count of grievous bodily harm. He has been refused bail and is due before court this morning. Earlier on Friday, police said they had since arrested and charged a teenager over an attack on an Uber driver in Perth’s north.



Related Article Taxis Uber is winning the rideshare war, but our addiction to the app may backfire Officers said two young boys were collected from a house in Balga by a rideshare car, and once inside, they began threatening him and brandished capsicum spray. The driver pulled over at a petrol station in Greenwood and got out, but the boy followed him and allegedly sprayed him. The two boys then left on foot, but were later picked up by police. A 15-year-old from Balga has been charged with administering poison, attempting to steal a car and aggravated arm robbery. He was in Perth Children’s Court yesterday.

World.title: Vincent Pastore, whose Sopranos character ratted out Tony, dies aged 80
World.content:
CultureTV & radioVale Vincent Pastore, whose Sopranos character ratted out Tony, dies aged 80 August 2, 2026 — 10:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Vincent Pastore, a veteran actor who played mobsters and tough guys, and was best known for playing Salvatore “Big Pussy” Bonpensiero on The Sopranos, has died. He was 80. Bob McGowan, who had managed Pastore since his run on The Sopranos, told the Associated Press that he learnt of his death on Saturday from another client and actor on the show, Vincent Curatola. Vincent Pastore, the veteran actor known for his role in The Sopranos, has died. Pictured in 2024. Getty He said that he had been found in his home on New York’s City Island after not being heard from for a few days. McGowan said he’d been trying to reach Pastore about a possible job.



“He was the most loyal client and he always gave to charity,” McGowan said, “and he was the kind of guy who would help anybody, which is rare in my business.” Michael Imperioli, a longtime friend and collaborator with Pastore, said on Instagram that it seemed as though he had known Vinny forever. The Sopranos cast, with James Gandolfini centre and Vincent Pastore at the far right. Reuters “We did lots of work together and travelled all over the USA as well as Italy and Australia. Lots of good times. Lots of laughs,” Imperioli said. “Vinny was a kind-hearted brother who cared deeply about his family and friends. I will miss him always.” Pastore appeared in movies dating back to the 1980s and had roles in big movies, including Goodfellas and Awakenings, both in 1990.



He often played gangsters. And it was one of those roles he’s best known for: his 30-episode run as Salvatore “Big Pussy” Bonpensiero, the friend of Tony Soprano who becomes an FBI informant in The Sopranos. He was born in the Bronx and grew up in suburban New Rochelle, New York. He enlisted in the navy during the Vietnam War and later attended Pace University, according to his biography on IMDb. He is survived by his daughter, Renee Pastore. AP Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.
