World.title: New Zealand First Kiwi Kids Grant plans to pay parents for having children
World.content:
New Zealand First wants more people to have babies - and would pay them to do it.

The party also confirmed former Defence Minister Ron Mark was returning to the party, and will stand in the election.

At a public meeting in Masterton, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said New Zealand was facing a "population precipice," and the rate of New Zealand citizens having children had fallen dramatically.

"We need more Kiwis having more children, and one way to do that is to substantially lower the main barrier most are facing, that is the cost," he said.

The party's Kiwi Kids Grant would seek to arrest that fall, by paying parents $5,000 a year for the first three years, and for up to three children.

Peters announced the grant at an NZ First public meeting. RNZ/Giles Dexter

To qualify, one parent would need to be a New Zealand citizen.

"New Zealand needs to get our birthrate increasing before it's too late," Peters said.

Peters said the tax-free payment would be administered through the Inland Revenue Department.

The policy, which the party had costed at $400 million over three years, would would be funded through operating baselines.

ACT leader David Seymour said he could see what New Zealand First was trying to do, but many countries had tried to pay people to have children without results.

"It doesn't seem to have worked where it has been tried in other countries. And bear in mind, if you have one income and you earn $100,000, the earned income tax credit and Working for Families are giving you about the same amount already."

New Zealand First also confirmed Ron Mark was returning to the party.

Ron Mark. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

World.title: ACT candidate Paul Henry unveils plan to let teachers use 'reasonable force' on students
World.content:
ACT wants to give teachers the legal power to remove "seriously or persistently disruptive" students from a classroom.

The party's new policy would allow teachers to send disruptive students to a supervised space and staff would be protected when using a "reasonable and proportionate" intervention to prevent harm or destruction of property.

Announcing the policy in Auckland on Sunday, ACT candidate Paul Henry said the law would give teachers clear legal protections and the power to regain "order" in the classroom.

"Let's be honest, there are a lot of little shits in classrooms, and we need to address that if we're going to lift education standards.

"Teachers need to know they're respected [and] they need to know the law is actually on their side."

ACT would "clarify" the boundaries already set under Section 99 of the Education and Training Act 2020 so teachers know what is permitted and are protected when they act reasonably.

Henry said teachers would be allowed to use "reasonable force" in specific circumstances, but denied "corporal punishment" would be allowed.

"We can't have the situation where that line is blurred. This has nothing to do with corporal punishment. This has nothing to do with punishing the child who is the problem."

The current guidelines allow school staff to physically restrain students as a last resort to prevent harm. The method must also be "reasonable and proportionate".

Asked how the policy was different from the current guidelines, Henry said his party would be "very specific what that behaviour the teacher can use is".

"The ambiguity that exists at the moment means many teachers just can't even face the prospect of doing it. They will take the easy road out, and the easy road out is a long way away from easy or preferable."

ACT would make it so assaulting a teacher, staff member or student would cause an immediate removal and mandatory stand-down or suspension. Serious assaults would be referred to Police Youth Aid.

Parents would be required to get involved when behaviour became serious or repeated, and could be held liable for deliberate property damage caused by their child.

If a parent failed to attend a mandatory meeting without a reasonable excuse they could be fined up to $300 for a first offence and up to $3000 for subsequent offences.

Parents may also be held financially responsible for the cost of deliberate property damage caused by their child at school, which could be recoverable as a debt if unpaid.

Henry said parents were part of the solution.

"The expectation with the parents is that they show - or guardians - up at school, and so they are engaged with the school [and] we are engaged with them.

"There are parents that presumably just don't give a damn so they're the ones that will be fined. The parents that do give a damn but don't know what to do and need help, we'll engage with them and we'll help them - we will not fine them."

'Make classrooms less safe'

Labour education spokesperson Ginny Andersen told RNZ that teachers, parents and student deserved to feel safe at school, but ACT's policy would do the opposite.

"This policy will just make classrooms less safe by letting potentially untrained staff physically drag students out of the room.

Ginny Andersen. RNZ / REECE BAKER

"This is not the sort of education system that New Zealand wants or needs... our teachers are there to teach, and their job should be to do that, not to physically restrain children."

Andersen said there was already a clear process in place.

"My real concern is for parents of children who need additional learning support for their kids, and they can't properly access learning support now and we should be looking about how we support learning, not how we further restrain children."

She said Henry using "little shits" to describe misbehaving children was unacceptable.

"It's not appropriate, and it's yet another example of the coalition lowering standards, and New Zealanders are quite frankly sick of it."

Andersen said fining parents for their children's behaviour would not solve the issue.

World.title: Eighth recent SH3 Awakino Gorge closure: Businesses say they're hurting
World.content:
Correction: The headline has been amended to say eighth recent closure of SH3

It's a case of grin and bear it for Mōkau businesses facing yet another complete closure of the Awakino Gorge - the link between Taranaki and Waikato - on State Highway 3.

The Transport Agency has announced the gorge will be closed between the rest area near the Historic Tunnel and the intersection of SH3 and Manganui Road, for four days from 6am Saturday 22 August to 6pm Tuesday 25 August.

During the closure, crews will be working to install three culverts to drain water, which is currently flowing over the road, at the massive slip that came down in April.

It's the ninth closure of the Awakino Gorge for weather-related incidents or repairs in recent times.

Owner of the River Run Cafe in Mōkau, Dev Rawat, said road closures were devastating for his business.

"We depend on the people who passing through State Highway 3 and when the road is shut no one come into the cafe and that impact us lots.

"So, we have to shut our business for those days, and last time we were shut for five days and there was no business."

He would like the government to offer compensation.

"Last year, the store was closed more than six or seven times, and that's affecting our business lots. It's hard to pay our staff, pay bills and everything.

"And the government's not think about the local businesses around here. They're supposed to think about it and give some compensation, so we can get some relief."

Waka Kotahi incident controller Kendra Ludeke said closing the road was always a last resort.

"We wouldn't be closing the road unless there was another way. We've looked at a number of other options, but this is the most efficient way to install these culverts, which means installation happens quicker and the road open quicker."

Waka Kotahi's Kendra Ludeke RNZ / Robin Martin

Ludeke said the work requires heavy machinery to be on the road to make a deep excavation, with large open trenches and there was no space for vehicles to pass around or safely through the worksite.

"It is quite narrow and we're working under what's already a single lane due to the slip above it. So, it's paramount due to safety for the road workers and for crews and for people that drive the road every day that we close it to be able to complete this work.

Ludeke thanked the local community and the travelling public for their patience.

"People travelling through Awakino Gorge and local communities have been incredibly understanding and patient over the past few months. We don't take that for granted. We understand a four-day closure of the road will be highly disruptive for local communities, businesses, freight operators, emergency services and people travelling between regions.

"Doing this work next month over a four-day full closure will be a big step forward in the recovery of this stretch of road and sets the area up for the next stage of recovery work.

The Mōkau Butcher, Bryan Lester, says there's no point opening when the Awakino Gorge is closed. RNZ / Robin Martin

Mōkau Butcher owner Bryan Lester said NZTA found themselves between a rock and a hard place.

"Yeah, well, I've got mixed emotions, the work has to be done. Those culverts do need replacing and I know it's pretty hard for them to do the culverts while trying to get in and out with trucks with dirt and stuff like that. But yeah, it's certainly ... mixed emotions because it's not good for my business.

"It has a huge impact."

Lester said he'd consider shutting shop during the road closure too.

"Well, we might ... close as well. I mean the last closure, I think I served five customers for a whole day when they had the road closed only a week or so ago. So yeah, pretty much we close our doors."

New Plymouth mayor Max Brough said closures on SH3 at Awakino were becoming routine.

"Oh, it's hard work, isn't it? But, you've got to do the work. The problem it comes back to is that there's no alternate route, you know, no easily accessible alternate route, right?

"Look, it's disappointing, but you can't fix something without doing the work, can you?

"But it's a tough call, right? Tough call for Taranaki yet again this year. Will it be nine closures, I think? Nine if we get to the end of the year without any more closures."

SH3 through the Awakino Gorge has been pummelled by the weather this year, creating the need for major repairs. Supplied / NZ Transport Agency

The culverts were being delivered separately from the $50 million Awakino Gorge resilience package that was announced in May. It was focused on reducing the risk of slips and similar events happening in the future and was currently in development.

This work would be focused on reopening this section of road to two lanes following the April weather event and slip.

World.title: 'Wasn't perfect': What we learnt from Warriors victory over Titans
World.content:
Analysis: With their season entering the home straight and threatening to stall as it had last year, the NZ Warriors have produced the biggest win of their season to keep hopes of a home playoff alive.

After a listless defeat to Canterbury Bulldogs last week, they turned up to their second home of Cbus Super Stadium - where they lost by 60 points only two years ago - to dismantle the Gold Coast Titans 42-6 on Saturday night.

That equalled the most points scored by the Warriors in 38 meetings between the two clubs and also their highest score this season, matching their output against Sydney Roosters in the opening round and Brisbane Broncos at 'Magic Round'.

It also beat their 40-6 win over Canberra Raiders in week two for their biggest margin of the campaign.

"What we wanted to do, we certainly did for big parts," reflected coach Andrew Webster. "Wasn't perfect, but it's not going to be.

"We always leave with work-ons, but we nailed the things we wanted to do and that was eliminate fast starts, and we looked good.

"The last eight minutes, we probably could have been more ruthless. We obviously saw a lot of opportunities, wanted to score and went away from what was working for us, but happy."

Here's what we learnt from the Warriors win over the Titans.

Best players

In 2024, wing Alofiana Khan-Pereira feasted on the Warriors, scoring four tries in that 66-6 embarrassment.

Now on the other side of the field, AKP reminded the Titans what they had let slip through their fingers, with a first half that saw him cut infield for a try, break from his own half for an assist to five-eighth Chanel Harris-Tavita and then offload for another to new centre partner Leka Halasima.

That pairing mixed it up on that edge, with Khan-Pereira often coming infield to take an early touch, which led to the Harris-Tavita try.

Wing Dallin Watene-Zelezniak showed his intent early with an intercept that regained the league lead in that statistical category.

Although he was cut down by fullback Keano Kini in cover defence a few minutes later, he found the right corner for the game's opening try and his 77th for the Warriors, tying assistant coach Stacey Jones for third on the club all-time list. He also topped 200 metres running.

Hooker Wayde Egan showed his craftiness, luring defenders into set restarts time and again, directly leading to Eddie Ieremia-Toeava's try.

Eddie Ieremia-Toeava had his best first-grade performance against Gold Coast. Jason O'Brien/Photosport

After a shocker seven days before, when he was pulled early, second-rower Jacob Laban returned with another powerful display that produced 146 metres running and a team-high 39 tackles.

Erin Clark's recent form has somewhat reflected his team's, but the 2025 Dally M Lock of the Year returned to his best with his ball distribution on point. He provided the final pass for Te Maire Martin's first try.

If there was any temptation to bring Luke Metcalf into the line-up, Martin has surely muted that with his double, and canny option-taking that laid on Laban's try.

Ieremia-Toeava had his best first-grade performance, running for 191 metres and making 35 tackles, while Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad continued to knock on the door of a regular starting spot, leading the game in running metres (245) and saving several tries with last-ditch heroics.

Best try

About 10 minutes before halftime, Laban made a halfbreak and threatened to score himself. His fast play-the-ball saw Martin look right, then pass left, before former halfback, now lock Erin Clark put up a perfect kick to his left edge.

Khan-Pereira leapt high for a catch and offload to Halasima, who powered through the Titans defenders, still trying to comprehend what they had just seen, to score.

"We're never going to hear the end of that," Webster rolled his eyes.

Remember, this came a week after front-rower Mitch Barnett chipped ahead on the last tackle for five-eighth Chanel Harris-Tavita to score against the Bulldogs.

You can't afford to sleep on the Warriors middle forwards - nor their edge forwards for that matter.

With Taine Tuaupiki and Adam Pompey out of the line-up, Laban was entrusted with kickoff duties.

Key moment

Late in the first half, the Warriors led 20-6, but the Titans were hot on attack with a new set restart metres out from the tryline.

Six points right then would have brought the home side back within single figures and kept them in the contest.

Instead, as they shifted right in front of the posts, Josh Patston could not take a hot pass and bobbled the ball directly into the hands of Tanner Stowers-Smith.

The front-rower rumbled 60 metres upfield and over halfway, bumping off Kini in the process.

Tanner Stowers-Smith rumbled 50 metres, turning desperate defence into attack against the Titans. NRL Photos/Photosport

The set ended with Halasima unable to claim a high kick to the corner and Nicoll-Klokstad was subsequently held up over the line, before Clark's bomb for Laban's try.

Instead of closing within 10, the Titans trailed by 20 at the break - and the Warriors don't lose from there.

Key stat

The Warriors have now won 10/10 when leading at halftime this season.

Injuries etc

Before kickoff, Webster pulled a fast one, switching Halasima into centre for Adam Pompey.

The coach insists he doesn't follow social media, but the keyboard coaches have been calling for Pompey's head for a few weeks now and they finally got it.

Whether that's a long-term fix - and Halasima certainly did enough to retain the job - or is just a ploy to get Rocco Berry another week of reps in his injury comeback remains to be seen.

The Warriors also lost the services of interchange forward Demitric Vaimauga and his power off the bench to a rib injury at captain's run, but his absence left the door open for Riley Price's surprise club debut and a piece of history.

Price and dad Steve, who captained the club for 91 games from 2005-09, became the organisation's first father-son representatives, beating out the Clearys and the Mellars.

Barnett left for a concussion check, but passed and returned before halftime.

Riley Price's surprise debut created Warriors club history. Jason O'Brien/Photosport

Martin sat out the final moments of the game, but by then, Webster had pulled his veterans, so that early exit may have been a precaution.

Webster also offered that Vaimauga should be good to go next week.

Titans

After back-to-back wins and in their captain's 100th game for the club, Gold Coast never really fired a shot and still seem a long way from escaping the bottom half of the competition table.

They also suffered a cruel blow, when promising half Zane Harrison limped off with a hamstring injury late in the game.

Centurion Tino Fa'asuamaleaui was probably their best, running for 172 metres, including 75 after contact, and making 29 tackles, but was reduced to exchanging taunts with Watene-Zelezniak, who had a one-sided scoreboard to point at in his defence.

What does the result mean

The Warriors at least retain their third spot on the points table and restore some of the valuable points differential advantage over their rivals that had been whittled away in recent weeks.

They are four points behind the Panthers and two behind Sydney Roosters, who may be the form team of the competition right now.

The Warriors currently need three more wins to mathematically clinch their playoff spot, although their differential means maybe just two, but they will still have eyes on a top-four position and a home playoff.

Those two things hang in the balance.

What's next

Two months ago, the Warriors went toe to toe with a Panthers outfit at CommBank Stadium, eventually bowing 20-18 in an encounter of such high quality, many commentators described as a preview of the grand final.

They combined for 91 percent set completion and the result barely dented the Warriors' standing on the table.

Since then, both teams have hit mid-season blues, both going 3-3 into this weekend, as teams around them surge.

Both scored convincing wins this week and will want to keep that momentum into the final weeks of the regular season.

Its Indigenous Round and former Penrith star James Fisher-Harris - now Warriors co-captain - can't wait.

"Pretty keen to play in that jersey, it looks pretty nice" he admitted. "Another great challenge and good to be back home."

The five-game run to the post-season looked pretty daunting a few weeks ago, when the Panthers, Broncos, South Sydney Rabbitohs, Newcastle Knights and Manly Sea Eagles had a combined 46-33 record.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Ellesse Andrews says track return in Glasgow has been 'an adjustment'
World.content:
Fresh off her first podium finish in Glasgow, track cycling star Ellesse Andrews admits her return to the track has required some getting used to.

Taking into account the elite peaks she's scaled during her decorated career, the four-time Olympic medallist and double Olympic champion has had a somewhat mixed bag at her third Commonwealth Games.

Three golds in Birmingham four years ago, a Commonwealth Games defence in the team sprint ended before it had really begun on Thursday.

A day later Andrews was ousted at the quarter-final stage of the individual sprint, another premature end to a games title defence.

The 26-year-old scrapped her way to a bronze medal overnight in the 1km time trial final, and now has her sights set on defending her Commonwealth Games Keirn title on the final day of racing.

After receiving her fifth Games medal, and first ever bronze, Andrews said she was delighted with the result.

"I'm really stoked to be walking away with a bronze medal today. The kilo is a really brutal event, so I'm just really happy I was able to put it out there," she told reporters.

"It's so hard. I think before we go into it, we know that we need to absolutely punch the first lap and the second lap and then the third, we need to really keep it rolling and the fourth is just about holding on."

For the next 24 hours it was all about recovery ahead of her fourth and final event of her games campaign.

Andrews has spent much of the year in the Keirin world series circuit in Japan and said the limited time on the track had required some adjustment.

"I knew that it was always going to be interesting, I think, coming off the back of, I guess, my campaign in Japan, not having a whole lot of racing on the track.

"So I think, just getting back into this environment has been different. Not really challenging as such, but just really different to what I've been used to.

"So I guess that has been a bit of an adjustment, but not in a negative way."

World.title: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's 'parent-child mentality' description of NZ businesses 'valid' in some cases - Seymour
World.content:
The prime minister's office is defending comments Christopher Luxon made to Rotorua businesspeople that New Zealand businesses had a "parent-child mentality" and looked too often to the government for help.

Labour has accused the prime minister of being "out of touch" and "telling struggling business owners to grow up, instead of taking responsibility for a weak economy under his watch".

But ACT party leader and deputy prime minister David Seymour has been more sympathetic in his assessment, telling RNZ Luxon has possibly got "two groups of people mixed up here".

"It's important to differentiate that there are some people who call themselves businesspeople and yet always have their hand out to the government, and there are a whole lot of people not like that doing it bloody tough, for reasons not of their fault."

Luxon was in Rotorua last week and on Friday morning held a breakfast chat with the local business chamber.

It was there that Rotorua Business Chamber chief executive Melanie Short, who was moderating the talk, raised the "challenge" businesses were facing "taking on some extra costs".

"We do not want to pass them on because we're also getting less customers through the door," she said. "So, it's a matter of time - how long can we hang on?"

In a long response, Luxon said since returning to New Zealand he noticed "there's a parent-child mentality".

"I have literally sat in boardrooms across New Zealand, and the conversation goes: 'I wonder what the government's going to do? I wonder what the government's going to think?'

"Who cares what the government thinks or does? Our job is to be adult, adult, adult," he told the business audience.

Below is the transcript of the prime minister's full response to Short's question, provided to RNZ by his office.

"I think that's a negative view, to be honest. Like we're entrepreneurs and business people, and I get it. You know, if you're not retooling and radically disrupting your business, you ain't doing the job.

"You know, you have to disrupt yourself aggressively before you get disrupted by global events, and if you keep thinking you want the same business model, the same customer mix, the same margin structure, you know you've got to be retooling and refinancing and rehoming, and that's just the reality of business people all around the world.

"So, my job is to make sure I'm setting up the conditions for you to be able to go create that growth. And I think some of the subtext and assumption in your question is that...I think in New Zealand I'll be honest with you as a business person who was... I sat in Illinois for six years in Chicago, and the last person I wanted to ever talk to as a CEO was the government. I didn't sit there in Chicago saying I wonder what the government thinks and I wonder what they're doing to help me for my business? Can I get some grant money to do something? No, no, I'm a business person.

"I'm building a kick-ass company that actually has commercially superior returns, great customer experience, and awesome internal culture. That is the job of what makes a great company, not a good one, a great one. And so that was my mentality.

"Come home to New Zealand, and there's a parent-child mentality. I have literally sat in boardrooms across New Zealand, and the conversation goes: 'I wonder what the government's going to do? I wonder what the government's going to think?'

"Who cares what the government thinks or does? Our job is to be adult, adult, adult. The business leaders, the political leaders, and the community leaders working together, doing things differently. I set up the operating system. You go out there and smack it and go create the road, and the community leaders see the pain, the hurt, the need, and the frustration, and the three actors do different things but complementary things to deal with the challenges and the opportunities.

"So I still think there's a little bit of.... okay, so in this chamber, how many of you are actually using Claude or Claude code? Okay great. How many sessions has the chamber run to help you understand that? Is that your number one focus right here, right now? Because that is going to disrupt your businesses, and it's a huge opportunity for you to do exceptionally well off the back of it.

"So how do we collectively lift our SME literacy on something like AI as a result? So I'm just pushing back to say my job is to set the conditions up. We're getting spending under control. We're getting inflation back into the band. We're at 2.9 percent, strip out the fuel pieces. We've got growth coming in. And that creates opportunity."

'Patronising lecture' - Labour

In response to those comments, first published on Saturday in the Rotorua Daily Post, Labour finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said businesses were not asking for a "patronising lecture and a handout from the prime minister - they're asking for an economy that works".

Labour leader Chris Hipkins and Labour's finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds. RNZ / Louis Dunham

"Christopher Luxon promised to fix the economy and now he says, 'Who cares what the government will think or do?' New Zealand businesses care very much what the government thinks and does, because his government's choices affect whether they keep their doors open."

However, the prime minister's office told RNZ Luxon's comments had been mischaracterised in the original write-up, and by Edmonds, who was not at the meeting.

"Labour is desperately trying to distract from the fact that they still haven't fronted up to New Zealanders about whether they intend to pay for their $18 billion spending plans with more taxes, more borrowing, or both," a spokesperson said.

Seymour told RNZ Luxon's point "is a valid one".

"At the end of the day you've got to have a product or service that customers want, at a price they can afford to pay, but it's certainly not true every business is waiting for the government to solve that problem."

World.title: Tori Moorby claims Commonwealth Games javelin silver
World.content:
After an "extremely difficult" year, Tori Moorby has produced the breakthrough performance of her career, winning silver in the women's javelin at the Commonwealth Games on Saturday - her first major championship medal.

The Hamilton-based athlete threw 60.04m to finish second behind Australia's Mackenzie Little, whose opening-round effort of 61.88m proved enough for gold. Kenya's Irene Jepkemboi claimed bronze.

For Moorby the silver medal improved on her fifth-place finish in Birmingham four years ago.

While Moorby claimed the Oceania title in Darwin earlier this year, she had been searching for a breakthrough medal at the sport's biggest international championships.

Following the event, a delighted Moorby struggled to put her feelings into words.

"I don't really know what to say. I've got a silver medal, what the heck," she told Sky Sport.

"This year has been extremely difficult for me. I went out there tonight and believed that I could bring home some silverware and I have.

"It's an awesome feeling and I'm so proud."

Moorby's silver rounded out a strong athletics campaign for New Zealand, taking the team's medal haul to seven.

The tally included memorable gold medals to Zoe Hobbs in the women's 100m and Eliza McCartney in the women's pole vault. Tom Walsh (shot put) and Lauren Bruce (hammer throw) also won silver, while Anna Grimaldi (para 100m) and Imogen Ayris (pole vault) collected bronze.

Zoe Hobbs' history-making feat in the women's 100m final was one of the highlights for New Zealand's team in Glasgow. Dean Mouhtaropoulos / Getty Images

Elsewhere on the final day of track and field competition, Sam Tanner finished ninth in a star-studded men's Commonwealth mile final.

The event returned to the Commonwealth Games programme for the first time in 60 years and attracted one of the strongest fields assembled for the discipline, featuring three of the last four world champions. Scotland's Josh Kerr entered the race fresh from his world-record 3:42.66 performance at the London Diamond League two weeks earlier.

Tanner found himself boxed in through the opening laps of the tactical race and was unable to work into contention as the pace lifted over the final circuit.

Roared on by a capacity crowd at Scotstoun Stadium, Kerr found clear running with 400 metres remaining before surging away to claim gold. Australia's Cameron Myers took silver, while Kenya's Timothy Cheruiyot secured bronze.

World.title: The House: We need to learn to live with bird flu, experts tell MPs
World.content:
The spread of bird flu is ongoing in New Zealand, and we will have to learn to live with it, officials told MPs this week.

In a briefing to Parliament's Primary Production Committee on Thursday, officials from the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) and the Department of Conservation (DOC) said the focus would be on surveillance, resilience, and protecting native species and poultry populations, as the number of cases potentially rises.

MPI chief veterinary officer Mary Van Andel told MPs the H5N1 strain of bird flu first emerged in the Northern Hemisphere in 2020 and has since spread around the world, likely arriving in New Zealand via Antarctic and subantarctic seafaring (pelagic) bird species.

VNP/Louis Collins

Van Andel said although the virus remains a low risk to humans, its spread has resulted in an increasing number of infections in mammals. However sustained mammal-to-mammal transmission remains rare.

This week Australia confirmed local transmission among a population of great crested terns in South Australia.

"This is kind of the pattern that we expect with this disease," Van Andel told MPs, explaining that it was only a matter of time before pelagic seabirds moving through the Southern Ocean brought the virus to New Zealand.

Deputy director-general of Biosecurity New Zealand, Stewart Anderson, told the committee that New Zealand's trade status remains unaffected, but that ultimately H5N1 is a disease the country is likely to have to live with.

"It seems very unlikely that this disease will be able to be eradicated from New Zealand wildlife. That's not what has happened in any other place in the world.

"So we need to focus our efforts on resilience, and on protecting the populations that we are able to, because we can't predict or know how this disease will behave here."

Suze Redmayne VNP/Louis Collins

Given that the Primary Production Committee has a heavy agricultural focus, questions arose about the potential economic challenges the virus could pose if the virus spreads further.

With mortality rates approaching around 90-95 percent in some affected species, National MP Suze Redmayne asked whether compensation would be on the cards for poultry farmers, citing the Mycoplasma bovis outbreak as a potential model.

Anderson told Redmayne that was unlikely. "The industry is going to need to live and manage with this, because it'll become an endemic disease, meaning it can't be eradicated. "We won't be seeking to exercise powers under the Biosecurity Act to undertake culling and so on, which means that compensation is not payable."

As the situation is evolving, and with officials continuing to monitor for any increase in local transmission the Primary Production Committee agreed it was likely MPI officials would need to return to Parliament for further updates.

What is a briefing?

Briefings are one of the non-legislative functions available to select committees, allowing MPs to hear directly from officials, experts, and members of the public on an issue or topic of particular interest to the committee. While they can lead to a more formal select committee inquiry, committees are under no obligation to launch one.

You can listen to the audio version of this story by clicking the link near the top of the page.

World.title: Quick hits: Sprinter's surprise, a bored prince and a stunning upset
World.content:
An Australian sprinter receives a surprise visit, Jamaica celebrates in style after beating the Diamonds and Prince George looks bored at the cycling.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Surprise guests shock Aussie sprinter

Chloe Mannix-Power (right) had some fans she was not expecting to see in the stands. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Chloe Mannix-Power somewhat controversially missed out on an individual 100-metre berth at these Games, but hit the track for the first time in the women's 4x100m heats.

In the moments after she and teammates Ebony Lane, Monique Hanlon and Georgia Harris made it through to the women's 4x100m final, Mannix-Power looked up into the stands and received quite a shock.

"I thought [my parents] were at home watching on the lounge, but no they're up in the top of the grandstand cheering me on," she said.

"My parents love a surprise moment, they've done it before, so to be honest I kind of had a little feeling they would be up there, but they never tell me they're here until the end of the race."

Mannix-Power later helped Australia finish fourth in the final.

2. Prince George bored?

Prince William, Princess Catherine and their three children took in a few of the sports on day nine.

Prince George, however, seemed as though he wanted to be anywhere else when they visited the velodrome.

Prince George watches on at the velodrome. (AP: Andrew Milligan)

Earlier, the royals watched on as the Diamonds lost 46-45 to Jamaica in a major upset in the netball semifinals.

The Prince and Princess of Wales took to Instagram to thank the athletes for putting on a show.

The Prince and Princess of Wales and their family watching the netball at the Hydro in Glasgow. (Getty Images)

"Incredible atmosphere at the Commonwealth Games today," a post from their official Instagram account read.

"Watching world-class talent compete and seeing the power of sport to bring people together is truly special.

"Thank you to everyone involved for such a wonderful day."

3. 'Absolute scenes'

Jamaica celebrates its win over the Diamonds. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Not only did the Royals take in Jamaica's shock victory, but they also witnessed some of the wildest celebrations seen at the Commonwealth Games.

After Sophie Dwyer missed the shot that would have sent the semifinal to extra time, the entire Jamaican squad celebrated like they never had before.

We lost count of how many social media videos featured the caption: "Absolute scenes."

Loading Instagram content

For the Jamaicans, this was personal.

They were still hurting from their loss to the Diamonds in the 2022 Commonwealth Games final in Birmingham.

"We're carrying a bit of vengeance from the last Commonwealth Games," Jamaica captain Shamera Sterling-Humphrey said.

"We've graduated from bronze medals. We didn't want bronze this year."

Jamaica faces New Zealand in the final, while the Diamonds meet England in the bronze medal play-off.

4. Montag admits to being 'selfish'

Elizabeth McMillen led Jemima Montag for most of the race, but did not win gold. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

It was an Australian sweep of the medals in the women's 10,000m race walk, but the fight for the gold medal between teammates was a fierce one.

Australian Elizabeth McMillen and Jemima Montag broke clear from the pack early and led for the entire race.

McMillen was at the front, with Montag her shadow just behind.

Montag's strategy was to use McMillen as protection from the wind, a tactic which worked to perfection.

McMillen's lead for the better part of 23 laps of the 25-lap race, before Montag ducked out from behind her and put on the burners in a decisive attack to claim gold.

It was a move she had no regrets over.

"In a race you have to be selfish. Unfortunately it's an individual sport, not a team," Montag said.

"If it was cycling or something with drafting, where you do change the lead around then absolutely.

"But as much as I would love to, sometimes you have to forget it's a teammate that you care about and just remember it's another competitor and it's another body that in front of you and to ultimately be selfish."

McMillen was not particularly happy, but understood.

"What can you do? That's racing for you," McMillen said.

"I did look back a few times thinking, 'Are you going to help out here?', but no. I was the rabbit today, so what are you going to do?"

5. Indian boxer explains celebration

Arundhati Choudhary celebrates in her unique way. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

India boxer Arundhati Choudhary is a beacon of positivity inside and outside the ring.

Choudhary, who won gold in the women's 70-kilogram category in Glasgow, takes inspiration from a Hindu deity, Lord Rama.

This is why she opts for a bow and arrow celebration.

"In India we have Lord Rama, who killed negativity with his bow," Choudhary explained.

"Last year I was suffering from surgery and my family was also suffering from many problems.

"So I just throw the bow and arrow and shoot all the negativity out."

World.title: 'Pattern of missteps': Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke
World.content:
Successfully stopping Gianni Infantino's FIFA plan to sell World Cup profits to private investors was the first half of a high-stakes game in global soccer politics.

The second half kicked off overnight with what seemed a clear aim of ending Infantino's decade-long presidency.

"No option should be off the table," said European soccer body UEFA, whose president Aleksander Čeferin has led the fight against Infantino in a seismic week for FIFA.

"The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family."

Aleksander Čeferin (left) has been a vocal critic of Gianni Infantino's latest quest to privatise part of FIFA. (Getty Images: Nicolò Campo/LightRocket)

After that comment, the governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) called for accountability, saying: "A [World Cup] proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place."

Mr Infantino had proposed creating a $US20 billion ($28.5 billion) company to run the World Cup with private investors but drew backlash that grew every day since Tuesday's announcement.

The FIFA president was forced to scrap the plan early Saturday after his senior adviser who sat on a White House panel resigned and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), joined Europe and North America in opposing it.

UEFA's blistering statement

UEFA, the governing body of European soccer, issued its blistering statement hours after FIFA announced it was withdrawing its private equity plan.

"We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game," UEFA said.

"We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

"It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again."

Lise Klaveness (right) looks on as Gianni Infantino takes a selfie with a fan during the World Cup. (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Norwegian soccer federation president Lise Klaveness, an elected member of the UEFA executive committee, said steps must be taken to protect the integrity of the sport.

"The entire framework of international football cooperation was unnecessarily put at risk in pursuit of individual interests rather than the best interests of the game," Mr Klaveness said.

"This has been visible to many for a long time, including those of us elected to positions intended to safeguard checks and balances and provide ongoing oversight. We have to recognise that these mechanisms have not worked well enough."

Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa (right) also criticised the way the privatisation plan had been rolled out. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

The president of the AFC, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, said, "The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game."

Mr Infantino's audacious bid fell apart after UEFA's 55-member nations agreed Thursday to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions. CONCACAF and the AFC also said they opposed the plan.

CONCACAF's statement added that FIFA leaders have "a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional".

FIFA's internal revolt

There was also an internal revolt.

Mr Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

Hours later, FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour issued a statement to the Associated Press, saying FIFA staff were deceived by Infantino's lack of openness in planning the sale over recent months and that the project must not continue.

Kevin Lamour says the FIFA plan is a project of "one person". (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

"It is the project of one person," wrote Mr Lamour, a longtime colleague of Mr Infantino at both FIFA and UEFA.

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Mr Infantino had proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $US20 billion subsidiary with 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The "anchor investor", described by FIFA, is a New York-based investment firm launched by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

This is not Infantino's first big plan to flop

A tumultuous week in international soccer is at least the third time Mr Infantino has rocked it with an ambitious plan many in the sport saw as reckless.

But the fallout from FIFA's Joshua Kushner-backed plan is the first time UEFA has acted quickly to create momentum for removing the man who was its former long-time employee.

In 2018, Mr Infantino pushed a secretive offer of $US25 billion from Japan's SoftBank to create new competitions, which posed a long-term risk to continental events for clubs and national teams.

Vladimir Putin awarded an Order of Friendship to Gianni Infantino after the 2018 World Cup in Russia. (Getty Images: Mikhail Metzel/TASS)

In 2021, Mr Infantino proposed playing World Cups every two years instead of four — an idea that also angered the International Olympic Committee where he is an elected member.

Both plans created big rifts in the sport and were eventually dropped by FIFA.

Despite the turmoil, Mr Infantino was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

The third time is shaping up to be different.

November 18 is the deadline for candidates to enter the next presidential contest, exactly four months ahead of the vote in Rabat, Morocco, where FIFA has its African headquarters.

FIFA statutes allow Mr Infantino one more four-year term in office. The failed spin-off venture seemed like a way to create a commissioner-like role for Mr Infantino beyond 2031, likely paying much more than his current annual salary and a bonus deal of more than $US6 million.

Gianni Infantino with Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani and Jordan's Crown Prince Hussein at the FIFA Arab Cup 2025. (Getty Images: Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto)

It would take 106 votes to ensure a majority in a contested election. Continents surely do not vote uniformly en bloc, but most of Europe's 55, plus Asia's 46 and CONCACAF's 35 FIFA members would be a solid base.

The Qatar FA issued a statement in support of Infantino on Saturday.

Its president, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa bin Ahmed Al Thani, said: "We welcome FIFA President Gianni Infantino's decision to withdraw the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal in the interest of the global football community.

"While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among Member Associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports president Infantino's efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: One final clean sweep proves Aussie track stars are the real deal
World.content:
The main event for most of the crowd at Scotstoun Stadium lived up to the hype.

Scottish world record holder Josh Kerr utterly bossed a chaotic men's mile final, teaching Australian hope Cameron Myers a lesson in competition racing.

Twenty-year-old Myers came into the Games in phenomenal form and pledged to not let the hometown favourite out of his sight in the final, but once he was boxed in and Kerr got a break, it was curtains with half a lap to go.

Josh Kerr lit up Scotstoun. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

"He smashed me," a visibly disappointed Myers said.

The inexperienced young gun pledged to learn from it and clearly enjoyed his time in the "electric" atmosphere.

But the finale for a historic athletics program for Australia came about half an hour later, when three Australian stars lined up in the women's mile.

We're used to see it in the swimming, but this time it was an international track meet that staged a replay of the Australian championships as Abbey Caldwell, Jess Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth went around the track four times.

Stunning day of Comm Games success for Australia Australia stuns the field to claim gold in the men's 4x100m relay for the first time since 1974 on a packed night final night of athletics action.

When they ran the equivalent 1,500 metres at the national championships in April, it was a debacle.

Hollingsworth tripped Hull, which held up Caldwell, who was pipped by Sarah Billings.

Hull and Caldwell lodged protests, Hollingsworth was disqualified, and Billings was installed as national champion.

After her unusual elevation to the crown, Billings chose to only race the 800m in Glasgow, winning bronze, and her competitors from that night in Sydney stepped in as the clear fastest milers in the country.

The women pulled off the triumph Camweon Myers (right) could not. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

Lining up in the Commonwealth Games final right next to Hull, Caldwell burst off the line, while Hull held back and watched as Hollingsworth settled into the pack ahead of her.

Like the nats, it was a slow race, raising the risk of another late calamity.

Instead, with 200 metres to go, Caldwell burst clear and Hull joined her.

Hull couldn't match Caldwell but, just like when she won silver behind Rose Davies in the 5,000m, she was beaming as her teammate crossed the line ahead of her.

Abbey Caldwell crossed ahead of Jess Hull, the woman who paved the path for her. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Meanwhile, the in-stadium announcer broke the news that the podium sweep was on as Hollingsworth, seemingly boxed in with the typically rambunctious peloton, found the space and energy to burst past Naomi Korir and claim bronze.

Caldwell had predicted a podium sweep before the athletics program started in a manner portraying matter-of-fact confidence, rather than arrogant bluster.

Even after the prediction came true, it was the importance of their presence on the start line, 9.34 metres behind the spot where Caldwell snared gold 4 minutes and 39.31 seconds later, that Hull remarked upon.

"The Aussies are a force; on that start line we're a threat," she said.

"We've done it at Commonwealth level and the next step is to do it at [world] championships, get three of us in the final and then the odds are pretty high that you're gonna bring home a couple of medals."

The women's middle distance has been the jewel in the Australian track crown before the sprinters joined the party in the past couple of years.

But this podium sweep in the first female Commonwealth mile in history, Caldwell said, truly "put [them] on the map".

"We are the best and I think we can prove that we are the best and we will come and compete for those [Olympic and world] medals," she said.

"We do all wanna keep competing and we are worldwide competitors.

"Jess paved that path for us; we're here to compete internationally, we've accomplished the Commonwealth and now we move onto the big world stage."

If Glasgow 2026 was the coming-out party for Australia's new short-track guns, it marked the coming of age for Caldwell, Hull, Hollingsworth and Billings, who were holding up the tartan long before it was cool.

World.title: Riders sent flying in spectacular crash as Aussie avoids carnage to medal
World.content:
A Malaysian rider was stretchered off the track and two others also needed medical attention after a mass pile-up in Commonwealth Games cycling.

As riders jockeyed for position with one lap left in the men's 10 kilometre scratch race, a crash in the back half of the bunch took down seven riders, with all who crashed not finishing the race.

The three Australians dodged the carnage and Tom Cornish went on to win silver behind England's Henry Hobbs.

But Malaysian New Joe Lau was taken from the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome on a stretcher. Red Walters of Grenada has a suspected broken collarbone and Canadian Jonathan Hinse was also in the hands of medical staff for several minutes before he was able to walk gingerly back to the team pits.

It was the first major crash after three days of track cycling at the Games.

"In racing, we're pretty used to the chaos. When you hear something like that and it's behind you, it's almost a sigh of relief — just because you're in front of it and you don't have to dodge anyone," Cornish said.

"So that was quite lucky.

"At that point, it's an all-out sprint anyway and there's not really much you can change.

"I was lucky to hold it up, I think."

Australia's Tom Cornish holds up his silver medal after avoiding the carnage in the men's 10km scratch race. (Getty Images: Molly Darlington)

The old maxim in cycling is that there are two types of riders — those who have crashed and those who are about to crash.

Cornish has crashed five times this year already and knows he is lucky not to break any bones.

"If it just happens to be one person further forward, you crash. If it doesn't then you make it through and that's kind-of how it is," Cornish said.

"It's something we're used to. I've been doing the sport for almost 20 years and it just becomes part of it."

Fellow Australian Oli Bleddyn did well to avoid the falling riders, while Blake Agnoletto was clear of the carnage.

"I was lucky enough to have the boys working for me today. Both of them are so strong in their own right, they probably could have been up there as well," Cornish said of their team riding.

"I was pretty lucky to have them."

World.title: The new wave of working women taking up golf
World.content:
Melissa Miegel found a new love at 37 years of age.

It happened when she least expected it on a quiet Sunday about five months ago.

At her father's invitation, she tagged along to his weekend activity.

She and golf have not been apart for a weekend since.

She is one of a growing cohort of women who have started spending time on the green.

Melissa Miegel has been playing golf for almost six months. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

According to Golf Australia, women's participation is increasing at almost double the rate of men.

It estimates around 60 per cent of people who started playing golf in the past two years were women.

As a mental health worker, Ms Miegel has found the pace and setting of golf to be a safe space.

"I have a very busy brain a lot of the time, so I think it's been a really good opportunity to get outside and actually be more focused on the thing that's directly in front of me," she said.

"For me it's about practising, being more present in what I'm doing and in the moment and slowing down.

"It's a good way to challenge myself as well."

Melissa Miegel is working with a local coach to encourage more women in her region to try the sport. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

Encouraging more women to join her in her home region of South Australia's Riverland has become a focus for Ms Miegel.

She believes it is a space where women who are already juggling family, work and life commitments can slow down and find time for themselves.

"I've done a lot of questioning about what it actually looks like for golf because I think people have perceptions of 18 holes, going out there [and] spending hours on end," Ms Miegel said.

Women finding their way

While golf has had a long history as a sport for men that takes hours to play, women are finding ways to make it work around life's busyness.

For this reason, driving ranges and simulators have become popular with women, making up 50 per cent of users with an average age of 38.

Most new golfers begin playing off-course. (ABC News: Dallas Freedman)

Women are also playing three times more nine-hole rounds of golf than men.

"You can play a round of golf in two hours, you can play the driving range, and you still get that social connection that you're really craving," said Golf Australia's head of women and girls Tamara Mason.

"You can wear what you want, you can show up with whoever you want, when you want, and you can fit that in."

She said those less traditional formats were also more accessible.

"You can show up 10 minutes later if the kids are late to school or if the meeting ran over," she said.

"You don't have that fear of disappointing people if you don't show up at your tee time."

Tamara Mason says regional golf clubs are finding the most success at fostering community to welcome in women. (ABC News: Dallas Freedman)

Beyond the format, Ms Mason said there was also a need for change around the culture of many clubs.

"We do have some work to do with our clubs and venues that perhaps only see things a particular way," she said.

"We know that there's a whole other customer base out there looking for something different.

"We know that women being physically active don't want to be judged when they're playing the sport."

Driving the change

Back in the Riverland, ex-PGA professional and coach Jamie Clutterham has been working with Ms Miegel, trying to break stereotypes by running clinics and programs for women and girls.

Jamie Clutterham believes including women in the golf community makes it stronger. (ABC Riverland: Anita Ward)

"In the past 21 months we've activated some programs, and we're seeing the start of, hopefully, a new women's golf world up here in the Riverland," he said.

" A lot of them will say to me 'I'm never going to get off the ground' and they walk away half an hour later happy that they've hit a shot. "

He said around 90 women have become regular golfers in the region across four local clubs.

Women now make up 42 per cent of all golfers in Australia, according to Golf Australia. (ABC Riverland: Shannon Pearce)

A group of community coaches also help him run the sessions to try and make a space in the sport that does not require competition.

"I try and bring new golfers into a coaching space and give them some confidence and competence, and hand them over to some mentors who help with the golf course play, become comfortable with the etiquette and the club environment," Mr Clutterham said.

"If we can activate even just a few people to enjoy that, enjoy some golf and be in a happy space, then I think we're ticking a box there."

Ms Miegel's advice is to give it a go.

"You don't have to be good enough to start playing, but I think you have to start playing to be at least trying to improve yourself and get better," she said.

World.title: Denny completes 68-year first to claim discus gold for Australia
World.content:
Matt Denny has embraced a special moment with his young son Roman after becoming the first man in 68 years to defend a Commonwealth Games discus title with victory in Glasgow.

Denny threw 67.73m in difficult conditions to beat Jamaica's Fedrick Dacres (65.10) and his English training partner Lawrence Okoye (64.45).

The Paris Olympics bronze medallist adds another Commonwealth gold medal to his Birmingham 2022 triumph, after taking hammer throw silver on his Games debut at Gold Coast 2018.

The last man to successfully defend a Commonwealth discus title was South Africa's Fanie du Plessis, who won in 1954 and 1958.

Matt Denny (centre) with silver medallist Fedrick Dacres of Jamaica and bronze medallist Lawrence Okoye of England. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

"I knew that there was that pressure there and I clearly had the best [throw] so far this season and had been performing the best, so there was that expectation there," Denny said.

"More so I think the expectation was from myself, but it is very special to make these kind of marks and do what people haven't done for a long time.

"It's not an easy sport to do and I'm in good company, so I'm pretty proud of the fact I can still prove myself against those guys and put some good distances out."

Denny did a lap of honour around the Scotstoun Stadium track with seven-month-old Roman in his arms.

The 30-year-old has had Roman and wife Mia with him on the road over the past few weeks in the United States and Europe, and said daily tasks like bath time had helped keep him grounded.

"[Roman] is not going to remember it but I know I will when I'm old and grey," Denny said.

"It's a tough sport and there's a lot that goes into it behind the scenes, so you have to have people who understand how you need to operate.

"She [Mia] has been one of those people who just know how I operate, so to be able to share these moments with them … is the most important thing."

World.title: Granny Grommets connect women far beyond the waves
World.content:
It's a crisp winter morning as the sun rises over the ocean and a group of older women laugh as they catch waves on their bodyboards.

They're members of a newly formed Granny Grommets group at North Haven on the New South Wales Mid North Coast, sparking a surge of interest.

"It brings back my youth, and I feel so free in the ocean," said 70-year-old Annie Milne, the group's founder.

" It's just fabulous, and we squeal in the waves and roll around in the sand. It's the camaraderie. I have friends here now that I wouldn't have had. "

Annie Milne enjoying the surf at North Haven. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

The first Granny Grommets group, for women aged 50 and over, was started about 26 years ago at Albany on Western Australia's southern coast, gradually spreading across Australian and overseas shores.

Ms Milne created the North Haven group after moving to the area, having been part of the Newcastle Granny Grommets and was surprised by the number of older women seeking connection while staying active.

"I was inundated. There's nearly 200 on the Facebook page already, and it's been only a few weeks," she said.

"Quite a few of the ladies I've spoken to are relatively new to the area. It's much harder to connect with people in our age group as we don't have connections with kids, school or sport.

" We're a group of older women who love the outdoors, in particular the ocean, and this group brings us all together in such a fun way. "

Granny grommets enjoy an early morning surf at North Haven. (ABC News: Emma Siossian )

The group's Kit Poole said it had strengthened her social network.

"I'm new to the community so it allows me to meet more people," she said.

"It's fitness, fun and friendship … watching the sun come up, and sometimes we see whales and dolphins."

Stephanie McMahon had never surfed before she joined the group, having moved to the area from the Hawkesbury region.

Loading...

"I thought what a great way to meet other like-minded women that don't feel like they are too old to get amongst it and have a bit of fun," she said.

" It's nice finding that special place where you can develop those community relationships. "

Sharon Taylor has also signed up. So far she has kept her feet on dry sand, but plans to change that.

"I have a fear of the ocean," she said.

"I am going to make it my goal to overcome my fear and put a wetsuit on and buy a board and get in there".

Connecting women of all ages

The North Haven chapter of Granny Grommets on a clear winter morning. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

Rebecca Olive is a vice-chancellor's senior research fellow at Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology who has conducted extensive feminist studies on the role of women's recreational sport and leisure in society.

Her 2025 research paper investigated how water sports can help build communities and meaningful friendships.

Rebecca Olive, pictured during an outdoor swim at Byron Bay, says outdoor swimming and surfing groups play an important role. (Supplied: Rebecca Olive)

She said she was "thrilled" to see the continued success of Granny Grommets groups Australia-wide, which also created a place for older women rediscovering their own interests after raising children.

"We often see women come back to physical activities as they age and … there's definitely an interest in these very playful, fun activities that are really immersive, literally in this case, in the ocean," she said.

"You don't have to be good at it to enjoy it.

" They can push themselves to try new things and be in nature, be with other people, and laugh with each other. "

Morning light hits the waves at North Haven. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

She said the Granny Grommets were also helping break down stereotypes about older women's abilities.

"It may be the first opportunity the women have had to access surfing in this way," she said.

" Even women walking along the beach seeing older women aging in public … can find it inspiring and be reminded they can keep doing things as they age. "

Dr Olive said outdoor surfing and swimming groups also fostered greater care for the natural environment.

Swimmers at Williamstown Beach in Melbourne arriving for a pre-dawn swim. (ABC News: Rudy De Santia)

She said that was evident in Melbourne where outdoor swimming groups, including the Williamstown Jellyfish, regularly converged at Port Phillip Bay.

Women in their sixties and seventies were also helping lead conservation initiatives there.

"They are getting scientists down to talk about how to take better care of that area. So spending time there has shown them this whole other part of this place they live," she said.

The Granny Grommets meet for a morning cuppa after their bodyboarding session at North Haven. (ABC Mid North Coast: Emma Siossian)

Back at North Haven, the Granny Grommets group is surging forward with plans for related social catch-ups.

"I love it. Joining Granny Grommets was a game changer for me," Ms Milne said.

"I couldn't imagine my life without it now."

World.title: 'Who says girls can't play baseball?': America's pastime goes pro for women
World.content:
The jaunty tune of Take Me Out to the Ball Game takes a fun spin in the trailer for the 1992 classic baseball movie A League of Their Own.

"Who says girls can't play baseball? Who says women can't throw," the jingle goes.

Turns out, for decades, that is exactly the message that has been sent to countless girls and women who have wanted to play 'America's pastime' at the highest level.

The film depicted the All American Girls Professional Baseball League which ran from 1943 to 1954.

And in the 72 years since it folded, there has not been another professional women's league in the USA. Until now.

Loading...

Anyone can play ball

Justine Siegal is the Commissioner and co-founder of the inaugural Women's Pro Baseball League (WPBL), which is getting underway this weekend.

Siegal is a pioneer in the sport. She is the first woman to coach a professional men's team, and the first female coach of a Major League Baseball team, with the Oakland Athletics.

Justine Siegal is the co-founder and Commissioner of the WPBL. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

"We're fighting this myth that baseball is for men and softball is for women," Siegal told ABC Sport at a fan day for the league in Brockton, Massachusetts.

"You can now see that there's 25 countries as national teams. There is growth at the high school level here in the US and in Canada, and there's just more girls playing baseball than ever.

"So it is a great time to ride the wave of women's pro sports like soccer and ice hockey and basketball with the WNBA, and start what we deserve."

Siegal has been instrumental in growing opportunities at the grassroots level too, founding the non-profit girls' baseball organisation Baseball for All in 2010.

"[In the WPBL] about 25 or 30 per cent of the players have played or participated in Baseball for All," she said.

"So for me as Commissioner, it's super exciting to have known a kid when they were 13 and their dream was to keep playing baseball."

Just such a kid is Sabrina Robinson, 23, who represents the Boston Hunters in the WPBL.

Sabrina Robinson started playing to follow in her brother's footsteps. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

"I didn't think this day would come in my lifetime. I thought I'd be in the stands supporting the next generation and the next generation," she told ABC Sport.

"My main motivation is to be the person that I didn't have growing up. I didn't see women playing baseball on the TV.

"So I really want to represent women's baseball players the best for the next generation coming up.

"It's very important that we build those communities and we show them that they can do it and that there's a path for them… maybe they get cut from their boys team but you can still come play women's."

Robinson plays first base for the Boston Hunters. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

Nylah Ramirez, 29, is a pitcher from Brooklyn, and is another member of the Hunters.

She has represented Puerto Rico at World Cup level, and also works as a youth coach.

"It means everything. It means my life's work is finally being paid off," she said.

"I hope that this blows up. I hope that the whole world knows that we're meant to be here.

" Just because you're a man, doesn't mean that you're a ballplayer. Ballplayers come in all shapes and sizes, all forms. "

Players were drafted from all over the world, including Australia. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

Take the early bet

The WPBL is starting small with four teams from Boston, New York, Los Angeles, and San Francisco, playing at one venue in Springfield, Illinois, across August and September.

Anna Palmer is one of the investors in the league, and also a co-founder of the National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) franchise Boston Legacy.

Anna Palmer is an investor in the WPBL. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

She understands the potential in women's sport.

"WPBL is a league that can hopefully be in every small town across America too. Baseball is America's sport," she told ABC Sport.

She said the investment in NWSL clubs like the Legacy, which came into the league this year, and is currently developing a purpose-built stadium and performance centre, shows the opportunities.

"The money that is now going into those teams through private equity and really sophisticated investors means that there's going to be the resources there to have the fan experiences that these women deserve and to pay the athletes the way that they should be paid, which is exciting," she said.

"I think on the sponsorship level, you're seeing companies realise that women's sports is big business and that they can attach their brand to these athletes and reach a different customer and live out their values in a different way."

The inaugural WPBL season will be played in Springfield, Illinois. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

She also urged investors to have the foresight to take "early bets".

"We went in with a franchise fee with Boston Legacy that was a little over $US50 million that seemed crazy at the time. And now Atlanta just came in over $US200 million," she said.

"If you're willing to take that bet, you're seeing the fandom and the energy and the ecosystem now catching up to that.

"And so I would say don't wait, lean in. Now is the moment for women's sports.

"We're going to be, 10, 15 years from now I think, seeing these valuations in the franchises look very, very different."

Players hope the league can expand to other cities in the future. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

The players echo those high hopes.

"I really hope for team expansions so we can get around to people's hometowns and get out to where all the younger girls are and get to new cities where girls don't even know that you could play baseball," Robinson said.

Siegal says the growth of the league and fan engagement is important, but the enduring message it sends is what will be most impactful.

"A long-term solution is that this league provides systemic change where girls are often told they don't have a future in baseball," she said.

"But now they do and they can have the same dream that their brothers do, and that's to be a professional baseball player."
