Tech.title: I Used Every AI Cheating App and Detector and Came to One Conclusion
Tech.content:
Education is at a crossroads. People are having fewer kids, which means schools are bracing for lower enrollments. You can’t throw a rock on TikTok without running into an exhausted teacher ready to tear their hair out. And on top of this is the now-pervasive, often institutionally sanctioned use, and practically unprovable abuse, of AI both in and out of the classroom.

Detectors, homework helpers, essay writers, AI math wizards and even sneaky backdoor test assistants have entered the student-focused chats on cheating in a big way. Here’s a roundup of all the biggest tools and how they’re being used to get around old-school schooling.

Have AI write, and then rewrite it again

The big names like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook) still appear to be the gold standard for getting away with skipping out on writing in school. I spent an afternoon slinging assignments in PDF format into all these tools and each generated polished, accurate responses in the form of persuasive and well-researched essays.

Most students and educators already know about these use cases, but what is surprising is the closed loop created by AI and plagiarism-detection tools. In essence, the cops are helping the culprits get away with the heist. These companies are having their cake, eating it, throwing it up and selling it again as a muffin-of-the-month subscription.

I tried a number of AI text humanizers and tested them against AI detector tools, and after being “humanized,” every single blurb passed with flying colors.

There’s a lot of talk in and out of academic circles about whether AI-detection tools are accurate or useful. From my research for this piece, I can confidently say they are worthless. Unless you’re a student who used AI to write your work and want to prove you didn’t use AI to write your work.

Do your homework, but don’t

The idea that students are at least absorbing some part of the materials in assignments or school work when they use AI, because they have to copy and paste things and put together a cohesively structured output that illustrates learning outcomes they can review, has reached One Wish Willow levels of delusion.

I threw a PDF of an assignment that’s supposed to be AI-proof into Claude — one of those “make something out of your work” assignments that educators like to point to as a better outcome, even if AI is involved.

The only instruction I gave the tool was: “Do this assignment. Complete all the required elements, including the visual elements, and put them into a standardized, cohesive format for submission. pdf please.”

The tool produced a couple of slick infographics that looked good enough to be made by someone using a Canva template and not slick enough to raise any alarm bells on the part of an educator.

Created by Rachel Kane using Claude

This is just the right level of mediocre that passes classes, and at no time did I ever read the assignment or review the generated work. These types of deliverables from assignments were actually the most difficult to pin down as AI within the confines of my research. I used several AI image detectors, and the results were mixed.

In one case, a tool called Winstonai flagged my AI created infographic as 100% AI, but it also flagged a graphic I created long before generative AI was available to the masses as 100% AI.

Another AI image detector, AI or Not, determined my entirely AI infographic was just 1% AI.

AIorNot/Screenshot by CNET

So it’s not a foolproof method, and a student looking to get away with passing this work off as their own just has to point to conflicting detectors to shut down an argument.

Hard problems call for easy solutions

There were exactly zero AI apps, tools and services used in the research for this piece that claimed to be “cheating apps.” Instead, words like “study guide,” “homework helper,” and even the bold promise to provide an “A+ result” were used to advertise each tool’s capabilities.

That didn’t mean any of them balked at being asked for outright solutions to complete problems. or stop them from highlighting features like the Advanced Assignment Solver right next to Homework Helper. I wonder which appeals to a student using these tools.

Services like Gauth AI, a paid study helper, and Studocu, a free study helper with a paid tier that starts at $7 a month, either explicitly offered to do student work wholesale, or put up zero resistance to solving multipage, complex assignments when simply prompted with “do this assignment.”

I used Studocu to generate answers to a complex, five-page astronomy assignment (PDF) from the University of Northern Iowa that included explicit instructions to use a dataset unique to each student based on their student IDs.

Studocu/Screenshot by CNET

In a matter of seconds, the tool used the unique data given and the five-page assignment to generate customized answers to every problem. Gauth AI was also more than up to the task, for a price ($12 a month, or $100 for a year).

Gauth/Screenshot by CNET

Not bad, considering you could probably pass the class without ever having to look at an HR diagram, or even learn what one is.

Test taking when you didn’t study

Testing is supposed to be the time-honored, proven ground for measuring competency, but in the age of AI tools, it’s just another hurdle to limbo under.

Some universities are now doing testing differently, using randomization of questions from large pools and more in-person testing.

For those schools still testing with lockdown browsers and through timed digital, students can get around protections with a variety of easily available tools that utilize “stealth” or discreet windows and integrate AI software, like ChatGPT, to provide on-demand answers.

Tools like Hiding AI even use data on how test scores improved using their subscription-based software that claims to provide an undetectable experience ($192/year).

Hiding AI/Screenshot by CNET

Another covert AI tool that advertises itself as an exam helper, Pluely (starting at $15/month and up to $120 for a lifetime subscription), is particularly adept at call-and-response. All a student needs to do is read out the questions to the exam they’re taking, and Pluely will provide the answers in a discreet, undetectable window. All the student has to do is click.

The bottom line

For every AI app, service or tool designed to build and generate all the different mediums and modes educators are asking students to demonstrate competency, there is an equal and opposite AI app, service or tool designed to help them argue that the work was done by a human.

It’s a marketplace of double dips where the primary customer — the thousands of people keeping investors interested in a growing consumer base — is the student, not the educator.

No matter what it says in the marketing materials, these tools aren’t made to help teachers teach or students learn. They’re made to serve the core customer who most likely just wants to get it over with.

Correction, July 31: A previous version attributed tools and functionality to Turnitin that do not exist on that website.

Tech.title: Sony’s Plan to Kill Physical PlayStation Discs Faces Gamer Backlash
Tech.content:
The age of the physical disc is ending on the Sony PlayStation. Despite backlash from gamers, the company intends to continue with its plans to end PlayStation disc sales as of January 2028.

“Following this date, new games will be available on PlayStation Store and at retailers in digital formats only. This transition has no impact on games that already released, or will be releasing, prior to January 2028 in disc format,” Sony said in a PlayStation blog post on July 1 . The post said the change is driven by consumer trends and a general preference for digital media.

Many PlayStation gamers clearly felt otherwise, with some players calling for a worldwide boycott of Sony platforms beginning in August. The PSBlackout urges gamers to keep their systems powered off for the entire week of Aug. 23. A petition on Change.org called “Don’t Kill the Disc” has also racked up over 350,000 verified signatures so far.

Sony wants to abandon fans? Let's give them a small taste of their own medicine!



Together with other creators we call for a 1 week #PSBlackout in August. No logins, no play sessions, no purchases on any of Sony's platforms. pic.twitter.com/v6JvdvbHLD — Does it play? (@DoesItPlay1) July 26, 2026

The backlash prompted Sony to respond to gamers in a Q&A session with shareholders, but the company isn’t changing its decision. Sony CFO Lin Tao said that the brand intends to continue moving forward with its plan to end physical disc sales and that the company doesn’t believe the backlash will negatively affect sales, though Tao noted the company will proceed “cautiously” with its plans.

Tao also said that the company is deciding how to address feedback from gamers unhappy with the decision. She said that Sony wants to consider the emotions of upset players, since the games are “connected to people’s fond memories.”

She also said the company might take measures in the future to lessen the blow, without specifying what those measures might be, and said that Sony wanted to engage with gamers in the future digital ecosystem.

A Sony representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Currently, the PlayStation 5 Slim Disc is the only model that comes with a built-in disc drive for physical games. However, you can still buy a separate disc drive for the PS5 Digital Edition and PS5 Pro console.

Some players plan to boycott Sony platforms to protest the loss of physical games. SOPA Images/Getty Images

Unless the August boycott significantly affects Sony’s bottom line, the company is unlikely to back down on this decision. Discs, after all, can be resold, creating a secondary market from which the company doesn’t profit. All digital sales are controlled solely by the company, no matter how old the title is. This is also likely to affect resale platforms like GameStop and eBay, where gamers can usually get used titles at significant discounts.

As many commentators point out, digital titles grant a revocable license for the game, not ownership. So it’s technically possible for Sony to pull a game you’ve paid for and downloaded onto your system, though it’s rare that a company does this if there isn’t a copyright or licensing issue.

This is a transition that PC gamers made ages ago, with purely digital storefronts like Steam, Epic, GOG and others now being the most common ways PC gamers play games. These days, you really need to go out of your way to include an optical drive in your PC build since it’s not a default option. I’ve also found that many of my older disc games, like Age of Empires 3 and the first Rome: Total War, aren’t compatible with Windows 11, and you can’t even install or run them properly.

IGN reported that Project Helix, Xbox’s next console, will not have a disc drive and that Microsoft is exploring ways to digitize physical games. That may leave Nintendo as the sole company to continue supporting physical game media for the foreseeable future, in the form of cartridges for the Switch 2, which can also play games made for the original Switch.

Tech.title: Prices Are Going Up for More AT&T Legacy Plans, Starting Tomorrow
Tech.content:
When AT&T introduced new plans early this year, it retired the old ones – common practice among carriers. However, customers who signed up for those freshly shelved plans as recently as Nov. 1, 2025, are about to see a price increase tomorrow.

In April, long-term customers hanging onto old phone plans learned they would see mandatory monthly surcharges added to their bills. Now, the pool of affected subscribers has expanded, with charges arriving in August for people who activated plans as recently as November.

On a support page that went live when it announced its revamped “2.0” unlimited phone plans, the carrier revealed that the prices of its “retired” unlimited wireless plans — the ones that customers who haven’t upgraded are still using — would go up by as much as $20 starting in April.

Originally, it applied to plans activated before July 24, 2025. Now, the support page includes a notice that the fees will also apply to plans between July 24 and Nov. 1, 2025. That includes Unlimited Premium PL, Unlimited Extra EL and Value Plus VL plans.

Making sense of the hiked prices

AT&T implemented two price changes. If your account with a “retired” plan has a single line, the price went up $10. If you have two or more lines on an account, the price increase was capped at $20 for the account.

Perhaps to offset the sting, affected plans get an extra 20GB of high-speed hotspot data each month.

However, not everyone is seeing the same deal.

As an AT&T mobile plan subscriber myself, when I signed into my own AT&T account to compare options, I was directed to a different support page that said prices would go up $5 per smartphone line. For hotspot, AT&T added 10GB of extra high-speed data — presumably to each line, but that’s not specified. The page reads, “Starting in August 2026, accounts with wireless lines that didn’t have an increase in April and activated or moved to an affected plan between July 24, 2025 and November 1, 2025 will now see the price change on your bill.”

There’s also a third support article for customers on retired Mobile Share plans. If your plan includes less than 6GB of data, the price increased $5 per month. If it’s a plan with more than 6GB per month, the price increases by $10 per month.

Based on those articles, the following plans are subject to the added fees:

AT&T Unlimited Plus, AT&T Unlimited Choice, AT&T Unlimited Choice II

AT&T Unlimited Plus Enhanced, AT&T Unlimited Choice Enhanced

AT&T Unlimited &More, AT&T Unlimited &More Premium

AT&T Unlimited Plan (Double Play)

AT&T Unlimited Starter SL, Unlimited Extra EL, Unlimited Premium PL

AT&T Unlimited Starter, Unlimited Extra, Unlimited Premium

AT&T Mobile Share Value, Mobile Share Value – Double Data

AT&T Mobile Share Plus

AT&T Mobile Share Advantage

As for why the prices are going up, AT&T’s support pages read, “This change helps us continue providing reliable network service, quality products, and great customer experiences.”

In an earlier statement to CNET, an AT&T spokesperson said, “We recognize that any price increase matters to our customers and their budgets. This increase reflects the real cost of continuing to deliver the speed, reliability and support our customers expect every day.”

AT&T maintains that its new plans are priced competitively with other carriers’ plans and “better aligned with how our customers use our services.”

When the increases were first announced, they applied only to wireless plans activated prior to July 24, 2025, according to the support note posted at the time. That included legacy plans, not just the recently discontinued plans that the 2.0 plans replace.

Asked about why more customers are now affected by the price increase, an AT&T spokesperson replied via email, “Customers who activated those plans beginning July 24, 2025, through November 1, 2025 were excluded from the April 2026 pricing because they were on their plan for less than 9 months.”

The increases make it worth comparing prices between holding onto an existing plan and switching to the new plans. For example, the first change makes the Premium 2.0 plan more appealing. When it was announced, the Premium 2.0 plan was more expensive than the older Unlimited Premium PL plan: $90 per month for a single line instead of $86, or $220 per month for four lines instead of $204. With the new price increase, the Unlimited Premium PL plan will cost $96 per month for a single line and $240 per month for four lines.

AT&T isn’t the only one to take action to encourage subscribers to move up to current plans. T-Mobile took a more drastic approach by automatically forcing thousands of customers on legacy plans onto its latest plans.

And this year has seen a lot of change in pricing among all the carriers. After Verizon replaced its CEO, it dropped prices across the board to be more competitive and then introduced a new Simplicity plan. T-Mobile introduced a new limited-time Better Value plan priced similarly to its Experience More plan but with more perks intended to appeal to families.

If AT&T’s increases prompt you to shop around, we have recommendations for the best cellphone plan and the best unlimited data plan, as well as a comparison of AT&T and Verizon plans.

Tech.title: Sony Is Paying Out $7.85M in PlayStation Store Credit. Here’s How to Claim Part of the Settlement
Tech.content:
You may be eligible to claim part of an upcoming $7.85 million settlement payout if you’re a PlayStation customer who lives in the US. The case centered on an allegation that Sony “unlawfully eliminated competition and monopolized the market for [its] digital games” by no longer selling game-specific vouchers that let PlayStation owners buy digital games from other online shops.

The class-action lawsuit Caccuri v. Sony Interactive Entertainment alleged that Sony’s actions caused “consumers to pay more for certain digital games than they otherwise would have paid on the PlayStation Store.” It alleges that this action is a violation of antitrust laws, as it forces PlayStation customers to buy from a single storefront at an inflated price.

Put simply, the lawsuit alleges that Sony limited the sale of digital games on other marketplaces, funneling customers into its own PlayStation Store. Some of these games include PlayStation exclusive titles, such as The Last of Us, as well as third-party games, like Mass Effect Trilogy and Resident Evil 4.

The lawsuit was initially settled in 2024, but the settlement was rejected twice during the approval process — most recently in July 2025 (PDF), when the presiding judge said the proposed plan “[did] not provide an estimated recovery or a range of potential recovery for class members.” The approval process was reinitiated in April.

Sony denied that it engaged in any wrongdoing or that settlement class members were damaged by its actions, and the court has not decided if the company violated any laws. Despite this, the court has preliminarily approved the $7.85 million settlement payment, subject to the court’s final approval hearing.

The settlement website is live now. The hearing is scheduled to take place on Oct. 15, and it’s meant to confirm the settlement sum, allocate up to 25% of the funds for attorneys’ fees and create a plan to distribute the rest of the money to eligible class members.

If you fit all of the criteria to be part of the Sony PlayStation game-voucher settlement, you’re automatically a class member in this lawsuit and will be able to collect a portion of the settlement money — added directly to your PlayStation Network account wallet — sometime after the final approval hearing.

Gamers who have deactivated their PlayStation Network accounts can apply for the settlement payment by sending qualifying purchase information to the email address info@PSNDigitalGamesSettlement.com. Customers with deactivated accounts will receive cash payments instead of PSN account accreditation.

The option to opt out of the settlement to retain your right to sue Sony separately in regard to its game-voucher sales practices closed on July 2. A written request to the court opting out of or objecting to the settlement had to be received by then; otherwise, you will remain part of the settlement class.

Who can be part of the Sony PlayStation settlement?

Not every PlayStation owner is automatically eligible. The money is reserved for those who purchased a digital game through the PlayStation Store during a period after Sony ceased its sales of game-specific vouchers for alternative online storefronts.

In order to join, you must meet the following qualifications:

Be a living individual human being in the US or its territories. Have purchased one of the eligible digital games (PDF) through the PlayStation Store between the period of April 1, 2019 and Dec. 31, 2023.

Affected individuals are automatically part of the settlement class and will receive their compensation through their PlayStation Network account wallet, subject to approval at the final hearing, the date and time of which could change. Any updates will be posted to the settlement website.

How much will the Sony PlayStation settlement pay?

It’s unclear how much each settlement class member will receive, though we know affected parties will automatically receive compensation in the form of PlayStation account funds.

Up to a quarter of the $7.85 million settlement will be used to pay attorneys’ fees, taxes and other administrative costs. The remaining settlement money will be administered equally to every settlement class member. Settlement class members will likely see a couple of dollars added to their PlayStation accounts once the funds are fully allocated.
